concept.learningObjective: Select early scar assessment after large piecemeal adenoma resection.
concept.historyMigration: None. Unchanged meanings reuse stable IDs. New meanings keep prior definitions and histories separate.

record.title: Early surveillance after piecemeal EMR
fairness: Six-month surveillance is the best offered answer under the named framework. Four overlapping captures establish piecemeal removal despite the single container/aggregate; a free edge on one fragment cannot establish clearance of the entire perimeter.
The resident must resolve procedure versus pathology provenance before applying surveillance timing. The three-year choice credibly overweights the adenoma histology or apparent local clearance.

Adequate whole-colon examination is explicit and options are parallel. The endoscopic absence of a remnant is appropriately included as a competing observation, not as a guarantee of complete histologic clearance.
Standalone and high-yield. This is surveillance timing, not an authored runtime test-wait duration.

concept.displayName: Complete favorable invasive-polyp excision
concept.learningObjective: Integrate specimen adequacy, depth and adverse-feature assessment before colectomy.
concept.historyMigration: None. Unchanged meanings reuse stable IDs. New meanings keep prior definitions and histories separate.

record.title: Complete favorable invasive-polyp excision
fairness: Surveillance is the best offered plan: an intact oriented specimen, shallow invasion, explicit lateral and deep clearance, favorable grade and absent adverse features support local treatment despite the presence of submucosal carcinoma.

The lateral-margin repair supplies a previously important adequacy boundary. Regional colectomy remains a plausible overreaction to invasion; scar excision incorrectly treats a resolved local-clearance problem.

Interpretation of whole-specimen adequacy followed by local-versus-regional management is consequential and high-yield. The negative findings are needed to justify the best answer rather than simply decorate it.
Standalone and self-contained. The exact numerical observations are patient data; this review does not derive a new universal cutoff or adjudicate a disputed close-margin zone.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Biopsy confirms sigmoid adenocarcinoma and distant staging is negative. The outside exploration record describes a firm focal attachment to the bladder dome, with the neck, trigone and ureteric entries separate from the tumor. The remainder of the bladder wall is uninvolved and would retain a substantial reservoir after dome removal. No peritoneal deposits were found. The patient is being considered for curative surgery, and the attachment has not been divided.
decisionNodes.stem: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded anatomy, subject to confirmation of clear margins at surgery?

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc partial cystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: A focal dome attachment can be removed en bloc with a bladder portion while retaining uninvolved neck, trigone and reservoir; the plan still requires an achievable clear margin.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with en-bloc total cystectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented attachment is focal at the dome; the record does not show neck/trigone involvement or loss of a usable remaining bladder requiring total removal.

answerChoices.label: Sigmoid colectomy with separation of the bladder attachment
answerChoices.rationale: An adherent cancer interface should not be divided to decide whether the adhesion is malignant; partial bladder resection preserves an en-bloc specimen.

decisionNodes.explanation: First preserve the adherent tumor-organ interface. Then use the involved anatomy to choose the planned bladder extent: a focal dome attachment with separate neck/trigone and a usable remnant supports en-bloc partial cystectomy, provided a clear margin is achievable. Adherence does not itself establish histologic invasion, and total cystectomy is not automatic.

concept.displayName: Plan en-bloc resection while preserving uninvolved bladder
concept.learningObjective: Use the location and extent of an adherent colon cancer to plan en-bloc bladder resection without automatically sacrificing the whole bladder.

record.title: Plan en-bloc resection while preserving uninvolved bladder
fairness: En-bloc sigmoid colectomy with partial cystectomy is the best offered plan, contingent on clear margins. The learner must preserve the adherent interface, then determine whether the described bladder anatomy requires partial or total removal.

The options independently test interface violation and excessive organ removal. Focal dome involvement, separate trigone/ureteric entries and a usable remaining reservoir are necessary to distinguish the two en-bloc operations.
The task's margin contingency protects fairness rather than providing the extent of resection. Adherence is not equated with histologically proven invasion in the explanation.
The retrospective clinic frame is coherent and standalone. En-bloc resection of an adherent colon cancer and extent appropriate to anatomy are high-yield.

answerChoices.rationale: The record lacks clinical or radiographic obstruction and other primary-related complications. For incurable metastatic disease in this setting, systemic treatment generally precedes prophylactic primary surgery.

record.title: Initial treatment of an asymptomatic metastatic primary
fairness: Systemic treatment planning with the primary in place is the best offered sequence. An adult scope failing to pass does not by itself establish clinically significant obstruction when a smaller scope passes, bowel function continues and CT shows no proximal dilation.

Interpret primary-related complication status first, then apply the documented noncurative metastatic setting to treatment sequence. Colectomy and diversion are concrete, credible responses to overcalling obstruction.

The absence of bleeding/transfusion need closes another reason to intervene locally. These facts are decision-critical and do not amount to an author-supplied 'asymptomatic' diagnosis in the visible text.
Standalone and high-yield. The explanation appropriately uses 'generally preferred' rather than prescribing systemic treatment regardless of future symptoms or individual goals.

record.title: Choose reconstruction after emergency sigmoid resection
fairness: Rectal-stump closure with end colostomy is the best offered reconstruction at the stated decision point. Persistent vasopressor requirement, fecal contamination and edematous bowel favor avoiding an anastomosis; proximal diversion does not eliminate anastomotic failure risk.

The current question separates the completed source-control resection from the remaining reconstruction decision. Viable ends and feasible fascial closure make the scope clear without requiring the learner to invent a damage-control/open-abdomen plan.

All options are concrete reconstructions with comparable specificity; there is no uniquely generic emergency-treatment answer. The two steps are assessment of present anastomotic risk and selection of the appropriate reconstruction.

The retrospective clinic frame is coherent and self-contained. This is high-yield emergency colorectal judgment, moderate rather than hard, and the explanation appropriately avoids a universal Hartmann rule.

record.title: Integrate baseline and first surveillance
fairness: Five-year surveillance is the best offered answer under the named USMSTF framework. Interpret the baseline 14-mm adenoma category, then modify the subsequent interval using the normal first surveillance examination.

The three-year option incorrectly carries the initial advanced-adenoma interval forward unchanged; the ten-year option erases the relevant prior adenoma history. Both are credible errors and neither is a lexical outlier.
Both examinations, their adequacy, the complete initial resection and relevant exclusions are supplied. This standalone node does not rely on a preceding surveillance question.
Serial surveillance planning is high-yield. Guideline timing is assessed from established knowledge offline, not newly verified current guidance.

record.title: Actual beta-blocker exposure before surgery
fairness: Best answer: omit tomorrow's metoprolol and review its longer-term indication. Actual administration history defeats literal continuation of the copied list; controlled hypertension without another represented indication defeats postponement merely to establish beta blockade.

Two consequential judgments remain: distinguish current treatment from an old prescription, then decide whether the indication warrants starting treatment or delaying surgery. This is a high-yield perioperative medication-reconciliation error.
The task, named age/sex presentation and timing are complete. This is a standalone case with no earlier feedback supplying the answer.

Review-wide limitation: this is an offline editorial review of the 21 executable candidate nodes, not independent source verification or clinical sign-off. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative. Historical kept/retired records and nine parked/unkeyed attempts were noted but not graded. All candidates remain needs_clinician_review. The reviewed input SHA-256 is de31ee9a99add949870b91b84f5704508ffd334a2f4209633d2afcf6453dca28.

record.title: Contrast-event phenotype and actual culprit agent
fairness: Best answer: gadobutrol-associated immediate hypersensitivity-type reaction. Transient warmth without wheals at the iohexol visit does not support the same event classification as generalized itchy raised plaques after gadobutrol.

The learner must distinguish physiologic symptoms from an allergic-like phenotype and then attribute that event to the administered agent rather than the referral header. Both agent names occur in the exhibit and in plausible choices; word matching to a single named drug cannot solve the item.

The explanation correctly limits inference: the record does not prove an IgE mechanism or determine another agent's safety or a prophylaxis protocol. The complete standalone exhibit supports one documentation answer. Accurate contrast reaction history is a high-yield diagnostic-safety concept.

record.title: Medication removal without withdrawal or undertreated pain
fairness: Best answer: discontinue the admission-added bedtime diphenhydramine. Abruptly discontinuing a confirmed longstanding benzodiazepine introduces withdrawal concerns, while the observed pain response provides a reason not to simply remove necessary analgesia.

The learner must identify medication-related delirium risk and then use actual exposure and indication to distinguish the safest immediate discontinuation among three potentially problematic drug classes. These are consequential competing considerations, not merely three unrelated medicines.

The admission chronology, exhibit and complete task stand alone. The explanation limits the immediate decision and does not endorse indefinite clonazepam use or supply an unsupported taper. Delirium prevention with avoidance of withdrawal and undertreated pain is high yield.

record.title: Original PCI indication and elective surgery timing
fairness: Best supported scheduling target: at least twelve months after PCI for the represented ACS-related DES and elective surgery requiring clopidogrel interruption. The acute symptoms, new ECG findings, troponin rise and culprit thrombus support the ACS pathway rather than the generic coronary-disease header.

Two consequential steps are present: reconstruct the PCI indication from the original record, then combine it with elective urgency and antiplatelet interruption when choosing the timing pathway. Six months and the current interval represent different plausible pathways rather than arbitrary numerical filler.

The explanation preserves the ideally-delayed elective context and distinguishes a time-sensitive exception without claiming that every post-PCI operation has the same timing. The standalone task is complete. This is high-yield perioperative stent management; current source wording was not independently retrieved in this offline review.

record.title: Extended prophylaxis after cancer surgery
fairness: Best supported answer: continue prophylactic LMWH to about four postoperative weeks. The prior DVT, major cancer operation and limited mobility support extended prevention; the nonexpanding bruise and unchanged serial hemoglobin do not establish recurrent major bleeding warranting a new hold.

The learner must reinterpret current bleeding concern after an earlier serious event, then apply persistent VTE risk to discharge duration. Stopping at discharge and carrying forward the earlier bleeding restriction are distinct, credible errors.

The explanation appropriately distinguishes total postoperative duration from four additional weeks after discharge. This high-yield standalone discharge record contains the relevant earlier course without requiring another node's answer. No new numerical eligibility threshold is inferred.

record.title: Progressive hand injury after contrast extravasation
fairness: Best answer: urgent hand-surgical assessment. Progressive tense swelling, sensory deterioration and marked pain with passive extension after initial elevation warrant escalation for threatened tissue rather than continuation of the same observation plan.

The learner must separate the present local injury trajectory from the prior systemic hives event and then recognize that the progression changes the management of extravasation. Continued local observation is a credible plan for a different, nonprogressive course; antihistamine treatment addresses the wrong represented process.

The explanation requests assessment rather than claiming a pressure-defined diagnosis or mandating an operation. This high-yield escalation principle is clear in the standalone historical record. Necessary warning signs should not be weakened to create difficulty.

record.title: Severe delayed drug reaction and allergy evaluation
fairness: Best answer: retain the reaction record and obtain drug-allergy specialist assessment. The retrieved blistering, mucosal disease and organ injury do not fit a routine remote benign-rash delabeling pathway.

The two consequential judgments are recognition of a severe delayed phenotype from the fuller history and understanding why neither direct challenge nor an immediate-hypersensitivity skin-test-then-challenge pathway resolves that risk. The elapsed years and reassuring abbreviated header are credible distractors.

The item need not name one exact severe delayed syndrome to establish that routine challenge is inappropriate. It does not claim that a particular alternative perioperative antibiotic is safe. The standalone task is clear and the allergy-evaluation boundary is high yield.

record.title: Recurrent collection with improved function
fairness: Best supported plan: observation with reassessment. Prior aspiration and increased measured dimensions make repeat intervention tempting, but present function, minimal symptoms, closed noninflamed wound and uncomplicated ultrasound appearance do not establish a need for drainage.

Two consequential interpretations are needed: classify the current collection in its wound context, then weigh its current effect against its persistence/size trend and the earlier reason for aspiration. Repeat aspiration is a credible error; catheter drainage is a more aggressive escalation without the represented burden to support it.

The explanation bases observation on current effects rather than an invented size cutoff. All relevant earlier treatment and current reassessment findings are included in this standalone case. Postoperative seroma management is high yield.

record.title: Wrong-site negative study after breast surgery
fairness: Best answer: targeted ultrasound at the current 2 o'clock incision. The complete acquisition record and sonographer confirmation establish that the negative examination concerns the old 6 o'clock scar, rather than merely an incomplete export of a correctly performed study.

The learner must assess whether the negative study answers the current question, then select focused characterization of an early postoperative fullness rather than mammographic escalation or sampling an uncharacterized target. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is not established as the next investigation before a drainable collection is demonstrated.

Both the key and aspiration option name the current site, and both contain ultrasound; exact site matching alone does not uniquely select the key. The standalone case is coherent. Imaging-target adequacy and postoperative collection evaluation are high-yield practical concepts.

record.title: Postoperative ketotic acidosis with modest glucose
fairness: Best answer: intravenous insulin with dextrose-containing fluid. Diabetes/SGLT2 exposure, substantial ketonemia and acidosis support DKA despite the modest glucose. The supplied potassium and completed initial volume replacement make the proposed next-infusion comparison interpretable.

Two consequential steps are present: recognize the acid-ketone disorder without relying on marked hyperglycemia, then choose glucose-containing support while insulin treats ketogenesis. Insulin with dextrose-free fluid and withholding insulin for saline are credible glucose-driven errors.

The options compare the same infusion decision. The explicit dextrose distinction is the clinical variable being tested, not an explanatory giveaway. The constructed exhibit and historical decision point stand alone; the explanation does not invent a dose or rate. This is high-yield perioperative metabolic safety.

record.title: Valve assessment before nonurgent major surgery
fairness: Best answer: defer the nonurgent operation for valve-team assessment. The concordant valve measurements and exertional presyncope support a symptomatic severe aortic-stenosis concern despite preserved ejection fraction.

The learner must interpret valve severity and symptoms, then apply the nonurgent major-operation context to preparation. Proceeding with surveillance treats preserved systolic function as sufficient reassurance; dobutamine stress testing misapplies a strategy for a different diagnostic question to already concordant high-gradient findings.

The key appropriately calls for specialist assessment rather than declaring a particular valve intervention mandatory. All needed context is present in this standalone case. This is a commonly tested perioperative cardiac decision.

concept.displayName: sglt2 acid ketone pattern
concept.learningObjective: Interpret postoperative ketone-associated acidosis despite modest glucose and select an insulin/fluid plan that can correct it without creating hypoglycemia.

record.title: Postoperative ketotic acidosis with modest glucose
fairness: Best answer: intravenous insulin with dextrose-containing fluid. Diabetes/SGLT2 exposure, substantial ketonemia and acidosis support DKA despite the modest glucose. The supplied potassium and completed initial volume replacement make the proposed next-infusion comparison interpretable.

Two consequential steps are present: recognize the acid-ketone disorder without relying on marked hyperglycemia, then choose glucose-containing support while insulin treats ketogenesis. Insulin with dextrose-free fluid and withholding insulin for saline are credible glucose-driven errors.

The options compare the same infusion decision. The explicit dextrose distinction is the clinical variable being tested, not an explanatory giveaway. The constructed exhibit and historical decision point stand alone; the explanation does not invent a dose or rate. This is high-yield perioperative metabolic safety.

decisionNodes.stem: Which medication discontinuation best fits {patientName}’s postoperative delirium-prevention plan?

answerChoices.label: Discontinue the bedtime diphenhydramine order
answerChoices.rationale: The newly added sleep medicine contributes anticholinergic exposure. The competing medicines have represented withdrawal-prevention or analgesic roles that cannot simply be discarded.

answerChoices.label: Discontinue the nightly clonazepam order
answerChoices.rationale: Longstanding daily benzodiazepine exposure makes abrupt elimination different from avoiding a newly prescribed sedative. Prevention of withdrawal needs a deliberate plan.

answerChoices.label: Discontinue the as-needed oxycodone order
answerChoices.rationale: Opioid exposure deserves careful titration, but the record shows substantial movement-related pain despite acetaminophen and meaningful response. Simply removing analgesia can leave another delirium contributor untreated.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret why each medicine is present and what Helen has actually been receiving. The admission-added anticholinergic sleep order can be removed without abruptly withdrawing a longstanding benzodiazepine or abandoning treatment of substantial pain. This does not approve indefinite clonazepam use or prescribe a taper; it identifies the best immediate order change.

concept.displayName: delirium anticholinergic order
concept.learningObjective: Identify an avoidable anticholinergic order while preserving useful symptom prevention.

record.title: Medication removal without withdrawal or undertreated pain
fairness: Best answer: discontinue the admission-added bedtime diphenhydramine. Abruptly discontinuing a confirmed longstanding benzodiazepine introduces withdrawal concerns, while the observed pain response provides a reason not to simply remove necessary analgesia.

The learner must identify medication-related delirium risk and then use actual exposure and indication to distinguish the safest immediate discontinuation among three potentially problematic drug classes. These are consequential competing considerations, not merely three unrelated medicines.

The admission chronology, exhibit and complete task stand alone. The explanation limits the immediate decision and does not endorse indefinite clonazepam use or supply an unsupported taper. Delirium prevention with avoidance of withdrawal and undertreated pain is high yield.

decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should {patientName} undergo next for the current 2 o’clock incision-site fullness?

answerChoices.label: Targeted ultrasound at the marked 2 o’clock incision
answerChoices.rationale: The completed examination covered the old inferior scar, so its negative result does not characterize the current site. Ultrasound can characterize the localized postoperative collection.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic mammography of the left breast
answerChoices.rationale: This may be appropriate for a different new palpable-lesion workup, but it does not replace the missing targeted characterization of this early localized postoperative site.

answerChoices.label: Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the 2 o’clock fullness
answerChoices.rationale: A drainable collection at the current site has not been demonstrated. Targeted imaging should establish what the finding is before a therapeutic aspiration is selected.

decisionNodes.explanation: First match the actual acquisition to the current clinical target. A complete negative study of the 6 o’clock scar does not assess the 2 o’clock postoperative bed. Then choose focused characterization of that early wound-site change rather than escalate because of a supposedly adequate negative study or aspirate uncharacterized tissue.

fairness: Best answer: targeted ultrasound at the current 2 o'clock incision. The complete acquisition record and sonographer confirmation establish that the negative examination concerns the old 6 o'clock scar, rather than merely an incomplete export of a correctly performed study.

Ultrasound-guided aspiration is not established as the next investigation before a drainable collection is demonstrated.

Both the key and aspiration option name the current site, and both contain ultrasound; exact site matching alone does not uniquely select the key. The standalone case is coherent. Imaging-target adequacy and postoperative collection evaluation are high-yield practical concepts.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 53-year-old woman, attends clinic four weeks after excision of a benign breast lesion without an implant. The record shows one earlier needle aspiration when the incision-site pocket made reaching and dressing painful. She now reaches the upper shelf and dresses without assistance; she notices the pocket only when pressing on it. Repeat ultrasound shows a thin-walled 3.0 × 0.8 × 1.5 cm fluid pocket, compared with 2.4 × 0.6 × 1.2 cm previously, with no solid component or surrounding hypervascularity. Temperature is 98.4°F and the skin moves freely over the closed incision, without erythema.

decisionNodes.stem: Which current management plan best fits {patientName}’s postoperative incision-site collection?

answerChoices.label: Clinical observation with reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The current functional course differs from the earlier symptomatic episode. Reappearance or a modest imaging increase does not by itself establish a need for another invasive procedure in this uncomplicated pocket.

answerChoices.label: Repeat image-guided needle aspiration
answerChoices.rationale: Aspiration helped the earlier painful pocket, but the present functional limitation has resolved. Repeating it solely because the image is larger adds a procedure without the former indication.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided catheter drainage
answerChoices.rationale: This is a real option for selected difficult recurrent collections, but one recurrence with recovered function is not evidence that a drain is now needed.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret recurrence and current effect separately. The earlier aspiration addressed pain and restricted use; those effects are no longer present despite a persistent image. Observation with reassessment fits this current uncomplicated pocket. Repeat aspiration and catheter drainage remain real interventions for different clinical burdens, not automatic responses to persistence.

concept.displayName: postoperative seroma observe
concept.learningObjective: Use current symptoms and wound effect, rather than persistence of fluid alone, to rank intervention versus observation.

record.title: Recurrent collection with improved function
fairness: Best supported plan: observation with reassessment. Prior aspiration and increased measured dimensions make repeat intervention tempting, but present function, minimal symptoms, closed noninflamed wound and uncomplicated ultrasound appearance do not establish a need for drainage.

Two consequential interpretations are needed: classify the current collection in its wound context, then weigh its current effect against its persistence/size trend and the earlier reason for aspiration. Repeat aspiration is a credible error; catheter drainage is a more aggressive escalation without the represented burden to support it.

The explanation bases observation on current effects rather than an invented size cutoff. All relevant earlier treatment and current reassessment findings are included in this standalone case. Postoperative seroma management is high yield.

decisionNodes.stem: Which agent-specific hypersensitivity entry is supported by {patientName}’s original records?

answerChoices.label: Gadobutrol-associated immediate hypersensitivity-type reaction
answerChoices.rationale: The administration record links the generalized wheal-type event to gadobutrol. The iohexol event has an isolated warmth phenotype.

answerChoices.label: Iohexol-associated immediate hypersensitivity-type reaction
answerChoices.rationale: This preserves the referral’s agent attribution even though the original iohexol event describes warmth without the generalized skin findings.

answerChoices.label: Hypersensitivity-type reactions to both named agents
answerChoices.rationale: This merges a physiologic warmth event with a separate generalized skin event and loses the distinction needed for future planning.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the event phenotype, then check which agent was actually administered for that event. The generalized wheal-type event follows gadobutrol, while the iohexol visit records isolated transient warmth. Document the actual agent and symptoms. This does not prove an IgE mechanism, permit every other agent or select a premedication protocol.

concept.learningObjective: Reconcile contrast administration provenance and event phenotype before updating an agent-specific hypersensitivity record.

record.title: Contrast-event phenotype and actual culprit agent
fairness: Best answer: gadobutrol-associated immediate hypersensitivity-type reaction. Transient warmth without wheals at the iohexol visit does not support the same event classification as generalized itchy raised plaques after gadobutrol.

The learner must distinguish physiologic symptoms from an allergic-like phenotype and then attribute that event to the administered agent rather than the referral header. Both agent names occur in the exhibit and in plausible choices; word matching to a single named drug cannot solve the item.

The explanation correctly limits inference: the record does not prove an IgE mechanism or determine another agent's safety or a prophylaxis protocol. The complete standalone exhibit supports one documentation answer. Accurate contrast reaction history is a high-yield diagnostic-safety concept.

record.title: Progressive hand injury after contrast extravasation
fairness: Best answer: urgent hand-surgical assessment. Progressive tense swelling, sensory deterioration and marked pain with passive extension after initial elevation warrant escalation for threatened tissue rather than continuation of the same observation plan.

The learner must separate the present local injury trajectory from the prior systemic hives event and then recognize that the progression changes the management of extravasation. Continued local observation is a credible plan for a different, nonprogressive course; antihistamine treatment addresses the wrong represented process.

The explanation requests assessment rather than claiming a pressure-defined diagnosis or mandating an operation. This high-yield escalation principle is clear in the standalone historical record. Necessary warning signs should not be weakened to create difficulty.

record.title: Severe delayed drug reaction and allergy evaluation
fairness: Best answer: retain the reaction record and obtain drug-allergy specialist assessment. The retrieved blistering, mucosal disease and organ injury do not fit a routine remote benign-rash delabeling pathway.

The two consequential judgments are recognition of a severe delayed phenotype from the fuller history and understanding why neither direct challenge nor an immediate-hypersensitivity skin-test-then-challenge pathway resolves that risk. The elapsed years and reassuring abbreviated header are credible distractors.

The item need not name one exact severe delayed syndrome to establish that routine challenge is inappropriate. It does not claim that a particular alternative perioperative antibiotic is safe. The standalone task is clear and the allergy-evaluation boundary is high yield.

record.title: Valve assessment before nonurgent major surgery
fairness: Best answer: defer the nonurgent operation for valve-team assessment. The concordant valve measurements and exertional presyncope support a symptomatic severe aortic-stenosis concern despite preserved ejection fraction.

The learner must interpret valve severity and symptoms, then apply the nonurgent major-operation context to preparation. Proceeding with surveillance treats preserved systolic function as sufficient reassurance; dobutamine stress testing misapplies a strategy for a different diagnostic question to already concordant high-gradient findings.

The key appropriately calls for specialist assessment rather than declaring a particular valve intervention mandatory. All needed context is present in this standalone case. This is a commonly tested perioperative cardiac decision.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 62-year-old woman, attends clinic four months after drug-eluting coronary stent placement to plan repair of a reducible incisional hernia. The catheterization referral header says “coronary disease.” The original admission record describes new chest pressure at rest, new ST depression and troponin rising from 18 to 860 ng/L (the assay’s female upper reference limit was 14). Angiography identified a thrombus-containing culprit coronary lesion that was stented. She is now taking aspirin and clopidogrel. The elective repair requires clopidogrel interruption.

concept.learningObjective: Integrate ACS stent indication, early interval and operation urgency before accepting antiplatelet interruption.

record.title: Original PCI indication and elective surgery timing
fairness: Best supported scheduling target: at least twelve months after PCI for the represented ACS-related DES and elective surgery requiring clopidogrel interruption. The acute symptoms, new ECG findings, troponin rise and culprit thrombus support the ACS pathway rather than the generic coronary-disease header.

Two consequential steps are present: reconstruct the PCI indication from the original record, then combine it with elective urgency and antiplatelet interruption when choosing the timing pathway. Six months and the current interval represent different plausible pathways rather than arbitrary numerical filler.

The explanation preserves the ideally-delayed elective context and distinguishes a time-sensitive exception without claiming that every post-PCI operation has the same timing. The standalone task is complete. This is high-yield perioperative stent management; current source wording was not independently retrieved in this offline review.

record.title: Persistent combined internal and external hemorrhoidal disease
clarityIssues: The presentation's phrase her later bleeding evaluation refers to an event not used or described in this standalone node. The update nevertheless identifies the treatment visit clearly, so this is residual framing clutter rather than a key-changing ambiguity.
fairness: Manual reduction establishes more advanced internal prolapse, while the symptomatic external disease and prior failed banding make excisional hemorrhoidectomy the strongest offered choice. Stapling or arterial ligation does not address the same external symptom source.

The two steps are to distinguish combined hemorrhoidal disease from rectal prolapse, then choose a procedure that treats the clinically important components after prior office treatment. External-component symptoms are decision data, not a supplied operation label.
The choices are parallel named procedures without explanatory qualifiers. All decision-critical information is present in this node; the later bleeding companion is not needed.
suggestions: No blocking clinical or reasoning revision. If a new wrapper version is authorized, remove the unused later bleeding evaluation reference and retain the explicit retrospective treatment visit.

record.title: Posterior source control and sphincter preservation in a horseshoe abscess

cues.phrase: Modified Hanley drainage with loose seton
cues.why: The key is the only eponym and the only label not repeating with lateral drainage. This is a modest style outlier, not a reliable nonmedical solution: lateral drainage is explicitly shared in the update, and selecting the seton still requires anatomical knowledge.

fairness: The posterior cavity below the levator with bilateral lateral communication supports a horseshoe source-control approach. The high external-sphincter crossing independently argues against complete fistulotomy. Modified Hanley drainage with a loose seton best combines these requirements among the offered choices.

The existing catheter is not treated as proof that the whole collection is drained. The update explicitly supplies continued left drainage and new right access, so the scored question concerns the remaining central access and tract decision. This resolves a potential incompleteness in the abbreviated keyed label.

This is hard because central cavity access and muscle-crossing consequences must both be interpreted; either isolated rule can lead to a different offered operation. The standalone outside-record review is coherent. The exact operative variant still requires clinician approval, but no confident error is apparent in the described principle.
suggestions: No blocking revision. In a future label revision, state central access and tract treatment in the same format for every choice, leaving the already agreed lateral drainage in shared context. Keep the high crossing and below-levator posterior source explicit.

record.title: Office treatment of persistent spontaneously reducing internal hemorrhoids
fairness: The spontaneous reduction and absent important external component establish the relevant disease pattern; persistent symptoms after conservative care then support rubber-band ligation. Excision and artery ligation are possible hemorrhoid procedures, but neither is the best initial procedural escalation for this record.

The task is specifically procedure selection at the treatment visit, not a claim that all rectal bleeding requires no further evaluation. No diagnostic-workup omission is needed to answer the stated task.

Office is an accurate setting descriptor, not a unique feasibility permission in the stem. No option contains its rationale. The standalone wrapper and update establish a coherent retrospective treatment visit without needing the formerly associated diagnostic node. This is lower-moderate, high-yield stage-based management.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Keep the failed conservative care, spontaneous reduction and external-component information together in the standalone context.

record.title: Sphincterotomy after unsuccessful fissure treatment with preserved continence
fairness: Persistent chronic fissure after diltiazem and botulinum treatment establishes a reason to escalate. Elevated resting pressure plus intact continence and no previous sphincter injury then favor LIS over the offered non-sphincter-dividing procedures. Failure of treatment alone would not establish that selection.

The diagnosis in the task is appropriate because the scored objective is operation selection, not recognition of a fissure. The request for an operative discussion does not pick LIS from the other operative options.

The later visit is fully described in this standalone node; no earlier medication-choice answer is required. The explanation appropriately retains continence risk and does not promise universal suitability. No confident inaccuracy was identified in its tailored-division teaching point during this offline review.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Retain pressure, functional reserve and prior treatment as separate selection facts; do not turn failed medical therapy into an unconditional indication for sphincter division.

record.title: Operation for a long rectal prolapse with substantial anesthetic risk

cues.phrase: Anesthesia advised against general anesthesia and pneumoperitoneum but considered regional anesthesia acceptable.
cues.why: This substantially narrows access selection. It is a legitimate patient-specific constraint rather than an invented convenience: it still does not distinguish Delorme from perineal rectosigmoidectomy without interpreting the long full-thickness segment.

fairness: The long full-thickness prolapse favors perineal rectosigmoidectomy over a mucosal sleeve procedure, while the anesthetic assessment disfavors the offered laparoscopic abdominal operation. These are two independent, consequential selections. Viability and reducibility make this an elective planning question rather than an untreated ischemic emergency.

The stated 12 cm is a fictional observation, not an asserted universal procedural cutoff. I find no confident clinical inaccuracy in the intended best answer, but exact procedure suitability remains a clinician judgment; this editorial PASS does not resolve the packet's separate clinical-sign-off question.
The standalone context fully supplies the prolapse and anesthetic findings. No prior diagnostic answer is required, and no prior explanation is now rehearsing the operation.
suggestions: No blocking editorial revision. Retain the length and anesthetic constraint, and do not generalize the explanation into an absolute length threshold or a rule that all older patients require a perineal operation.

record.title: Evacuation retraining despite a coexisting rectal pouch
fairness: The concordant abnormal expulsion and anal pressure rise during attempted evacuation support a coordination problem. The resident must then prioritize biofeedback over treating an anatomically visible pouch or using botulinum toxin before first-line retraining.

The resting MRI does not establish that the pouch causes the evacuation failure; splinting makes repair tempting without proving that it should precede functional treatment. This is a meaningful, high-yield functional-versus-structural sequencing comparison.

For evacuation coordination modestly expands the biofeedback label but does not repeat a diagnosis supplied in the stem or independently disclose the answer. No blocking length, grammar or convergence cue was found. The standalone context provides the stool-care history and both physiological observations.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the two concordant functional findings and avoid converting the resting MRI description into proof of a mechanically obstructing rectocele.

record.title: Symptomatic rectocele after successful coordination treatment
fairness: Current relaxation and adequate balloon expulsion reduce the case for further treatment directed at nonrelaxation. Retained contrast that is released by vaginal support then connects the pouch to the persisting disability, supporting discussion of native-tissue rectocele repair.

The item requires both functional reassessment and attribution of residual mechanical obstruction; merely identifying a pouch is insufficient. Botulinum treatment is the wrong physiological target here. STARR is a recognizable procedural competitor, and its adverse-complication teaching point is consistent with the intended comparison; no confident inaccuracy was identified offline.

Native-tissue rectocele repair leaves route selection open, but that is appropriate to the stated repair-versus-other-procedure task; no unsupported choice between vaginal and transanal routes is imposed. None of the options includes a rationale or uniquely cautious wording.

Although the update calls the study returned, it supplies all relevant observations and does not require the previous test-choice node. The case is coherent and answerable on its own. The explanation correctly describes a reasonable procedural discussion rather than guaranteed symptom resolution.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the contrast-retention/release finding and current coordination results; do not turn a rectocele on static imaging alone into an indication for repair.

record.title: Mapping recurrent fistula extensions despite a known sphincter defect
fairness: The current distribution cannot be reduced to the old short tract or its known muscle defect. The resident must infer possible secondary or higher extension, then select a study for that operative problem rather than focus solely on the continence injury. MRI is the strongest offered answer for that objective.

Expert three-dimensional endoanal ultrasound is a credible competitor and can map fistulas, not just sphincter defects. The explanation correctly retains that capability. I do not identify a confident factual error or an equally strong key from the represented higher-extension concern, although this is a comparative clinical judgment rather than an absolute exclusion of ultrasound.

The parallel modality labels contain no key-specific rationale, lexical shortcut or convergence pattern. The old ultrasound and new examination are temporally distinguishable, and the case is independently answerable without an earlier test-selection node.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the new higher distribution and the genuine ultrasound alternative; do not simplify feedback into MRI is always required or ultrasound only evaluates continence. Exact comparative ranking remains for named clinical sign-off.

record.title: Fistulotomy with limited muscle crossing and intact continence
fairness: Lay-open fistulotomy is the best offered procedure for the represented very low, unbranched posterior tract with intact muscle and gas/liquid/solid continence. LIFT and advancement flap are real alternatives for a different muscle-division risk, not nonsensical procedures.

The resident must combine tract extent with functional reserve, then judge whether the extra sphincter-preserving procedure is justified. This is a lower-moderate core surgical decision; changing baseline continence would materially change its interpretation.

The options have parallel procedure labels and comparable specificity. No nonmedical wording, absolute, unique rationale or convergence selects the key. The standalone clinic history supplies the relevant prior abscess and operative findings.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Retain both the limited crossing and explicit baseline function; neither a tract label nor persistent drainage alone establishes suitability for fistulotomy.

record.title: Procedural escalation after late deterioration of sphincter repair
fairness: The long initial improvement followed by gradual deterioration without a new injury makes an old anatomical gap an insufficient reason to repeat reconstruction. Persistent formed-stool leakage despite conservative care then supports an SNM trial rather than immediate permanent implantation or routine bulking injection.

The old defect gives repeat sphincteroplasty a credible attraction; the temporal course is consequential rather than decorative. The task asks for a procedural pathway, so test stimulation appropriately competes with reconstructive and injection pathways at the escalation decision.

No nonmedical wording attack selects SNM. Repeat overlapping sphincteroplasty overlaps the history but cues a distractor, not the key. The standalone case carries the necessary prior repair, response and recurrence sequence.
suggestions: No blocking revision. For clearer clinical specificity in a future version, name the actual conservative measures already tried rather than only conservative care, without inventing doses or durations. Preserve the distinction between test stimulation and permanent implantation.

record.title: Treating the residual stool-consistency contributor to leakage
clarityIssues: Continence-focused rehabilitation does not specify whether the completed course included instrumented biofeedback or only exercises. This leaves the precise relationship to the biofeedback distractor less clear than it could be, although stool-directed treatment remains best supported by the represented residual pattern.
fairness: The resident must compare retained formed-stool function and improved squeeze against persistent loose-stool urgency, then target the remaining contributor instead of treating the old ultrasound defect as sufficient reason for surgery. Fiber intolerance and the stated assessment of the loose stool support a monitored loperamide trial.

The chosen plan is not merely the only novel option: recognizing why stool consistency matters despite an anatomical defect requires clinical interpretation. Biofeedback is a real continence intervention, and the explanation correctly avoids conflating it with evacuation retraining.

The explanation does not promise cure or prescribe an invented dose. The prior defect, rehabilitation response, diary and current symptom pattern are all supplied in the standalone node. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical keying shortcut was found.
suggestions: No blocking revision. In a future clarification, state the actual completed rehabilitation modality so a resident need not guess whether continence biofeedback has already been tried. Preserve the formed-versus-loose-stool contrast and avoid implying that an old structural defect is irrelevant to long-term management.

record.title: Drainage of an externally originating supralevator abscess

cues.phrase: There is no abdominal visceral source.
cues.why: The word abdominal permits lexical elimination of Transabdominal drainage through the pelvic cavity. This is a partial cue, not a way to distinguish the remaining two routes without anatomical knowledge; absence of a visceral source also supplies relevant origin information.

fairness: The positive continuity from lateral ischioanal fat into the high collection supports transperineal drainage; supralevator location by itself does not select internal drainage. The source-plane inference and its effect on drainage route are both consequential. Moderate difficulty is at the lower end because the other-plane negatives narrow the comparison.

The retrospective clinic presentation and MRI update form a coherent standalone record. No previous scored answer is needed. Named patient, age and sex are supplied by the case wrapper; the complaint is short and appropriate.

Review scope for this report: all 16 current executable candidate nodes were assessed from Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task, Options and Explanation, including six previously passed candidates. The two Keep inventory rows, 65 retirement proposals, six parked attempts and held/unkeyed records were noted but not rescored. Historical multipart cases were not treated as current cases. Author verdicts and key-position markers were not evidence of quality.

This is an offline editorial assessment, not new source verification or clinical approval. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured performance or verified examination frequencies. Runtime rendering, randomization and wait previews are outside the visible-text assessment. These limitations apply to every row.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the positive lower-to-upper continuity; do not make the upper location alone determine the route.

If a future wording version is authorized, replace the interpretive Other planes wording with concise actual imaging observations while retaining the information needed to exclude a visceral source. Do not silently alter the preserved exact version.

record.title: Drainage of an intersphincteric-origin supralevator abscess
clarityIssues: The update repeats that the founder reviews outside records after the presentation has already established that setting. This is removable framing, not a clinical ambiguity.
fairness: The uninterrupted lower-to-upper fluid column supplies the origin inference rather than simply labelling the abscess. Recognizing an intersphincteric origin then determines internal drainage, despite the distracting high location.

Internal and external occur together in the anatomical description; neither is a unique word match to a keyed option. All options name comparable access routes without a teaching rationale. Transabdominal access represents a high-location error, not an equally supported source-control route here.

The retrospective clinic context and MRI observations stand alone. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the explanation. The text describes observations rather than promising an unavailable diagnostic image.
suggestions: No blocking revision. A future prose cleanup can shorten the duplicate record-review sentence while retaining the positive anatomical continuity.

concept.learningObjective: Choose external drainage when an ischioanal cavity extends above the levator.

record.title: Drainage of an externally originating supralevator abscess

cues.phrase: There is no abdominal visceral source.
cues.why: The word abdominal permits lexical elimination of Transabdominal drainage through the pelvic cavity. This is a partial cue, not a way to distinguish the remaining two routes without anatomical knowledge; absence of a visceral source also supplies relevant origin information.

fairness: The positive continuity from lateral ischioanal fat into the high collection supports transperineal drainage; supralevator location by itself does not select internal drainage. The source-plane inference and its effect on drainage route are both consequential. Moderate difficulty is at the lower end because the other-plane negatives narrow the comparison.

The retrospective clinic presentation and MRI update form a coherent standalone record. No previous scored answer is needed. Named patient, age and sex are supplied by the case wrapper; the complaint is short and appropriate.

Review scope for this report: all 16 current executable candidate nodes were assessed from Presentation, Current update, Exhibit, Task, Options and Explanation, including six previously passed candidates. The two Keep inventory rows, 65 retirement proposals, six parked attempts and held/unkeyed records were noted but not rescored. Historical multipart cases were not treated as current cases. Author verdicts and key-position markers were not evidence of quality.

This is an offline editorial assessment, not new source verification or clinical approval. Difficulty and high-yield judgments are qualitative, not measured performance or verified examination frequencies. Runtime rendering, randomization and wait previews are outside the visible-text assessment. These limitations apply to every row.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the positive lower-to-upper continuity; do not make the upper location alone determine the route.

If a future wording version is authorized, replace the interpretive Other planes wording with concise actual imaging observations while retaining the information needed to exclude a visceral source. Do not silently alter the preserved exact version.

Examination under anesthesia shows one unbranched tract crossing only the lowest external sphincter fibers. The remaining muscle is intact. There has been no previous fistula operation.
decisionNodes.stem: Which definitive procedure best fits {patientName}'s demonstrated tract?

answerChoices.label: Ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract
answerChoices.rationale: LIFT is a real sphincter-preserving alternative for transsphincteric anatomy, but this very low unbranched tract with preserved function fits the simpler definitive fistulotomy pathway. It becomes more compelling when division would sacrifice substantial muscle or functional reserve.

answerChoices.label: Endorectal advancement flap
answerChoices.rationale: A flap is an option for fistulas requiring preservation of sphincter muscle; it adds a repair procedure to a superficial tract that can be laid open.

answerChoices.label: Lay-open fistulotomy
answerChoices.rationale: The very low unbranched tract and intact baseline continence fit selected lay-open fistulotomy. Persistent drainage does not itself require a complex-fistula repair. The choice balances the represented limited crossing against actual function.

concept.displayName: Select fistulotomy for a very low unbranched fistula with intact function.
concept.learningObjective: Select fistulotomy for a very low unbranched fistula with intact function.

record.title: Fistulotomy with limited muscle crossing and intact continence
fairness: Lay-open fistulotomy is the best offered procedure for the represented very low, unbranched posterior tract with intact muscle and gas/liquid/solid continence. LIFT and advancement flap are real alternatives for a different muscle-division risk, not nonsensical procedures.

The resident must combine tract extent with functional reserve, then judge whether the extra sphincter-preserving procedure is justified. This is a lower-moderate core surgical decision; changing baseline continence would materially change its interpretation.

The options have parallel procedure labels and comparable specificity. No nonmedical wording, absolute, unique rationale or convergence selects the key. The standalone clinic history supplies the relevant prior abscess and operative findings.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Retain both the limited crossing and explicit baseline function; neither a tract label nor persistent drainage alone establishes suitability for fistulotomy.

record.title: Operation for a long rectal prolapse with substantial anesthetic risk

cues.phrase: Anesthesia advised against general anesthesia and pneumoperitoneum but considered regional anesthesia acceptable.
cues.why: This substantially narrows access selection. It is a legitimate patient-specific constraint rather than an invented convenience: it still does not distinguish Delorme from perineal rectosigmoidectomy without interpreting the long full-thickness segment.

fairness: The long full-thickness prolapse favors perineal rectosigmoidectomy over a mucosal sleeve procedure, while the anesthetic assessment disfavors the offered laparoscopic abdominal operation. These are two independent, consequential selections. Viability and reducibility make this an elective planning question rather than an untreated ischemic emergency.

The stated 12 cm is a fictional observation, not an asserted universal procedural cutoff. I find no confident clinical inaccuracy in the intended best answer, but exact procedure suitability remains a clinician judgment; this editorial PASS does not resolve the packet's separate clinical-sign-off question.
The standalone context fully supplies the prolapse and anesthetic findings. No prior diagnostic answer is required, and no prior explanation is now rehearsing the operation.
suggestions: No blocking editorial revision. Retain the length and anesthetic constraint, and do not generalize the explanation into an absolute length threshold or a rule that all older patients require a perineal operation.

record.title: Evacuation retraining despite a coexisting rectal pouch
fairness: The concordant abnormal expulsion and anal pressure rise during attempted evacuation support a coordination problem. The resident must then prioritize biofeedback over treating an anatomically visible pouch or using botulinum toxin before first-line retraining.

The resting MRI does not establish that the pouch causes the evacuation failure; splinting makes repair tempting without proving that it should precede functional treatment. This is a meaningful, high-yield functional-versus-structural sequencing comparison.

For evacuation coordination modestly expands the biofeedback label but does not repeat a diagnosis supplied in the stem or independently disclose the answer. No blocking length, grammar or convergence cue was found. The standalone context provides the stool-care history and both physiological observations.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the two concordant functional findings and avoid converting the resting MRI description into proof of a mechanically obstructing rectocele.

record.title: Drainage of an intersphincteric-origin supralevator abscess
clarityIssues: The update repeats that the founder reviews outside records after the presentation has already established that setting. This is removable framing, not a clinical ambiguity.
fairness: The uninterrupted lower-to-upper fluid column supplies the origin inference rather than simply labelling the abscess. Recognizing an intersphincteric origin then determines internal drainage, despite the distracting high location.

Internal and external occur together in the anatomical description; neither is a unique word match to a keyed option. All options name comparable access routes without a teaching rationale. Transabdominal access represents a high-location error, not an equally supported source-control route here.

The retrospective clinic context and MRI observations stand alone. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the explanation. The text describes observations rather than promising an unavailable diagnostic image.
suggestions: No blocking revision. A future prose cleanup can shorten the duplicate record-review sentence while retaining the positive anatomical continuity.

answerChoices.label: Complete posterior fistulotomy with lateral drainage
answerChoices.rationale: This reaches the communicating source but would divide the high muscle-crossing tract. A connected cavity does not make all involved sphincter safe to lay open.

answerChoices.label: Transrectal cavity drainage with lateral drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Internal drainage fits an upward intersphincteric source. The represented route crosses the external muscle to a posterior cavity below the levator, so transrectal access would establish a different communication.

answerChoices.label: Modified Hanley drainage with loose seton
answerChoices.rationale: Posterior access addresses the communicating deep postanal source while a loose seton avoids laying open the represented high muscle-crossing tract. The existing left opening remains part of lateral drainage; a redundant new left incision is not required.

cues.phrase: Modified Hanley drainage with loose seton
cues.why: The key is the only eponym and the only label not repeating with lateral drainage. This is a modest style outlier, not a reliable nonmedical solution: lateral drainage is explicitly shared in the update, and selecting the seton still requires anatomical knowledge.

fairness: The posterior cavity below the levator with bilateral lateral communication supports a horseshoe source-control approach. The high external-sphincter crossing independently argues against complete fistulotomy. Modified Hanley drainage with a loose seton best combines these requirements among the offered choices.

The existing catheter is not treated as proof that the whole collection is drained. The update explicitly supplies continued left drainage and new right access, so the scored question concerns the remaining central access and tract decision. This resolves a potential incompleteness in the abbreviated keyed label.

This is hard because central cavity access and muscle-crossing consequences must both be interpreted; either isolated rule can lead to a different offered operation. The standalone outside-record review is coherent. The exact operative variant still requires clinician approval, but no confident error is apparent in the described principle.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A prior operation described a short posterior tract. Current examination finds two draining openings separated by an indurated area that extends above the palpable sphincter ring. Gas leakage began after the prior operation, and an older ultrasound showed a posterior muscle defect. He is afebrile, and no superficial fluctuant cavity is palpable.
decisionNodes.stem: Which investigation should guide {patientName}'s next operative plan?

answerChoices.label: Three-dimensional endoanal ultrasonography
answerChoices.rationale: Expert ultrasound can assess the tract and sphincter anatomy. The concern for higher secondary extension, rather than an isolated low tract or defect, favors MRI in this record.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced pelvic computed tomography
answerChoices.rationale: CT can identify an acute abscess, but is less suited than MRI to defining recurrent tract anatomy and secondary extensions for planned repair.

answerChoices.label: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
answerChoices.rationale: The changed distribution and higher induration raise concern for secondary extensions beyond the old short tract. MRI is particularly helpful for complex secondary anatomy; expert endoanal ultrasound can also map fistulas and is not merely a defect study.

decisionNodes.explanation: The current openings and higher induration are not accounted for by the former short tract. MRI can delineate complex secondary extensions for operative planning. Three-dimensional ultrasound remains a useful fistula and muscle study; this comparison does not restrict it to the old continence defect.

concept.displayName: Select imaging that maps new extensions before reoperation for a recurrent fistula.
concept.learningObjective: Select imaging that maps new extensions before reoperation for a recurrent fistula.

record.title: Mapping recurrent fistula extensions despite a known sphincter defect
fairness: The current distribution cannot be reduced to the old short tract or its known muscle defect. The resident must infer possible secondary or higher extension, then select a study for that operative problem rather than focus solely on the continence injury. MRI is the strongest offered answer for that objective.

Expert three-dimensional endoanal ultrasound is a credible competitor and can map fistulas, not just sphincter defects. The explanation correctly retains that capability. I do not identify a confident factual error or an equally strong key from the represented higher-extension concern, although this is a comparative clinical judgment rather than an absolute exclusion of ultrasound.

The parallel modality labels contain no key-specific rationale, lexical shortcut or convergence pattern. The old ultrasound and new examination are temporally distinguishable, and the case is independently answerable without an earlier test-selection node.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the new higher distribution and the genuine ultrasound alternative; do not simplify feedback into MRI is always required or ultrasound only evaluates continence. Exact comparative ranking remains for named clinical sign-off.

decisionNodes.stem: Which procedure is best supported for {patientName}'s persistent fissure at this later visit?

answerChoices.label: Anocutaneous advancement flap
answerChoices.rationale: A flap is especially useful when limited continence reserve makes further sphincter relaxation undesirable. Those functional concerns are not represented here.

answerChoices.label: Anal fissurectomy
answerChoices.rationale: Fissurectomy removes the fissure tissue but does not offer the same established efficacy as selected LIS for the represented hypertonic persistent fissure.

answerChoices.label: Lateral internal sphincterotomy
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent disease after medical treatment, elevated resting pressure and intact baseline continence fit selected LIS. Continence counseling remains necessary; the choice is not a promise of zero risk. When LIS is selected, limiting division to the fissure apex is supported over routine extension to the dentate line.

concept.learningObjective: Choose selected LIS after appropriate medical treatment with preserved continence.

record.title: Sphincterotomy after unsuccessful fissure treatment with preserved continence
fairness: Persistent chronic fissure after diltiazem and botulinum treatment establishes a reason to escalate. Elevated resting pressure plus intact continence and no previous sphincter injury then favor LIS over the offered non-sphincter-dividing procedures. Failure of treatment alone would not establish that selection.

The diagnosis in the task is appropriate because the scored objective is operation selection, not recognition of a fissure. The request for an operative discussion does not pick LIS from the other operative options.

The later visit is fully described in this standalone node; no earlier medication-choice answer is required. The explanation appropriately retains continence risk and does not promise universal suitability. No confident inaccuracy was identified in its tailored-division teaching point during this offline review.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Retain pressure, functional reserve and prior treatment as separate selection facts; do not turn failed medical therapy into an unconditional indication for sphincter division.

record.title: Procedural escalation after late deterioration of sphincter repair
fairness: The long initial improvement followed by gradual deterioration without a new injury makes an old anatomical gap an insufficient reason to repeat reconstruction. Persistent formed-stool leakage despite conservative care then supports an SNM trial rather than immediate permanent implantation or routine bulking injection.

The old defect gives repeat sphincteroplasty a credible attraction; the temporal course is consequential rather than decorative. The task asks for a procedural pathway, so test stimulation appropriately competes with reconstructive and injection pathways at the escalation decision.

No nonmedical wording attack selects SNM. Repeat overlapping sphincteroplasty overlaps the history but cues a distractor, not the key. The standalone case carries the necessary prior repair, response and recurrence sequence.
suggestions: No blocking revision. For clearer clinical specificity in a future version, name the actual conservative measures already tried rather than only conservative care, without inventing doses or durations. Preserve the distinction between test stimulation and permanent implantation.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A prior obstetric ultrasound showed an anterior sphincter defect. With formed stools she can defer defecation and retain stool during activity. Her diary records accidents after sudden urges on days with loose stool. A completed continence-focused rehabilitation course improved voluntary squeeze but not those loose-stool episodes. Psyllium caused persistent bloating and was stopped. Assessment found no fecal loading or infectious or inflammatory cause of the chronic loose stool.
decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment should {patientName} try next for this remaining leakage pattern?

answerChoices.label: Continence biofeedback
answerChoices.rationale: Biofeedback is a genuine continence treatment. Here a completed course improved squeeze while the residual accidents remained tied to loose stools, making stool-directed medication the more useful next trial.

answerChoices.label: Overlapping sphincteroplasty
answerChoices.rationale: A defect can inform repair planning, but the ability to retain formed stool and the current treatment-response pattern argue for addressing stool consistency before proceeding from anatomy to reconstruction.

answerChoices.label: Loperamide therapy
answerChoices.rationale: The residual problem tracks loose-stool urgency despite retained formed-stool control and improved squeeze. A monitored stool-firming medicine is a reasonable next conservative trial after poorly tolerated bulking; the old defect does not by itself require reconstruction.

decisionNodes.explanation: Compare what improved with what still causes accidents. Voluntary squeeze improved and formed stools are retained, whereas loose-stool urgency remains. A monitored loperamide trial targets that residual contributor before an operation based on the old defect; continence biofeedback is not being characterized as evacuation training.

concept.learningObjective: Direct initial continence treatment at the observed stool and evacuation pattern.

record.title: Treating the residual stool-consistency contributor to leakage
clarityIssues: Continence-focused rehabilitation does not specify whether the completed course included instrumented biofeedback or only exercises. This leaves the precise relationship to the biofeedback distractor less clear than it could be, although stool-directed treatment remains best supported by the represented residual pattern.
fairness: The resident must compare retained formed-stool function and improved squeeze against persistent loose-stool urgency, then target the remaining contributor instead of treating the old ultrasound defect as sufficient reason for surgery. Fiber intolerance and the stated assessment of the loose stool support a monitored loperamide trial.

The chosen plan is not merely the only novel option: recognizing why stool consistency matters despite an anatomical defect requires clinical interpretation. Biofeedback is a real continence intervention, and the explanation correctly avoids conflating it with evacuation retraining.

The explanation does not promise cure or prescribe an invented dose. The prior defect, rehabilitation response, diary and current symptom pattern are all supplied in the standalone node. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical keying shortcut was found.
suggestions: No blocking revision. In a future clarification, state the actual completed rehabilitation modality so a resident need not guess whether continence biofeedback has already been tried. Preserve the formed-versus-loose-stool contrast and avoid implying that an old structural defect is irrelevant to long-term management.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: A completed biofeedback course is documented. Current manometry shows anal relaxation during bearing down, and balloon expulsion meets laboratory criteria. The returned contrast-evacuation study shows material retained in an anterior rectal pouch after the rest of the rectum empties; vaginal pressure releases it. Soft-stool evacuation still requires splinting and limits daily activities.
decisionNodes.stem: Which procedure is best supported for {patientName}'s persistent evacuation difficulty?

answerChoices.label: Puborectalis botulinum toxin injection
answerChoices.rationale: Current functional relaxation argues against residual nonrelaxing puborectalis as the treatment target. Injection does not correct the retaining pouch.

answerChoices.label: Stapled transanal rectal resection
answerChoices.rationale: STARR is not recommended for rectocele or internal intussusception because of its complication profile. A relevant anatomical target does not validate every operation directed at it.

answerChoices.label: Native-tissue rectocele repair
answerChoices.rationale: Retention linked to splinting and substantial symptoms supports a repair discussion after functional contributors have been addressed. This does not rank repair routes or prescribe mesh.

decisionNodes.explanation: The returned study links the pouch to incomplete evacuation, rather than merely showing an incidental rectocele. With functional treatment completed and objective coordination improved, native-tissue repair is a reasonable procedural discussion. Puborectalis injection targets persistent nonrelaxation, which is not represented. STARR is not recommended for this indication because of its complication profile; the item does not rank repair routes or prescribe mesh.

record.title: Symptomatic rectocele after successful coordination treatment
fairness: Current relaxation and adequate balloon expulsion reduce the case for further treatment directed at nonrelaxation. Retained contrast that is released by vaginal support then connects the pouch to the persisting disability, supporting discussion of native-tissue rectocele repair.

The item requires both functional reassessment and attribution of residual mechanical obstruction; merely identifying a pouch is insufficient. Botulinum treatment is the wrong physiological target here. STARR is a recognizable procedural competitor, and its adverse-complication teaching point is consistent with the intended comparison; no confident inaccuracy was identified offline.

Native-tissue rectocele repair leaves route selection open, but that is appropriate to the stated repair-versus-other-procedure task; no unsupported choice between vaginal and transanal routes is imposed. None of the options includes a rationale or uniquely cautious wording.

Although the update calls the study returned, it supplies all relevant observations and does not require the previous test-choice node. The case is coherent and answerable on its own. The explanation correctly describes a reasonable procedural discussion rather than guaranteed symptom resolution.
suggestions: No blocking revision. Preserve the contrast-retention/release finding and current coordination results; do not turn a rectocele on static imaging alone into an indication for repair.
