record.title: Biopsy follow-up
fairness: The resident must reconcile the needle/specimen evidence with the displaced clip to identify the actual sampled field, then use multifocal ADH and substantial residual abnormal calcification to choose diagnostic excision rather than further vacuum sampling. Both location and procedure matter.

Posterior-field excision is the defensible best offered plan. The benign-appearing retroareolar calcium and documented acquisition prevent the clip from being a substitute for the target. Repeat posterior vacuum biopsy is the closest credible error; ADH already represented in several foci with substantial residual abnormality favors excision. This does not imply that every ADH diagnosis invariably requires the same treatment.

The two-by-two procedure/location alternatives balance both components, so convergence does not assemble a unique key. No giveaway diagnosis is supplied for a diagnosis task: ADH is appropriately a prerequisite to this management decision.

ADH management and radiologic-pathologic localization are high-yield. The table and complete task stand alone, with no later part or preceding-feedback dependency. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

record.title: Growing breast mass
fairness: The learner must identify the microscopic fat-injury pattern, establish that the solid nodule rather than only its adjacent fluid was represented, and integrate same-target regression before choosing follow-up despite the prior phyllodes history. These observations distinguish postoperative change from an inadequately evaluated recurrent lesion.

Clinical and targeted ultrasound follow-up is the defensible best offered plan. Repeat tissue sampling and excision are plausible reactions to a new nodule after phyllodes, but the representative benign tissue and regressing matched lesion make them less appropriate now. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The numerical size change describes this fictional course rather than a universal threshold. The follow-up option is somewhat longer, but its clinical/ultrasound pairing does not independently reveal the key; all choices are concrete next plans.

Postoperative fat necrosis and imaging-pathology concordance are high-yield. The presentation supplies the prior surgery, aspiration and current biopsy, so this standalone case is coherent without an earlier node. The explanation's mention of fluid cytology is not needed to solve the task.
suggestions: Optional feedback cleanup: omit 'from fluid cytology' unless a cytology result is actually part of the visible history. Keep the distinction between fluid aspiration and representative solid-tissue cores.

record.title: Incidental classic LCIS with a separately explained target
fairness: The resident must identify sclerosing adenosis as the sampled calcification correlate, distinguish incidental classic LCIS from a nonclassic or unexplained target lesion, and choose local follow-up rather than automatic excision.
Imaging follow-up is the best offered local diagnostic plan for this represented, explained site. The explanation correctly separates local diagnostic clearance from future-risk assessment.
The negatives about florid expansion and pleomorphism are decision-critical subtype information, not gratuitous distractor exclusions. Named LCIS is legitimate data in this management task.
The case is self-contained. Its explanation does establish the concordance principle that the later discordance node reuses; that later node needs independent difficulty repair.

record.title: Enlargement after a concordant fibroadenoma core
fairness: The resident must reconcile earlier concordant benign tissue with substantial interval enlargement and contour change, then choose whole-lesion excision over repeating a limited sample or continuing surveillance. Excision is the best offered plan.
The measurements describe this fictional lesion; they are not stated as a universal size or growth threshold.
The update follows the preceding core request and supplies its result, growth and symptom consequence. With the shared presentation it stands alone; prior feedback did not disclose this new decision.

record.title: Persistent breast swelling
fairness: The resident must distinguish residual heterogeneous inflammatory tissue from a recurrent drainable collection, then use matched imaging and clinical regression to choose follow-up rather than immediate core biopsy of every persistent palpable area. The absence of an enclosed fluid space rules out repeat aspiration for a clinically necessary reason; it does not alone choose follow-up over biopsy.

Interval examination and targeted ultrasound is the defensible best offered plan for the improving, non-drainable residual finding. The prior culture-directed treatment and resolved erythema support that course. The explanation requires follow-up through resolution and renewed assessment for progression, rather than dismissing all lactational masses.

The size values describe observed regression rather than a management cutoff. Post-treatment lactational collections versus residual tissue are high-yield. The complete standalone presentation and comparison do not require prior-node results or teaching.
No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation's statement about mammography does not affect the current answer because mammography is not an offered alternative.
suggestions: Optional brevity edit: remove the unrelated final mammography sentence from feedback so the explanation remains focused on the tested residual-lesion decision.

record.title: Breast biopsy review
fairness: The resident must distinguish acquisition through the intended target from pathology that explains the target, then act on the unresolved increasing distortion rather than apply a blanket observation rule for classic LCIS. The histologic label does not itself answer this management question.

Localized surgical excision is a defensible best offered plan after this extensive targeted vacuum acquisition still fails to explain the increasing distortion. Surveillance ignores the discordance. Repeat vacuum sampling is the closest competitor; the already targeted central and radiating sampling makes simply repeating that same plan less persuasive.

Do not generalize the explanation to a prohibition on repeat percutaneous sampling for every discordant biopsy. That broader ranking is context-dependent; this offline review identifies no confident inaccuracy in the narrower presented case.

Concordance and the distinction between incidental classic LCIS and an unexplained imaging target are high-yield. This standalone case restates its current target and does not depend on the earlier calcification case or feedback.
suggestions: Optional brevity edit: the reference to a separate previously sampled calcification group can be removed if this remains a standalone encounter; it does not determine the offered plan. Re-review any changed exact version.

record.title: Persistent breast swelling
fairness: The resident must distinguish protected direct feeding from the separate contaminated collection pathway, then translate both exposure assessments into the plan for the next feed and this specific bottle. MRSA does not automatically imply that both routes have the same disposition.

Continue direct feeding under the described protected arrangement and discard the exposed collection is the defensible best offered answer for this healthy term infant. Visible clarity does not undo the documented drainage-to-flange-to-milk contact. The explanation appropriately limits the discard instruction to this collection and calls for cleaning and reassessment before reuse.

The four choices form a balanced two-by-two matrix with no component-majority or length cue. The contamination makes the bottle decision straightforward, but does not reveal whether protected direct breastfeeding should continue. Both route-specific observations remain necessary to choose the full plan.

Breastfeeding management during a treated breast abscess is high-yield. The standalone case specifies the infant context, wound protection and actual collection exposure without dependence on a previous abscess node. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; this editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Suspicious palpable finding despite adequate negative imaging
fairness: The update establishes actual ultrasound coverage, then supplies a hard irregular palpable focus and dynamic skin dimpling. The resident must distinguish adequate imaging from resolution of clinical suspicion and select tissue sampling.
Palpation-guided core is the best offered next diagnostic plan; negative imaging does not justify observation of this examination finding, and MRI need not precede tissue assessment.

The current update states the new examination and repeat-ultrasound result; the shared presentation supplies the earlier mammogram. This is coherent and independently answerable with those visible fields. The preceding explanation teaches coverage, not the new clinical-imaging discordance decision.

record.title: Biopsy follow-up
fairness: The resident must interpret ongoing regular menses as a relevant limitation on the aromatase-inhibitor option, then apply the prior proximal DVT to tamoxifen risk reduction. The combination changes the otherwise tempting preventive prescription after ADH; neither observation by itself resolves the entire offered set.

Withholding the offered endocrine drugs while continuing surveillance is the defensible best answer. Completion of anticoagulation does not erase the DVT history for this preventive tamoxifen decision. The explanation appropriately addresses prevention rather than importing treatment rules for established invasive cancer.

The no-medication choice is structurally different from the two prescriptions, but it is a concrete plan at the same decision stage, and wording alone does not establish its correctness. Menstrual and thrombosis observations are decision-critical, not gratuitous distractor exclusions.

Risk reduction after atypia and endocrine-agent eligibility are high-yield. The standalone presentation supplies the excision result and makes surveillance common to all choices. No previous ADH node or explanation is needed; no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

record.title: Pure FEA after retrieval of the calcification target
fairness: The resident must reconcile calcifications in the specimen and lesion with the absence of a residual group, then distinguish pure FEA from associated higher-risk atypia before choosing follow-up.

For the specifically described pure, explained and retrieved target, mammographic follow-up is the best offered plan; repeat vacuum sampling lacks a residual target and automatic excision is not compelled by FEA alone.

The explanation limits the inference to this sampled target and does not extend follow-up to associated atypia or an unsampled field. Contemporary local-policy applicability still requires named clinical sign-off; this editorial PASS is not that approval.
The case is self-contained and has no preceding-answer scaffold.

record.title: Biopsy follow-up
fairness: The resident must reconcile the needle/specimen evidence with the displaced clip to identify the actual sampled field, then use multifocal ADH and substantial residual abnormal calcification to choose diagnostic excision rather than further vacuum sampling. Both location and procedure matter.

Posterior-field excision is the defensible best offered plan. The benign-appearing retroareolar calcium and documented acquisition prevent the clip from being a substitute for the target. Repeat posterior vacuum biopsy is the closest credible error; ADH already represented in several foci with substantial residual abnormality favors excision. This does not imply that every ADH diagnosis invariably requires the same treatment.

The two-by-two procedure/location alternatives balance both components, so convergence does not assemble a unique key. No giveaway diagnosis is supplied for a diagnosis task: ADH is appropriately a prerequisite to this management decision.

ADH management and radiologic-pathologic localization are high-yield. The table and complete task stand alone, with no later part or preceding-feedback dependency. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

record.title: Biopsy follow-up
fairness: The resident must interpret ongoing regular menses as a relevant limitation on the aromatase-inhibitor option, then apply the prior proximal DVT to tamoxifen risk reduction. The combination changes the otherwise tempting preventive prescription after ADH; neither observation by itself resolves the entire offered set.

Withholding the offered endocrine drugs while continuing surveillance is the defensible best answer. Completion of anticoagulation does not erase the DVT history for this preventive tamoxifen decision. The explanation appropriately addresses prevention rather than importing treatment rules for established invasive cancer.

The no-medication choice is structurally different from the two prescriptions, but it is a concrete plan at the same decision stage, and wording alone does not establish its correctness. Menstrual and thrombosis observations are decision-critical, not gratuitous distractor exclusions.

Risk reduction after atypia and endocrine-agent eligibility are high-yield. The standalone presentation supplies the excision result and makes surveillance common to all choices. No previous ADH node or explanation is needed; no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

record.title: Incidental classic LCIS with a separately explained target
fairness: The resident must identify sclerosing adenosis as the sampled calcification correlate, distinguish incidental classic LCIS from a nonclassic or unexplained target lesion, and choose local follow-up rather than automatic excision.
Imaging follow-up is the best offered local diagnostic plan for this represented, explained site. The explanation correctly separates local diagnostic clearance from future-risk assessment.
The negatives about florid expansion and pleomorphism are decision-critical subtype information, not gratuitous distractor exclusions. Named LCIS is legitimate data in this management task.
The case is self-contained. Its explanation does establish the concordance principle that the later discordance node reuses; that later node needs independent difficulty repair.

record.title: Breast biopsy review
fairness: The resident must distinguish acquisition through the intended target from pathology that explains the target, then act on the unresolved increasing distortion rather than apply a blanket observation rule for classic LCIS. The histologic label does not itself answer this management question.

Localized surgical excision is a defensible best offered plan after this extensive targeted vacuum acquisition still fails to explain the increasing distortion. Surveillance ignores the discordance. Repeat vacuum sampling is the closest competitor; the already targeted central and radiating sampling makes simply repeating that same plan less persuasive.

Do not generalize the explanation to a prohibition on repeat percutaneous sampling for every discordant biopsy. That broader ranking is context-dependent; this offline review identifies no confident inaccuracy in the narrower presented case.

Concordance and the distinction between incidental classic LCIS and an unexplained imaging target are high-yield. This standalone case restates its current target and does not depend on the earlier calcification case or feedback.
suggestions: Optional brevity edit: the reference to a separate previously sampled calcification group can be removed if this remains a standalone encounter; it does not determine the offered plan. Re-review any changed exact version.

These observations distinguish postoperative change from an inadequately evaluated recurrent lesion.

Clinical and targeted ultrasound follow-up is the defensible best offered plan. Repeat tissue sampling and excision are plausible reactions to a new nodule after phyllodes, but the representative benign tissue and regressing matched lesion make them less appropriate now. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The numerical size change describes this fictional course rather than a universal threshold. The follow-up option is somewhat longer, but its clinical/ultrasound pairing does not independently reveal the key; all choices are concrete next plans.

Postoperative fat necrosis and imaging-pathology concordance are high-yield. The presentation supplies the prior surgery, aspiration and current biopsy, so this standalone case is coherent without an earlier node. The explanation's mention of fluid cytology is not needed to solve the task.

The absence of an enclosed fluid space rules out repeat aspiration for a clinically necessary reason; it does not alone choose follow-up over biopsy.

Interval examination and targeted ultrasound is the defensible best offered plan for the improving, non-drainable residual finding. The prior culture-directed treatment and resolved erythema support that course. The explanation requires follow-up through resolution and renewed assessment for progression, rather than dismissing all lactational masses.

The size values describe observed regression rather than a management cutoff. Post-treatment lactational collections versus residual tissue are high-yield. The complete standalone presentation and comparison do not require prior-node results or teaching.

record.title: Persistent breast swelling
fairness: The resident must distinguish protected direct feeding from the separate contaminated collection pathway, then translate both exposure assessments into the plan for the next feed and this specific bottle. MRSA does not automatically imply that both routes have the same disposition.

Continue direct feeding under the described protected arrangement and discard the exposed collection is the defensible best offered answer for this healthy term infant. Visible clarity does not undo the documented drainage-to-flange-to-milk contact. The explanation appropriately limits the discard instruction to this collection and calls for cleaning and reassessment before reuse.

The four choices form a balanced two-by-two matrix with no component-majority or length cue. The contamination makes the bottle decision straightforward, but does not reveal whether protected direct breastfeeding should continue. Both route-specific observations remain necessary to choose the full plan.

Breastfeeding management during a treated breast abscess is high-yield. The standalone case specifies the infant context, wound protection and actual collection exposure without dependence on a previous abscess node. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; this editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Gastroschisis: reduction-related physiological compromise
fairness: The reversible changes during reduction establish that returning all the bowel, rather than simply the choice of fascial suture, produces compromise. The resident then distinguishes gradual reduction from two methods of primary closure.

The sutureless option is a credible competing error: changing the covering technique does not necessarily resolve the intolerance to full reduction already demonstrated. Staged reduction with a silo is the best supported offered plan.
No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation does not invent a pressure threshold or require one to infer the relevant physiology.

Repeated 'Primary' in two alternatives does not independently select the key without understanding the reduction response. All choices are comparably concise operative plans, and the raw anatomical description is appropriate.
Standalone case: baseline physiology, trial response and reversal are supplied. No previous diagnosis task or feedback is needed.
suggestions: Preserve the improvement when the reduction is released; it makes the causal inference consequential.
Keep the explanation focused on intolerance of reduction rather than implying that every gastroschisis requires a silo or that sutureless closure is generally inappropriate.

record.title: Intussusception: partial reduction with continued stability
fairness: The resident must distinguish incomplete but progressive reduction from failed nonoperative treatment, then integrate the reassuring reassessment to choose another supervised attempt rather than operation. Residual intussusception prevents observation from being equivalent to successful reduction.

A delayed repeat enema is the best supported offered plan. Trapped fluid makes failure a credible concern but does not itself establish perforation or mandate surgery. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The child's older age raises concern for a lead point but does not by itself invalidate another reduction attempt. The exhibit does not establish that a lead point has been excluded; feedback should not imply that it has.
The choices are parallel care plans; there is no convincing nonmedical wording shortcut. Naming the established diagnosis is legitimate because the task concerns response and next management.
Standalone case: the initial diagnosis, procedure outcome and current assessment are all supplied. No earlier explanation is necessary.
suggestions: Retain partial anatomical progress, residual disease and the reassessment together; removing any of these would weaken the actual decision.
A minor copyedit would change 'a 8-year-old girl' to 'an 8-year-old girl'. Preserve the exact independently reviewed version unless a new version is authorized.
Clinical sign-off should retain the distinction between selecting another supervised attempt here and declaring that repeat enemas are appropriate indefinitely or that a lead point is absent.

record.title: Meconium obstruction: incomplete but progressive contrast decompression
fairness: The microcolon/ileal pellet pattern and contrast passage establish the relevant obstruction pattern. The learner must then distinguish useful partial response from completed decompression or treatment failure and apply the current complication assessment.

Another supervised therapeutic contrast attempt is the best supported offered plan. Persistent pellets and bilious drainage make passive observation a less adequate plan; anatomical progress and maintained physiology make immediate operative decompression less compelling.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation appropriately avoids a universal number of attempts or mandatory interval. It should not be read as permission to repeat a hyperosmolar intervention without continued fluid management and monitoring.

The complication negatives are clinically necessary eligibility information. Although they weaken surgery, residual obstruction still makes escalation a credible error after an incompletely successful first attempt. There is no decisive nonmedical phrase match or option-length outlier.
Standalone case: initial treatment, procedure findings and postprocedure condition are supplied without relying on a preceding diagnosis or treatment answer.
suggestions: Retain residual obstruction as well as procedural progress; either observation alone would flatten the decision.
Keep the explanation explicit that the repeat procedure is supervised and accompanied by continued resuscitation/monitoring. Do not add unverified dosing, attempt counts or intervals.
Do not infer cystic-fibrosis confirmation from this vignette or add it as an established diagnosis without separate evidence.

record.title: NEC: persistent loop during improving clinical course
fairness: The persistent loop creates a credible temptation to operate. The learner must assess its significance alongside improving abdominal findings and decreasing organ support, then choose continued monitored medical treatment rather than an invasive intervention.

The absence of free gas alone would not settle the decision. The concurrent clinical trajectory makes continued nonoperative treatment the best offered plan. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The key is somewhat longer than the two procedure labels, but not an explanatory or comprehensiveness outlier. Improvement is decision-critical evidence, not merely an authored statement that surgery is unnecessary.

Standalone case: the known NEC diagnosis, current treatment and relevant serial findings are supplied. The explanation appropriately calls for close reassessment rather than treating the fixed loop as harmless.
suggestions: Preserve both the concerning radiographic observation and the improving clinical trajectory. Do not turn this into the false rule that absence of pneumoperitoneum excludes a surgical indication.
Keep difficulty qualitative and retain clinician review of the exact clinical course; this editorial PASS is not clinical sign-off.

record.title: Preterm infant hernia: respiratory risk and repair timing
fairness: The learner must establish that this is a currently reducible hernia without an acute incarceration episode, then weigh ongoing respiratory disease against the risk of waiting. Planned repair after neonatal hospitalization is the best supported offered plan in this specific context.

Repair before discharge is a credible competing plan. Surveillance for spontaneous resolution is a weaker alternative, but represents confusing an inguinal hernia with a self-resolving pediatric groin condition; it does not create a second defensible key.

Reliable follow-up and warning-sign education favor the delayed strategy, but are legitimate safety conditions for that choice rather than unnecessary permission. Removing them would weaken the stated basis for waiting.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation appropriately avoids an exact age threshold, indefinite observation or a universal delay rule. The precise contemporary timing evidence was not freshly verified in this offline review.

Standalone case: gestational age, current chronological age, reducibility, respiratory support and follow-up context are supplied. The arithmetic is coherent, and no preceding hernia-diagnosis item is needed.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between a planned deferred operation and surveillance for spontaneous resolution.
Keep respiratory status, reducibility and follow-up reliability together when using this exact timing key; do not generalize it to an incarcerated hernia or unreliable access to reassessment.
Editorial PASS does not resolve any separate clinical timing hold or grant clinical approval. Preserve the exact version pending the named clinician's decision.

record.title: Wilms tumor: high caval extension under a COG pathway
fairness: The imaging defines continuous venous extension and its upper extent. The resident must apply that extent as an exception to the usual upfront nephrectomy approach, then preserve the histology-before-chemotherapy sequence under the explicitly stated COG framework.

Biopsy followed by preoperative chemotherapy and reassessment for resection is the defensible best offered sequence. Immediate nephrectomy with thrombectomy is a credible default-pathway error; chemotherapy before tissue diagnosis imports a different pathway. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified from the supplied text.

The exact hepatic-vein-level boundary and biopsy requirement are protocol-specific clinical claims. They were not freshly source-verified under the no-network restriction; this editorial assessment does not independently certify current COG criteria.

Naming Wilms tumor and the protocol is legitimate for a management-exception task. The key is not uniquely qualified or longer in a way that selects it; all choices are concrete tumor-directed sequences.

Standalone case: anatomy and protocol are present without another Noah item. Do not compose this directly with the separate upfront-nephrectomy node without supplying a coherent treatment interval and operative context.
suggestions: Preserve the exact thrombus extent and the named pathway; making either vague would create a real fairness problem.
Obtain named clinical confirmation of the exact protocol boundary and histologic sequence before promotion from needs_clinician_review.
Do not add unrelated metastatic findings or a diagnosis-recognition task merely to increase difficulty; the exception and treatment sequence already create the consequential reasoning.

record.title: Intussusception: partial reduction with continued stability
fairness: The resident must distinguish incomplete but progressive reduction from failed nonoperative treatment, then integrate the reassuring reassessment to choose another supervised attempt rather than operation. Residual intussusception prevents observation from being equivalent to successful reduction.

A delayed repeat enema is the best supported offered plan. Trapped fluid makes failure a credible concern but does not itself establish perforation or mandate surgery. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The child's older age raises concern for a lead point but does not by itself invalidate another reduction attempt. The exhibit does not establish that a lead point has been excluded; feedback should not imply that it has.
The choices are parallel care plans; there is no convincing nonmedical wording shortcut. Naming the established diagnosis is legitimate because the task concerns response and next management.
Standalone case: the initial diagnosis, procedure outcome and current assessment are all supplied. No earlier explanation is necessary.
suggestions: Retain partial anatomical progress, residual disease and the reassessment together; removing any of these would weaken the actual decision.
A minor copyedit would change 'a 8-year-old girl' to 'an 8-year-old girl'. Preserve the exact independently reviewed version unless a new version is authorized.
Clinical sign-off should retain the distinction between selecting another supervised attempt here and declaring that repeat enemas are appropriate indefinitely or that a lead point is absent.

record.title: NEC: persistent loop during improving clinical course
fairness: The persistent loop creates a credible temptation to operate. The learner must assess its significance alongside improving abdominal findings and decreasing organ support, then choose continued monitored medical treatment rather than an invasive intervention.

The absence of free gas alone would not settle the decision. The concurrent clinical trajectory makes continued nonoperative treatment the best offered plan. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The key is somewhat longer than the two procedure labels, but not an explanatory or comprehensiveness outlier. Improvement is decision-critical evidence, not merely an authored statement that surgery is unnecessary.

Standalone case: the known NEC diagnosis, current treatment and relevant serial findings are supplied. The explanation appropriately calls for close reassessment rather than treating the fixed loop as harmless.
suggestions: Preserve both the concerning radiographic observation and the improving clinical trajectory. Do not turn this into the false rule that absence of pneumoperitoneum excludes a surgical indication.
Keep difficulty qualitative and retain clinician review of the exact clinical course; this editorial PASS is not clinical sign-off.

answerChoices.label: Staged reduction with a silo
answerChoices.rationale: The response ties full reduction to respiratory and perfusion compromise. A silo permits gradual reduction while protecting the bowel; a different covering technique does not by itself solve inadequate abdominal capacity.

answerChoices.label: Primary sutured fascial closure
answerChoices.rationale: Completing the same full reduction under tension would recreate the observed compromise. Bowel viability before reduction does not establish that the abdomen can safely contain it now.

answerChoices.label: Primary sutureless cord closure
answerChoices.rationale: Avoiding sutures does not remove the pressure effect of returning all bowel to an inadequate abdominal domain. Primary sutureless closure still requires safe reduction.

record.title: Gastroschisis: reduction-related physiological compromise
fairness: The reversible changes during reduction establish that returning all the bowel, rather than simply the choice of fascial suture, produces compromise. The resident then distinguishes gradual reduction from two methods of primary closure.

The sutureless option is a credible competing error: changing the covering technique does not necessarily resolve the intolerance to full reduction already demonstrated. Staged reduction with a silo is the best supported offered plan.
No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation does not invent a pressure threshold or require one to infer the relevant physiology.

Repeated 'Primary' in two alternatives does not independently select the key without understanding the reduction response. All choices are comparably concise operative plans, and the raw anatomical description is appropriate.
Standalone case: baseline physiology, trial response and reversal are supplied. No previous diagnosis task or feedback is needed.
suggestions: Preserve the improvement when the reduction is released; it makes the causal inference consequential.
Keep the explanation focused on intolerance of reduction rather than implying that every gastroschisis requires a silo or that sutureless closure is generally inappropriate.

record.title: Meconium obstruction: incomplete but progressive contrast decompression
fairness: The microcolon/ileal pellet pattern and contrast passage establish the relevant obstruction pattern. The learner must then distinguish useful partial response from completed decompression or treatment failure and apply the current complication assessment.

Another supervised therapeutic contrast attempt is the best supported offered plan. Persistent pellets and bilious drainage make passive observation a less adequate plan; anatomical progress and maintained physiology make immediate operative decompression less compelling.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation appropriately avoids a universal number of attempts or mandatory interval. It should not be read as permission to repeat a hyperosmolar intervention without continued fluid management and monitoring.

The complication negatives are clinically necessary eligibility information. Although they weaken surgery, residual obstruction still makes escalation a credible error after an incompletely successful first attempt. There is no decisive nonmedical phrase match or option-length outlier.
Standalone case: initial treatment, procedure findings and postprocedure condition are supplied without relying on a preceding diagnosis or treatment answer.
suggestions: Retain residual obstruction as well as procedural progress; either observation alone would flatten the decision.
Keep the explanation explicit that the repeat procedure is supervised and accompanied by continued resuscitation/monitoring. Do not add unverified dosing, attempt counts or intervals.
Do not infer cystic-fibrosis confirmation from this vignette or add it as an established diagnosis without separate evidence.

answerChoices.label: Biopsy, preoperative chemotherapy, then resection
answerChoices.rationale: The caval extension reaches the hepatic veins, an exception to the usual up-front nephrectomy pathway. Under the stated framework, obtain histology and use preoperative chemotherapy before reassessing resection. The usual caution about biopsy upstaging does not erase this exception.

answerChoices.label: Nephrectomy with thrombectomy, then chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Up-front nephrectomy is usual for a typical resectable unilateral mass, but the superior caval extent changes the preferred sequence here. Localized staging does not by itself establish that immediate thrombectomy is the right first step.

answerChoices.label: Preoperative chemotherapy, then resection histology
answerChoices.rationale: This sequence postpones the tissue diagnosis until resection. The named COG pathway for this exception calls for biopsy with preoperative therapy; a different treatment framework should not be silently substituted.

answerChoices.label: Plan repair after the neonatal hospitalization
answerChoices.rationale: For a currently reducible hernia in a very preterm infant with ongoing respiratory disease, a delayed planned repair with follow-up is reasonable. The timing balances respiratory risk against incarceration during the wait; it is not indefinite observation or a universal age rule.

answerChoices.label: Plan repair before neonatal discharge

record.title: Preterm infant hernia: respiratory risk and repair timing
fairness: The learner must establish that this is a currently reducible hernia without an acute incarceration episode, then weigh ongoing respiratory disease against the risk of waiting. Planned repair after neonatal hospitalization is the best supported offered plan in this specific context.

Repair before discharge is a credible competing plan. Surveillance for spontaneous resolution is a weaker alternative, but represents confusing an inguinal hernia with a self-resolving pediatric groin condition; it does not create a second defensible key.

Reliable follow-up and warning-sign education favor the delayed strategy, but are legitimate safety conditions for that choice rather than unnecessary permission. Removing them would weaken the stated basis for waiting.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation appropriately avoids an exact age threshold, indefinite observation or a universal delay rule. The precise contemporary timing evidence was not freshly verified in this offline review.

Standalone case: gestational age, current chronological age, reducibility, respiratory support and follow-up context are supplied. The arithmetic is coherent, and no preceding hernia-diagnosis item is needed.
suggestions: Retain the distinction between a planned deferred operation and surveillance for spontaneous resolution.
Keep respiratory status, reducibility and follow-up reliability together when using this exact timing key; do not generalize it to an incarcerated hernia or unreliable access to reassessment.
Editorial PASS does not resolve any separate clinical timing hold or grant clinical approval. Preserve the exact version pending the named clinician's decision.

record.title: Interpret a burn surface culture in context
fairness: Continuing the current local regimen is the best offered plan: interpret a surface isolate against objectively improving wound behavior, then decide whether systemic treatment is indicated rather than selecting an antibiotic from susceptibilities.

Ciprofloxacin and cefepime are meaningful temptations because the report names susceptibility, while the wound trajectory and lack of newly described surrounding/systemic illness favor local care. The susceptibility language supports the distractors rather than uniquely cueing the key.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation appropriately calls for reassessment with deterioration rather than claiming a surface culture can never matter. Standalone chronology and task are complete.
suggestions: Retain the clinical trend and the surface-specimen distinction. If revising wording, replace 'surrounding skin are unchanged' with the actual relevant examination so readers need not infer that the previous baseline was benign.

record.title: Release a deep compartment after electrical injury
fairness: Forearm fasciotomy is the best offered procedure: evolving tension, passive-stretch pain and motor change identify a threatened deep compartment, then pliable skin and the electrical mechanism distinguish fascial decompression from eschar release.
Maintained Doppler signals are a useful competing observation and do not make thrombectomy preferable or exclude a compartment emergency. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The previous node establishes muscle injury but does not name the later procedure. The acquired examination changes the decision and contains sufficient current findings to stand alone with the shared presentation.
suggestions: Retain the pulse-versus-compartment distinction and the skin examination. Do not add a pressure cutoff or require a pressure measurement to manufacture difficulty in this clinically overt scenario.

record.title: Reassess oliguria after electrical-injury resuscitation
fairness: Reducing crystalloid while reassessing perfusion and balance is the single best offered direction. Interpret persistent oliguria in the context of recovered systemic perfusion, excluded bladder retention and accumulating respiratory/volume findings; then reverse continued fluid escalation despite the legitimate initial concern for pigment-associated renal injury.

Increasing fluid is a credible error because the patient has substantial muscle injury and worsening urine output; maintaining it is a credible failure to respond to the new overload evidence. The three labels differ only in infusion direction and provide no length, qualification, convergence or wording-overlap shortcut.

The task asks for direction, not an exact prescription. A current infusion rate would be needed to calculate a new rate, but its absence does not undermine the relative choice among increase, maintain and reduce in this stated course. No new fluid or urine-output threshold is required to solve it.

The explanation properly limits its conclusion: a change in crystalloid direction does not by itself determine a diuretic or dialysis decision. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The card supplies the earlier resuscitation and later review within one coherent standalone node; named patient, age/sex and complete task are present.
Electrical injury, occult muscle damage and reassessment of resuscitation rather than blindly chasing urine output are high-yield. The strong overload pattern makes this moderate, not hard.
suggestions: Retain both the initial reason to give fluid and the subsequent contradictory volume/perfusion evidence. Preserve the narrow infusion-direction task and urgent renal assessment.
Optional brevity improvement: place the serial output, weight and balance in a compact record, without adding an interpretive heading such as 'fluid overload.'

record.title: Start enteral support after burn resuscitation
fairness: A low-rate gastric enteral start is the best offered plan: infer improving perfusion from the support/lactate/urine trajectory, then distinguish quiet bowel sounds from a reason to withhold enteral nutrition.

Primary PN and waiting for stool represent credible common errors, although the latter is the weaker option. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the item does not claim a universal hour, pressor limit or calorie target.

The first feeding decision is coherent and does not reveal the later deterioration. With the shared presentation, its task is complete. The explanation's perfusion emphasis appropriately scaffolds, but does not answer, the later update.
suggestions: Keep the physiologic trajectory and cautious start. If polishing the presentation, identify the drainage as gastric for precision without adding unnecessary details or cutoffs.

record.title: Select a feeding route after perfusion recovery
fairness: Low-rate postpyloric enteral feeding is the single best offered route in the stated current assessment. First distinguish the recovered perfusion/abdominal course from the earlier unsafe feeding episode; then interpret persistent vomiting and large gastric aspirates despite a prokinetic as a gastric-tolerance problem rather than failure of the entire enteral route.

Repeating gastric feeding is tempting because it was previously tolerated; parenteral nutrition is tempting after repeated gastric failure and the alarming earlier abdominal episode. The acquired course, ongoing inability to eat and failed prokinetic trial make postpyloric access the best remaining offered route. The low-rate qualifier is shared by both enteral choices and does not uniquely mark the key.

The clinical review's absence of current ischemic concern is a supplied safety assessment, not proof that normal lactate or a benign examination alone excludes ischemia. Keeping a clear assessment of this issue is necessary after the prior bloody drainage and shock. Do not remove it merely to make the item harder.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. I have not independently verified the adequacy of the unspecified prokinetic regimen or the evidentiary basis of the exact aspirate examples offline; the item does not ask for a dose or a numerical cutoff, and vomiting plus persistent large aspirates supplies the intended intolerance finding. Exact clinical wording remains subject to named clinician review.

The sequential course is fully supplied and coherent as one standalone record review; the earlier episode is not silently reinterpreted as safe feeding. The named patient, demographics, short complaint and complete task are present. Enteral eligibility, gastric intolerance and route escalation are high-yield, with moderate two-step application rather than hard discrimination.
suggestions: Retain the earlier safety warnings, explicit current assessment and current failure of gastric delivery after a prokinetic. Avoid introducing a fixed restart interval or treating the reported aspirate values as a universal threshold.

Optional precision improvement at clinical sign-off: name the actual prokinetic treatment and relevant evaluation findings if they are documented and source-supported; do not invent a regimen or claim that one negative finding excludes ischemia.

record.title: Adjust fluids to the acquired response
fairness: Reduce crystalloid with reassessment is the best offered direction: interpret urine output relative to the 70-kg patient and current perfusion, then weigh the improving resuscitation markers against increasing edema.

Stable pressure, falling lactate, patent drainage and the excluded alternative causes of high output make the trend interpretable without inventing an exact rate reduction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The new update is consequential and coherent after the starting-rate calculation. It does not require recalling which numerical answer was previously chosen; current weight, response and task are available in the presentation/update.
suggestions: Retain the direction-only choices and reassessment. Do not turn this into a universal urine-output or percentage-reduction rule.

record.title: Choose local care versus transfer after a scald
fairness: Local wound follow-up with burn-service consultation is the best offered disposition: distinguish the small blistered dermal component from the larger intact erythematous area, then incorporate wound-care tolerance and reliable follow-up. Admission based on the combined visible area is a credible error.

The analgesia and follow-up observations establish a relevant care constraint rather than merely announce outpatient eligibility. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Standalone item; the task is complete when separated from the presentation.
suggestions: Retain the depth-versus-area distinction and concrete wound-care observations. Difficulty is a qualitative prediction, not demonstrated performance. This offline editorial PASS is not source verification or clinical approval.

record.title: Localize and address post-fire airway obstruction
fairness: Flexible bronchoscopy is the single best offered next procedure. First interpret the peak-pressure rise with unchanged plateau during valid passive measurements as predominantly increased resistance; then integrate tube patency/position, particulate material and focal volume loss to select inspection and clearance of the lower airway.

Tube exchange represents mislocalizing resistance to the endotracheal tube; thoracostomy represents treating a pleural cause of an acute ventilatory change. The supplied tube and pleural observations appropriately discriminate urgent alternatives. These are medically meaningful negatives, not a plain-language announcement that the distractors are wrong.

A freely passing suction catheter does not absolutely exclude every tube-related problem, and pleural sliding only informs the regions assessed. Nevertheless, the full supplied pattern and adequate current oxygenation make bronchoscopy the best of these choices. The explanation does not require an absolute exclusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The options are concise named procedures with comparable specificity. No diagnostic label, key-only task term, explanatory option or component-convergence cue was found. General airway mechanics are applied to a burn-specific particulate-obstruction problem, a high-yield resident decision.

The prior intubation is supplied as a completed event, so airway stabilization need not be reconstructed from another question. The retrospective record is coherent and independently answerable; the named patient, demographics and complete task are present. No separate image or exhibit is promised.
suggestions: Retain the conditions making plateau pressure interpretable, the current tube assessment and acquired lobar findings. Avoid adding an 'airway cast' diagnosis or a pre-answer statement that bronchoscopy is needed.
This is a moderate applied item; the readily discriminating observations do not justify a hard label. Runtime testing/procedure wait presentation was not assessed from these text-only review fields.

record.title: Choose empiric antidote treatment after a fire
fairness: Immediate hydroxocobalamin is the best offered plan: infer possible cyanide toxicity from the fire exposure, collapse and persistent marked lactate elevation, then account for concurrent CO exposure and hypotension when ranking hydroxocobalamin against nitrite/thiosulfate.

The antidote alternatives are clinically related; awaiting confirmation represents a consequential sequencing error. The send-out assay context is relevant to empiric treatment rather than a generic permission statement.

The explanation appropriately avoids a universal lactate cutoff or an absolute ban on nitrites. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this offline review; comparative antidote evidence and exact clinical sign-off remain for the clinician. Standalone and complete.
suggestions: Retain both the mixed-exposure evidence and the hemodynamic course. Do not turn the constructed lactate value into a diagnostic threshold or imply all smoke exposures require antidote treatment.

record.title: Apply regional depth to an excision plan
fairness: Planning excision and coverage of the central region is the best offered extent: interpret the repeated central findings alongside the advancing epithelial edge, then avoid applying a whole-wound operative or conservative plan.
The options test a meaningful regional consequence rather than merely naming burn depth. Whole-wound excision and continued dressings are recognizable over- and undertreatment errors.

The central observations support deeper injury but do not distinguish every possible depth with certainty. The wording asks for surgical planning, not an exact operative day or an unconditional claim that all similar wounds require immediate excision.

The first node establishes the operative-field decision without teaching the later donor-limited coverage material. The later operative findings appropriately need to establish bed readiness separately. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the planning wording, serial examination and independently healing peripheral region. Avoid upgrading these observations to an unsupported exact depth or fixed operation deadline.

record.title: Reconcile burn extent and the resuscitation clock
fairness: The supplied worksheet yields 22% dermal-burn TBSA; 3 x 70 x 22 = 4620 mL; half is 2310 mL; subtracting 800 leaves 1510 mL over the remaining four hours, or 377.5 rounded to 378 mL/hour. Exactly one offered answer matches.

693 mL/hour results from including the additional 12% intact erythema; 189 results from spreading the remaining first allocation over eight hours. Both are interpretable errors rather than numerical outliers.

The worksheet explicitly fixes the protocol; the explanation correctly limits the calculation to that worksheet rather than claiming a universal starting coefficient. First node of a coherent fluid sequence; it does not disclose the later response-based adjustment.
suggestions: Retain the explicit local worksheet and rounding instruction. This is burn-resuscitation arithmetic, not a statistics item subject to the single-skill statistics exception.

record.title: Reassess a regionally changing hand burn
fairness: A new burn-surgical assessment is best: worsening central blanching and touch response must be reconciled with less overall pain and epithelialization at the edge, then used to change the existing plan.

Continuing the previously prescribed plan is a credible error. Emergency eschar release is a weaker distractor because no circumferential restriction or distal perfusion deterioration is described, but it does not introduce an alternative defensible key.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The serial exhibit materially changes the decision; this is a standalone case rather than a later node relying on unseen feedback.
suggestions: Preserve the regional trajectory and misleading subjective improvement. If strengthening the third option, use a clinically plausible competing response to the changed wound without removing circulation information.

record.title: Prepare the burn bed and select staged coverage
fairness: Completing the necessary tangential excision and applying cadaveric allograft is the single best offered plan. The learner must interpret the central recipient bed independently of the bleeding margin, then select coverage using the still-open donor surfaces. Misreading either surface changes one consequential part of the operation.

The four choices form a balanced two-by-two set: each excision level and each coverage type appears twice. The key cannot be assembled from majority components, and all labels have comparable length, specificity and grammatical form.

The recipient-bed observations support further removal of the described adherent nonviable layer. The donor map supplies a real limit on immediate autografting rather than merely saying 'autograft unavailable.' Equipment availability does not provide a donor surface. The distractors represent using a partly prepared bed or choosing definitive coverage without a usable donor site.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation avoids inventing a donor-healing interval or fixed allograft deadline. The exact depth/extent of intraoperative excision still requires clinical judgment; the item asks for the staged strategy, not an unsupported measurement.

Burn excision, recipient-bed viability and temporary versus definitive coverage are high-yield. The two observations are fairly explicit, so this is moderate rather than hard. The later operation follows coherently from the original wound description, and all information needed for this singleton is present without prior feedback. Patient, age/sex and task are clear.
suggestions: Retain the balanced option matrix and separate recipient/donor observations. Do not replace them with labels such as 'inadequate bed' or 'no usable donors,' which would supply the interpretation.

Optional shortening: reduce the earlier peripheral-healing narrative if it has no role beyond establishing the previously observed wound; preserve the central-versus-margin distinction at the actual operation.

record.title: Recognize restrictive chest eschar
fairness: Thoracic escharotomy is the best offered procedure: simultaneous peak/plateau pressure rise during passive ventilation indicates a compliance problem, and the circumferential chest burn with poor excursion localizes a plausible restrictive cause.

The tube-patency and bilateral pleural findings are relevant checks against the offered alternatives. These are clinical observations requiring interpretation, not a diagnosis label or explanatory option.

The earlier limb-node explanation primes the general eschar-release principle and likely lowers difficulty, but it does not teach the pressure interpretation. The later update supplies its own current findings and can be solved without the earlier answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the passive-ventilation and inspiratory-hold details; they make the pressure comparison fair. Do not rate this as an unprimed hard item when shown immediately after limb escharotomy.
Remove the final explanation sentence about procedures not occurring in the founder's clinic if editing feedback; it adds no clinical reasoning.

record.title: Relieve restrictive thermal eschar
fairness: Forearm escharotomy followed by reassessment is the single best offered immediate intervention: first interpret worsening unilateral distal perfusion despite recovered systemic perfusion and external-pressure measures, then select the constraining tissue layer and release sequence.

Escharotomy versus fasciotomy is a consequential, commonly tested distinction. Arterial exploration is a weaker distractor, but reduced distal signals can tempt a learner to treat primary arterial pathology rather than external restriction. All options name parallel procedures with the same reassessment clause; no unique wording match, explanatory key or convergence shortcut was found.

The absence of crush/electrical injury does not prove that deep compartment syndrome is impossible. The item does not need that absolute: circumferential deep thermal injury supports initial eschar release, and the explanation explicitly allows deeper decompression when demonstrated or when perfusion fails to recover. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The outside-record timeline, named patient and age/sex are sufficient to answer independently. There is only one current scored node; no preceding answer is required. The phrase 'first decision below' and chest-burn detail are residual framing, not a decision-changing ambiguity.
suggestions: Retain failed external-pressure measures, the local-versus-systemic comparison and reassessment after release; do not replace them with an announced diagnosis.
Optional editorial cleanup: remove 'first' from 'first decision below' in this singleton and omit the chest detail if it has no remaining role. Do not present this as a difficult stretch item.

decisionNodes.stem: Using the outside hospital's stated worksheet, which starting infusion rate should have been recorded for {patientName} at arrival, rounded to the nearest whole mL/hour?

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 378 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: Count 14% plus 8%, giving 22%. The first allocation is 3 × 70 × 22 / 2 = 2310 mL. Subtract 800 mL, then divide the remaining 1510 mL by the four hours remaining: 377.5 mL/hour.

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 693 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: This result counts the additional epidermal erythema: (3 × 70 × 34 / 2 − 800) / 4 = 692.5. The intact red region does not belong in this dermal-burn estimate.

answerChoices.label: Crystalloid at 189 mL/hour
answerChoices.rationale: This result restarts an eight-hour window at arrival: (2310 − 800) / 8 = 188.75. The supplied worksheet measures time from the injury.

concept.displayName: Reconcile burn extent and the resuscitation clock
concept.learningObjective: Use only dermal-burn extent, elapsed time from injury and prior fluid when applying a specified burn-fluid starting estimate.
concept.historyPolicy: New burn-specific decision identity; no automatic migration of another concept history.

record.title: Reconcile burn extent and the resuscitation clock
fairness: The supplied worksheet yields 22% dermal-burn TBSA; 3 x 70 x 22 = 4620 mL; half is 2310 mL; subtracting 800 leaves 1510 mL over the remaining four hours, or 377.5 rounded to 378 mL/hour. Exactly one offered answer matches.

693 mL/hour results from including the additional 12% intact erythema; 189 results from spreading the remaining first allocation over eight hours. Both are interpretable errors rather than numerical outliers.

The worksheet explicitly fixes the protocol; the explanation correctly limits the calculation to that worksheet rather than claiming a universal starting coefficient. First node of a coherent fluid sequence; it does not disclose the later response-based adjustment.
suggestions: Retain the explicit local worksheet and rounding instruction. This is burn-resuscitation arithmetic, not a statistics item subject to the single-skill statistics exception.

concept.learningObjective: Reassess the initial burn-fluid prescription using the actual perfusion and urine-output trajectory.
concept.historyPolicy: New burn-specific decision identity; no automatic migration of another concept history.

record.title: Adjust fluids to the acquired response
fairness: Reduce crystalloid with reassessment is the best offered direction: interpret urine output relative to the 70-kg patient and current perfusion, then weigh the improving resuscitation markers against increasing edema.

Stable pressure, falling lactate, patent drainage and the excluded alternative causes of high output make the trend interpretable without inventing an exact rate reduction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The new update is consequential and coherent after the starting-rate calculation. It does not require recalling which numerical answer was previously chosen; current weight, response and task are available in the presentation/update.
suggestions: Retain the direction-only choices and reassessment. Do not turn this into a universal urine-output or percentage-reduction rule.

concept.displayName: Recognize restrictive chest eschar
concept.learningObjective: Use acquired ventilatory and examination findings to distinguish chest-wall restriction from tube obstruction or pleural disease.
concept.historyPolicy: New burn-specific decision identity; no automatic migration of another concept history.

record.title: Recognize restrictive chest eschar
fairness: Thoracic escharotomy is the best offered procedure: simultaneous peak/plateau pressure rise during passive ventilation indicates a compliance problem, and the circumferential chest burn with poor excursion localizes a plausible restrictive cause.

The tube-patency and bilateral pleural findings are relevant checks against the offered alternatives. These are clinical observations requiring interpretation, not a diagnosis label or explanatory option.

The earlier limb-node explanation primes the general eschar-release principle and likely lowers difficulty, but it does not teach the pressure interpretation. The later update supplies its own current findings and can be solved without the earlier answer. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the passive-ventilation and inspiratory-hold details; they make the pressure comparison fair. Do not rate this as an unprimed hard item when shown immediately after limb escharotomy.
Remove the final explanation sentence about procedures not occurring in the founder's clinic if editing feedback; it adds no clinical reasoning.

answerChoices.label: Forearm compartment fasciotomy
answerChoices.rationale: Progressive deep-compartment findings after electrical muscle injury require fascial release; preserved arterial signals do not make the deep tissue pressure problem disappear.

answerChoices.label: Forearm skin escharotomy
answerChoices.rationale: There is no constricting circumferential skin envelope to release, and skin incision would not decompress the affected deep compartments.

answerChoices.label: Forearm arterial thrombectomy
answerChoices.rationale: The deep tension and stretch-pain trajectory with maintained arterial signals points to compartment pressure rather than a demonstrated arterial occlusion.

decisionNodes.explanation: Integrate the deep pain/tension trajectory with the electrical mechanism and pliable skin. The threatened compartment lies beneath fascia, so skin eschar release does not address it. Maintained Doppler signals cannot by themselves exclude a deep compartment syndrome.

concept.displayName: Release a deep compartment after electrical injury
concept.learningObjective: Select fascial decompression for a deteriorating deep muscle compartment rather than an escharotomy based on the burn label.
concept.historyPolicy: New burn-specific decision identity; no automatic migration of another concept history.

record.title: Release a deep compartment after electrical injury
fairness: Forearm fasciotomy is the best offered procedure: evolving tension, passive-stretch pain and motor change identify a threatened deep compartment, then pliable skin and the electrical mechanism distinguish fascial decompression from eschar release.
Maintained Doppler signals are a useful competing observation and do not make thrombectomy preferable or exclude a compartment emergency. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The previous node establishes muscle injury but does not name the later procedure. The acquired examination changes the decision and contains sufficient current findings to stand alone with the shared presentation.
suggestions: Retain the pulse-versus-compartment distinction and the skin examination. Do not add a pressure cutoff or require a pressure measurement to manufacture difficulty in this clinically overt scenario.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 34-year-old woman, reviews her outside hospital records in clinic after an enclosed upholstered-furniture fire. She had soot in her mouth, lost consciousness and arrived with circulatory collapse. Her airway was secured and she received oxygen and circulatory support. Lactate remained 16 mmol/L, and blood co-oximetry showed COHb 19%. The hospital laboratory sent a cyanide assay to a reference laboratory.

decisionNodes.stem: Which antidote plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded hospital condition while supportive treatment continues?

answerChoices.label: Administer intravenous hydroxocobalamin now
answerChoices.rationale: The exposure, coma/collapse and profound persistent lactate support empiric treatment for suspected cyanide toxicity. Hydroxocobalamin avoids adding the nitrite-associated methemoglobin burden to documented CO exposure.

answerChoices.label: Administer sodium nitrite with thiosulfate now
answerChoices.rationale: This is a genuine cyanide regimen, but sodium nitrite can worsen hypotension and oxygen carriage through methemoglobin formation when CO poisoning coexists. The preferred available alternative here is hydroxocobalamin.

answerChoices.label: Await the blood cyanide result before antidote treatment
answerChoices.rationale: A reference-laboratory result should not defer treatment when severe exposure and clinical findings make suspicion high.

decisionNodes.explanation: Infer possible cyanide toxicity in addition to the measured CO exposure, then account for the oxygen-carriage and hypotension risks of sodium nitrite when choosing treatment. The history and collapse justify empiric hydroxocobalamin without waiting for a send-out result. Lactate here is a constructed observation, not a universal diagnostic cutoff.

concept.displayName: Choose empiric antidote treatment after a fire
concept.learningObjective: Integrate severe smoke toxicity and impaired oxygen carriage to choose empiric hydroxocobalamin rather than wait for confirmation or add a methemoglobin-forming regimen.
concept.historyPolicy: New burn-specific decision identity; no automatic migration of another concept history.

record.title: Choose empiric antidote treatment after a fire
fairness: Immediate hydroxocobalamin is the best offered plan: infer possible cyanide toxicity from the fire exposure, collapse and persistent marked lactate elevation, then account for concurrent CO exposure and hypotension when ranking hydroxocobalamin against nitrite/thiosulfate.

The antidote alternatives are clinically related; awaiting confirmation represents a consequential sequencing error. The send-out assay context is relevant to empiric treatment rather than a generic permission statement.

The explanation appropriately avoids a universal lactate cutoff or an absolute ban on nitrites. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this offline review; comparative antidote evidence and exact clinical sign-off remain for the clinician. Standalone and complete.
suggestions: Retain both the mixed-exposure evidence and the hemodynamic course. Do not turn the constructed lactate value into a diagnostic threshold or imply all smoke exposures require antidote treatment.

decisionNodes.stem: Which regional wound plan best fits {patientName}'s recorded trunk examination when planning burn excision and coverage?

answerChoices.label: Plan excision and coverage of the central region
answerChoices.rationale: The central pattern indicates deeper nonviable tissue, while the advancing peripheral epithelialization supports preserving that region rather than treating the field as uniform.

answerChoices.label: Plan excision and coverage of the entire wound
answerChoices.rationale: Uniform excision would remove the represented viable epithelializing periphery along with the deeper center.

answerChoices.label: Plan continued dressing care for the entire wound
answerChoices.rationale: Peripheral healing does not establish that the dry insensate center will close by the same pathway.

concept.displayName: Apply regional depth to an excision plan
concept.learningObjective: Distinguish nonviable central burn from viable epithelializing peripheral tissue when planning regional excision and coverage.
concept.historyPolicy: New scored clinical meaning: operative extent replaces a pure depth label. Keep previous concept/history intact; no FSRS transfer.

record.title: Apply regional depth to an excision plan
fairness: Planning excision and coverage of the central region is the best offered extent: interpret the repeated central findings alongside the advancing epithelial edge, then avoid applying a whole-wound operative or conservative plan.
The options test a meaningful regional consequence rather than merely naming burn depth. Whole-wound excision and continued dressings are recognizable over- and undertreatment errors.

The central observations support deeper injury but do not distinguish every possible depth with certainty. The wording asks for surgical planning, not an exact operative day or an unconditional claim that all similar wounds require immediate excision.

The first node establishes the operative-field decision without teaching the later donor-limited coverage material. The later operative findings appropriately need to establish bed readiness separately. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Retain the planning wording, serial examination and independently healing peripheral region. Avoid upgrading these observations to an unsupported exact depth or fixed operation deadline.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial nutrition plan best fits {patientName}'s first outside burn-unit assessment?

record.title: Start enteral support after burn resuscitation
fairness: A low-rate gastric enteral start is the best offered plan: infer improving perfusion from the support/lactate/urine trajectory, then distinguish quiet bowel sounds from a reason to withhold enteral nutrition.

Primary PN and waiting for stool represent credible common errors, although the latter is the weaker option. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the item does not claim a universal hour, pressor limit or calorie target.

decisionNodes.stem: Which antimicrobial plan best fits {patientName}'s wound at this clinic review?

fairness: Continuing the current local regimen is the best offered plan: interpret a surface isolate against objectively improving wound behavior, then decide whether systemic treatment is indicated rather than selecting an antibiotic from susceptibilities.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation appropriately calls for reassessment with deterioration rather than claiming a surface culture can never matter. Standalone chronology and task are complete.

concept.displayName: Relieve restrictive thermal eschar
concept.learningObjective: Distinguish circumferential skin restriction from systemic hypoperfusion and deeper muscle injury when selecting decompression.
concept.historyPolicy: New burn-specific decision identity; no automatic migration of another concept history.

record.title: Relieve restrictive thermal eschar
fairness: Forearm escharotomy followed by reassessment is the single best offered immediate intervention: first interpret worsening unilateral distal perfusion despite recovered systemic perfusion and external-pressure measures, then select the constraining tissue layer and release sequence.

Escharotomy versus fasciotomy is a consequential, commonly tested distinction. Arterial exploration is a weaker distractor, but reduced distal signals can tempt a learner to treat primary arterial pathology rather than external restriction. All options name parallel procedures with the same reassessment clause; no unique wording match, explanatory key or convergence shortcut was found.

The absence of crush/electrical injury does not prove that deep compartment syndrome is impossible. The item does not need that absolute: circumferential deep thermal injury supports initial eschar release, and the explanation explicitly allows deeper decompression when demonstrated or when perfusion fails to recover. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The outside-record timeline, named patient and age/sex are sufficient to answer independently. There is only one current scored node; no preceding answer is required. The phrase 'first decision below' and chest-burn detail are residual framing, not a decision-changing ambiguity.
suggestions: Retain failed external-pressure measures, the local-versus-systemic comparison and reassessment after release; do not replace them with an announced diagnosis.
Optional editorial cleanup: remove 'first' from 'first decision below' in this singleton and omit the chest detail if it has no remaining role. Do not present this as a difficult stretch item.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: His 80-kg preinjury weight has risen to 88 kg, with a recorded positive fluid balance of 8 L. Urine output over the last three hours is 15, 12 and 8 mL; creatinine has doubled from baseline. The urinary catheter flushes freely and bladder ultrasonography shows an empty bladder. Blood pressure is stable without vasopressors, extremities are warm and lactate has normalized. New bilateral crackles and an increasing oxygen requirement have appeared; chest radiography shows bilateral interstitial fluid. The renal team is evaluating reversible causes and electrolyte complications.
decisionNodes.stem: Which direction for {patientName}'s crystalloid infusion best fits this later outside-hospital review while renal assessment continues?

answerChoices.label: Reduce crystalloid and reassess perfusion and fluid balance
answerChoices.rationale: Low output now coexists with recovered systemic perfusion, marked accumulation and new respiratory findings. Continuing to chase output with crystalloid risks worsening overload rather than treating intrinsic renal injury.

answerChoices.label: Maintain crystalloid and reassess perfusion and fluid balance
answerChoices.rationale: An unchanged infusion continues substantial delivery despite new accumulation and respiratory consequences; the original electrical-injury fluid rationale is no longer sufficient.

answerChoices.label: Increase crystalloid and reassess perfusion and fluid balance
answerChoices.rationale: Oliguria and pigmenturia warrant urgent assessment, but do not establish an indication for still more fluid in this newly congested, systemically perfused patient.

decisionNodes.explanation: The small skin wounds underestimate muscle injury, so initial monitored fluid replacement was appropriate. The later decision uses the acquired volume and perfusion assessment: very low output persists after recovery of systemic perfusion while weight, fluid balance and respiratory findings worsen. Reduce unnecessary crystalloid while urgently evaluating renal injury and complications; neither a diuretic prescription nor automatic dialysis follows from this question.

fairness: Reducing crystalloid while reassessing perfusion and balance is the single best offered direction. Interpret persistent oliguria in the context of recovered systemic perfusion, excluded bladder retention and accumulating respiratory/volume findings; then reverse continued fluid escalation despite the legitimate initial concern for pigment-associated renal injury.

Increasing fluid is a credible error because the patient has substantial muscle injury and worsening urine output; maintaining it is a credible failure to respond to the new overload evidence. The three labels differ only in infusion direction and provide no length, qualification, convergence or wording-overlap shortcut.

The task asks for direction, not an exact prescription. A current infusion rate would be needed to calculate a new rate, but its absence does not undermine the relative choice among increase, maintain and reduce in this stated course. No new fluid or urine-output threshold is required to solve it.

The explanation properly limits its conclusion: a change in crystalloid direction does not by itself determine a diuretic or dialysis decision. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The card supplies the earlier resuscitation and later review within one coherent standalone node; named patient, age/sex and complete task are present.
Electrical injury, occult muscle damage and reassessment of resuscitation rather than blindly chasing urine output are high-yield. The strong overload pattern makes this moderate, not hard.
suggestions: Retain both the initial reason to give fluid and the subsequent contradictory volume/perfusion evidence. Preserve the narrow infusion-direction task and urgent renal assessment.
Optional brevity improvement: place the serial output, weight and balance in a compact record, without adding an interpretive heading such as 'fluid overload.'

answerChoices.label: Flexible bronchoscopy

answerChoices.rationale: The tube has a documented passable lumen and appropriate position. Those observations make a primary tube problem less compelling than retained material beyond it.
