record.title: Localize and address post-fire airway obstruction
fairness: Flexible bronchoscopy is the single best offered next procedure. First interpret the peak-pressure rise with unchanged plateau during valid passive measurements as predominantly increased resistance; then integrate tube patency/position, particulate material and focal volume loss to select inspection and clearance of the lower airway.

Tube exchange represents mislocalizing resistance to the endotracheal tube; thoracostomy represents treating a pleural cause of an acute ventilatory change. The supplied tube and pleural observations appropriately discriminate urgent alternatives. These are medically meaningful negatives, not a plain-language announcement that the distractors are wrong.

A freely passing suction catheter does not absolutely exclude every tube-related problem, and pleural sliding only informs the regions assessed. Nevertheless, the full supplied pattern and adequate current oxygenation make bronchoscopy the best of these choices. The explanation does not require an absolute exclusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The options are concise named procedures with comparable specificity. No diagnostic label, key-only task term, explanatory option or component-convergence cue was found. General airway mechanics are applied to a burn-specific particulate-obstruction problem, a high-yield resident decision.

The prior intubation is supplied as a completed event, so airway stabilization need not be reconstructed from another question. The retrospective record is coherent and independently answerable; the named patient, demographics and complete task are present. No separate image or exhibit is promised.
suggestions: Retain the conditions making plateau pressure interpretable, the current tube assessment and acquired lobar findings. Avoid adding an 'airway cast' diagnosis or a pre-answer statement that bronchoscopy is needed.
This is a moderate applied item; the readily discriminating observations do not justify a hard label. Runtime testing/procedure wait presentation was not assessed from these text-only review fields.

A tangential pass exposes punctate bleeding at the edge, but a broad central region remains dry and brown with an adherent layer and no punctate bleeding. decisionNodes.stem: Which operative plan best fits {patientName}'s current recipient-bed and donor findings?

answerChoices.label: Complete tangential excision, then apply cadaveric allograft
answerChoices.rationale: The center still requires recipient-bed preparation, while the donor map does not establish a healed harvestable source. Temporary allograft follows adequate removal of residual nonviable tissue.

answerChoices.label: Complete tangential excision, then apply meshed autograft
answerChoices.rationale: Further recipient preparation is appropriate, but the current donor surfaces have not re-epithelialized. Meshing does not create a harvestable donor site.

answerChoices.label: Use the current excision level, then apply cadaveric allograft
answerChoices.rationale: Temporary coverage addresses the donor limitation but does not correct a central recipient bed with retained adherent nonviable tissue.

answerChoices.label: Use the current excision level, then apply meshed autograft
answerChoices.rationale: This plan overlooks both the central recipient finding and the donor map. Neither a preferred definitive material nor meshing resolves those two readiness constraints.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read the two surfaces separately. Punctate bleeding at the margin does not make the adherent dry center ready for coverage; complete the necessary burn excision. The four choices form a balanced two-by-two set: each excision level and each coverage type appears twice. The key cannot be assembled from majority components, and all labels have comparable length, specificity and grammatical form.

The recipient-bed observations support further removal of the described adherent nonviable layer. The donor map supplies a real limit on immediate autografting rather than merely saying 'autograft unavailable.' Equipment availability does not provide a donor surface. The distractors represent using a partly prepared bed or choosing definitive coverage without a usable donor site.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation avoids inventing a donor-healing interval or fixed allograft deadline. The exact depth/extent of intraoperative excision still requires clinical judgment; the item asks for the staged strategy, not an unsupported measurement.

Burn excision, recipient-bed viability and temporary versus definitive coverage are high-yield. The two observations are fairly explicit, so this is moderate rather than hard. The later operation follows coherently from the original wound description, and all information needed for this singleton is present without prior feedback. Patient, age/sex and task are clear.
suggestions: Retain the balanced option matrix and separate recipient/donor observations. Do not replace them with labels such as 'inadequate bed' or 'no usable donors,' which would supply the interpretation.

Optional shortening: reduce the earlier peripheral-healing narrative if it has no role beyond establishing the previously observed wound; preserve the central-versus-margin distinction at the actual operation.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 46-year-old woman, reviews her outside burn-unit nutrition records with the founder in clinic. Extensive burns required intubation. Gastric feeding had initially been tolerated. A subsequent episode brought increasing vasopressor support, falling urine output, rising lactate, a tender distended abdomen and bloody gastric drainage. Enteral delivery was held while resuscitation and abdominal evaluation proceeded. The following feeding review occurred after that episode.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Vasopressors have been discontinued, lactate has returned to the reference range and urine output has recovered. Serial examinations now show a soft nontender abdomen without recurrent blood in drainage. Evaluation has found no bowel obstruction; current clinical review does not raise concern for intestinal ischemia. Gastric feeding restarts but produces vomiting and aspirates of 650 and 700 mL in consecutive six-hour collections despite a prokinetic trial. She remains unable to eat while intubated.
decisionNodes.stem: Which nutrition route best fits {patientName}'s current findings at this later outside-hospital review?

answerChoices.label: Low-rate postpyloric enteral feeding
answerChoices.rationale: The acquired course now supports controlled perfusion and a usable intestinal tract, while repeated large gastric aspirates persist despite a prokinetic. Moving delivery beyond the stomach addresses that remaining route problem.

answerChoices.label: Low-rate gastric enteral feeding
answerChoices.rationale: That route was actually retried after recovery and continues to produce vomiting and large aspirates despite the prokinetic; the current record supplies a reason to change access.

answerChoices.label: Intravenous parenteral nutrition
answerChoices.rationale: The earlier safety episode warrants reassessment, but it does not establish that the recovered intestine is unusable. Persistent gastric delivery difficulty can first be addressed through a postpyloric route under these findings.

concept.displayName: Select a feeding route after perfusion recovery
concept.learningObjective: Distinguish persistent gastric intolerance after recovery from the earlier unsafe perfusion/abdominal episode when selecting the next nutrition route.
concept.historyPolicy: New scored clinical meaning; previousConceptId records the prior objective. Keep previous concept/history intact; no FSRS transfer.

record.title: Select a feeding route after perfusion recovery
fairness: Low-rate postpyloric enteral feeding is the single best offered route in the stated current assessment. First distinguish the recovered perfusion/abdominal course from the earlier unsafe feeding episode; then interpret persistent vomiting and large gastric aspirates despite a prokinetic as a gastric-tolerance problem rather than failure of the entire enteral route.

Repeating gastric feeding is tempting because it was previously tolerated; parenteral nutrition is tempting after repeated gastric failure and the alarming earlier abdominal episode. The acquired course, ongoing inability to eat and failed prokinetic trial make postpyloric access the best remaining offered route. The low-rate qualifier is shared by both enteral choices and does not uniquely mark the key.

The clinical review's absence of current ischemic concern is a supplied safety assessment, not proof that normal lactate or a benign examination alone excludes ischemia. Keeping a clear assessment of this issue is necessary after the prior bloody drainage and shock. Do not remove it merely to make the item harder.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. I have not independently verified the adequacy of the unspecified prokinetic regimen or the evidentiary basis of the exact aspirate examples offline; the item does not ask for a dose or a numerical cutoff, and vomiting plus persistent large aspirates supplies the intended intolerance finding. Exact clinical wording remains subject to named clinician review.

The sequential course is fully supplied and coherent as one standalone record review; the earlier episode is not silently reinterpreted as safe feeding. The named patient, demographics, short complaint and complete task are present. Enteral eligibility, gastric intolerance and route escalation are high-yield, with moderate two-step application rather than hard discrimination.
suggestions: Retain the earlier safety warnings, explicit current assessment and current failure of gastric delivery after a prokinetic. Avoid introducing a fixed restart interval or treating the reported aspirate values as a universal threshold.

Optional precision improvement at clinical sign-off: name the actual prokinetic treatment and relevant evaluation findings if they are documented and source-supported; do not invent a regimen or claim that one negative finding excludes ischemia.

record.title: Surveillance after favorable anal-margin SCC excision
fairness: Clinical and anoscopic surveillance is the best offered next plan. The learner must identify a small skin-based anal-margin primary, then integrate differentiation, negative staging and complete clearance to avoid unnecessary re-excision or canal-cancer treatment.

The 12-mm clearance is an observed measurement, not an invented universal threshold. It makes the wider-excision alternative weaker for a clinical reason. A nonmedical reader might prefer observation after negative margins, but cannot resolve surveillance versus adjuvant chemoradiation from wording alone.

The task is complete, the options are comparable next-management plans, and the record supplies the operative and pathological facts needed to distinguish the limited-excision exception. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally defensible offered alternative identified.
The standalone case is coherent with outside excision already completed. Its explanation does not depend on the different, still-present poorly differentiated lesion in another case.
suggestions: Optional feedback cleanup: remove 'no minimum margin cutoff is taught.' It is an authoring comment rather than a clinical explanation. Preserve the observation and the reason surveillance is appropriate.
Do not extend this verdict to close/positive margins or to the held postoperative poorly differentiated scenario.

record.title: Isolated recurrence in a previously irradiated groin
fairness: Right inguinal lymph-node dissection is the best offered recommendation. The learner must localize the failure away from the controlled anal primary and apply the prior groin radiation history to the salvage choice.

The mobile, biopsy-confirmed node and restaging supply the information needed to favor a nodal operation over APR. Prior inclusion of both groins in the radiation plan distinguishes this case from an untreated nodal basin. Those are necessary observations, not disposable exclusion sentences.

Both the dissection and radiation choices address the right groin, so location-word matching does not uniquely reveal the key. The options name actual treatment plans and contain no key-only rationale or meaningful length outlier.

No confident clinical error identified. Individual reirradiation decisions are more nuanced than a universal prohibition; the explanation appropriately supports dissection planning rather than asserting that further radiation can never be used. Exact salvage eligibility still requires clinician review.
The standalone presentation and exhibit provide the prior treatment, current pathology and disease distribution. No continuity or missing-prerequisite problem identified.
suggestions: Retain the prior radiation-field observation and controlled-primary finding. Do not strengthen the feedback into an absolute contraindication to all reirradiation.

record.title: Systemic therapy after prior radiosensitizing chemotherapy
fairness: The combination of retifanlimab, carboplatin and paclitaxel is the intended best offered answer. The meaningful distinction is prior fluorouracil/mitomycin radiosensitization versus a prior platinum-containing systemic line for advanced disease, followed by combination therapy versus checkpoint monotherapy.

The supplied metastatic diagnosis is appropriate because this task concerns treatment line, not diagnosis. The distribution of disease and matched biopsy make the systemic-treatment frame coherent. The prior-drug record is necessary to distinguish the two retifanlimab options.

The combination choice is longer than monotherapy, but not anomalously more detailed than the named chemotherapy alternative. Retifanlimab occurs in two choices; chemotherapy occurs in two choices. No reliable nonmedical convergence or wording shortcut identifies the key.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, but the exact contemporary retifanlimab indications and monotherapy eligibility wording have not been independently verified in this no-network review. Do not interpret this editorial PASS as confirmation that the label or preferred regimen remains current.

This is useful contemporary oncology knowledge, but the exact retifanlimab regimen is less clearly a commonly tested general-surgery board target than chemoradiation, local-excision selection or salvage APR. highYield=false reflects that limitation, not evidence that it is never tested.
The current standalone case provides prior treatment and present disease status; no unseen prior node is required.
suggestions: Keep this as supplemental systemic-oncology coverage rather than representing it as a core high-frequency ABSITE question.
Have Melissa verify the exact combination/monotherapy indication distinction before clinical approval; retain the restrained 'supported ... option' explanation.

record.title: Initial treatment with inguinal nodal involvement
fairness: The best offered answer is concurrent fluorouracil/mitomycin with radiation. The learner must classify an inguinal metastasis as regional, then select initial treatment despite sphincter involvement. The systemic regimen and primary APR represent distinct staging and treatment-sequencing errors.

The known squamous diagnosis is appropriate for a treatment task. The negative distant assessment is necessary and does not itself supply the regional-node classification. No material key-only wording, length, convergence or explanatory-option shortcut identified.

The current standalone case supplies histology, local anatomy and distant assessment without needing the former workup companions. The named patient, age/sex and short complaint are coherent. No preceding explanation rehearses the answer in this current composition.

Review scope for this report: all ten nodes in reviewRound.current.cases, including the five still-executable rewritten/new v1 items, were independently assessed from their visible candidate fields. Superseded v1 revisions, four baseline kept items, retirement proposals, two parked diagnostic nodes and three clinical holds were not scored. No current case has a later decision node.

All verdicts in this report are offline editorial judgments, not clinical approval or fresh source verification. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative judgments, not measured resident performance or verified examination frequency. Drafts remain needs_clinician_review. Runtime rendering and wait estimates cannot be certified from these visible text fields.
suggestions: Retain the regional-node versus distant-disease distinction and the sphincter finding. They make a common, high-yield initial-treatment decision consequential.

record.title: Salvage treatment for isolated local recurrence
fairness: Salvage APR is the best offered plan. The learner must combine biopsy, documented earlier complete response and negative distant staging to identify isolated local recurrence, then apply prior definitive chemoradiation and current anatomy to select surgical salvage.

Repeat definitive chemoradiation and systemic therapy represent credible errors about prior treatment and recurrence extent. The explanation recommends multidisciplinary APR planning rather than guaranteeing that the brief vignette establishes every operative-fitness requirement.

The current task does not supply the classification 'local failure' before answering. Preserved planes and negative distant imaging are necessary to distinguish local salvage from a systemic approach; deleting them would weaken fairness rather than improve difficulty.

No material wording, length, convergence or teaching-sentence shortcut identified. 'Salvage' appears in the option, but no earlier visible answer or explanation announces salvage APR in this standalone case.

The presentation, functional update and exhibit are temporally coherent and contain the current biopsy, prior therapy and restaging. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally defensible offered answer identified. This is a core surgical-oncology decision, with moderate rather than hard predicted difficulty.
suggestions: Retain this standalone composition. If a diagnostic-confirmation companion is added later, review its feedback to ensure it does not announce APR before this choice.
Keep the distinction between recommending multidisciplinary salvage planning and asserting unconditional operative eligibility.

record.title: Representative tissue versus additional sections
fairness: Anoscopy-guided incisional biopsy is the best offered diagnostic step. Surface epithelial atypia does not characterize the palpable underlying nodule; the epithelial-only retained block then makes additional sections an inadequate solution to the missing tissue compartment.

These are linked, consequential inferences: distinguish location adequacy from architectural adequacy, then decide whether new acquisition or further processing can resolve the discrepancy. The block inventory is necessary to fairly reject additional sections; removing it would leave a genuine alternative.

The repeated epithelial description is decision-critical evidence, not a repeated keyed action. None of the three option labels uniquely echoes the nodule or ulcer location. The specialist-review choice is a credible near-miss, while repeat cytology is a weaker but recognizable tissue-versus-screening error.

The options are all diagnostic plans. No confident clinical error identified. The explanation preserves the surface finding rather than falsely calling the biopsy entirely useless or diagnosing invasion from the nodule alone.
The current standalone case supplies the outside procedure, specimen findings and present examination. It does not rely on later staging or another question's feedback.
suggestions: Keep the retained-material inventory and correct-site sampling detail. They distinguish this application from a simple 'biopsy an anal mass' recognition question.

record.title: Surveillance after favorable anal-margin SCC excision
fairness: Clinical and anoscopic surveillance is the best offered next plan. The learner must identify a small skin-based anal-margin primary, then integrate differentiation, negative staging and complete clearance to avoid unnecessary re-excision or canal-cancer treatment.

The 12-mm clearance is an observed measurement, not an invented universal threshold. It makes the wider-excision alternative weaker for a clinical reason. A nonmedical reader might prefer observation after negative margins, but cannot resolve surveillance versus adjuvant chemoradiation from wording alone.

The task is complete, the options are comparable next-management plans, and the record supplies the operative and pathological facts needed to distinguish the limited-excision exception. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally defensible offered alternative identified.
The standalone case is coherent with outside excision already completed. Its explanation does not depend on the different, still-present poorly differentiated lesion in another case.
suggestions: Optional feedback cleanup: remove 'no minimum margin cutoff is taught.' It is an authoring comment rather than a clinical explanation. Preserve the observation and the reason surveillance is appropriate.
Do not extend this verdict to close/positive margins or to the held postoperative poorly differentiated scenario.

record.title: Isolated recurrence in a previously irradiated groin
fairness: Right inguinal lymph-node dissection is the best offered recommendation. The learner must localize the failure away from the controlled anal primary and apply the prior groin radiation history to the salvage choice.

The mobile, biopsy-confirmed node and restaging supply the information needed to favor a nodal operation over APR. Prior inclusion of both groins in the radiation plan distinguishes this case from an untreated nodal basin. Those are necessary observations, not disposable exclusion sentences.

Both the dissection and radiation choices address the right groin, so location-word matching does not uniquely reveal the key. The options name actual treatment plans and contain no key-only rationale or meaningful length outlier.

No confident clinical error identified. Individual reirradiation decisions are more nuanced than a universal prohibition; the explanation appropriately supports dissection planning rather than asserting that further radiation can never be used. Exact salvage eligibility still requires clinician review.
The standalone presentation and exhibit provide the prior treatment, current pathology and disease distribution. No continuity or missing-prerequisite problem identified.
suggestions: Retain the prior radiation-field observation and controlled-primary finding. Do not strengthen the feedback into an absolute contraindication to all reirradiation.

record.title: Systemic therapy after prior radiosensitizing chemotherapy
fairness: The combination of retifanlimab, carboplatin and paclitaxel is the intended best offered answer. The meaningful distinction is prior fluorouracil/mitomycin radiosensitization versus a prior platinum-containing systemic line for advanced disease, followed by combination therapy versus checkpoint monotherapy.

The supplied metastatic diagnosis is appropriate because this task concerns treatment line, not diagnosis. The distribution of disease and matched biopsy make the systemic-treatment frame coherent. The prior-drug record is necessary to distinguish the two retifanlimab options.

The combination choice is longer than monotherapy, but not anomalously more detailed than the named chemotherapy alternative. Retifanlimab occurs in two choices; chemotherapy occurs in two choices. No reliable nonmedical convergence or wording shortcut identifies the key.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, but the exact contemporary retifanlimab indications and monotherapy eligibility wording have not been independently verified in this no-network review. Do not interpret this editorial PASS as confirmation that the label or preferred regimen remains current.

This is useful contemporary oncology knowledge, but the exact retifanlimab regimen is less clearly a commonly tested general-surgery board target than chemoradiation, local-excision selection or salvage APR. highYield=false reflects that limitation, not evidence that it is never tested.
The current standalone case provides prior treatment and present disease status; no unseen prior node is required.
suggestions: Keep this as supplemental systemic-oncology coverage rather than representing it as a core high-frequency ABSITE question.
Have Melissa verify the exact combination/monotherapy indication distinction before clinical approval; retain the restrained 'supported ... option' explanation.

record.title: Representative tissue versus additional sections
fairness: Anoscopy-guided incisional biopsy is the best offered diagnostic step. Surface epithelial atypia does not characterize the palpable underlying nodule; the epithelial-only retained block then makes additional sections an inadequate solution to the missing tissue compartment.

These are linked, consequential inferences: distinguish location adequacy from architectural adequacy, then decide whether new acquisition or further processing can resolve the discrepancy. The block inventory is necessary to fairly reject additional sections; removing it would leave a genuine alternative.

The repeated epithelial description is decision-critical evidence, not a repeated keyed action. None of the three option labels uniquely echoes the nodule or ulcer location. The specialist-review choice is a credible near-miss, while repeat cytology is a weaker but recognizable tissue-versus-screening error.

The options are all diagnostic plans. No confident clinical error identified. The explanation preserves the surface finding rather than falsely calling the biopsy entirely useless or diagnosing invasion from the nodule alone.
The current standalone case supplies the outside procedure, specimen findings and present examination. It does not rely on later staging or another question's feedback.
suggestions: Keep the retained-material inventory and correct-site sampling detail. They distinguish this application from a simple 'biopsy an anal mass' recognition question.
Keep the qualitative moderate rating; this does not yet warrant a hard rating.

record.title: Salvage treatment for isolated local recurrence
fairness: Salvage APR is the best offered plan. The learner must combine biopsy, documented earlier complete response and negative distant staging to identify isolated local recurrence, then apply prior definitive chemoradiation and current anatomy to select surgical salvage.

Repeat definitive chemoradiation and systemic therapy represent credible errors about prior treatment and recurrence extent. The explanation recommends multidisciplinary APR planning rather than guaranteeing that the brief vignette establishes every operative-fitness requirement.

The current task does not supply the classification 'local failure' before answering. Preserved planes and negative distant imaging are necessary to distinguish local salvage from a systemic approach; deleting them would weaken fairness rather than improve difficulty.

No material wording, length, convergence or teaching-sentence shortcut identified. 'Salvage' appears in the option, but no earlier visible answer or explanation announces salvage APR in this standalone case.

The presentation, functional update and exhibit are temporally coherent and contain the current biopsy, prior therapy and restaging. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally defensible offered answer identified. This is a core surgical-oncology decision, with moderate rather than hard predicted difficulty.
suggestions: Retain this standalone composition. If a diagnostic-confirmation companion is added later, review its feedback to ensure it does not announce APR before this choice.
Keep the distinction between recommending multidisciplinary salvage planning and asserting unconditional operative eligibility.

record.title: Source control after a sleeve leak with shock and peritonitis
fairness: Independent answer: urgent operative exploration with washout and drainage. The learner must integrate the distribution of fluid with new hypotension, tachycardia and diffuse guarding, then change from a potentially localized/endoscopic leak strategy to operative source control.

Percutaneous drainage and endoscopic treatment are credible approaches in other leak states; the current deterioration makes them inferior here. The shared resuscitation and antimicrobials prevent the key from winning merely by being the only complete treatment bundle.

The word 'Urgent' is appropriate to the actual operative option and is supported by necessary findings, not a gratuitous rhetorical cue. No confident clinical error or competing best answer identified. Preserve the instability findings rather than hide them for difficulty.

The progression from persistent symptoms to CT findings and deterioration is coherent. The preceding explanation does not select this route. The current update supplies sleeve anatomy, CT results and the decisive condition, so it remains solvable with the shared presentation even if the earlier answer is not recalled.

record.title: Acarbose efficacy versus reproducible intolerance
fairness: The table distinguishes fewer hypoglycemic episodes from an acceptable overall treatment response. Activity-limiting gastrointestinal symptoms recur on reintroduction and settle off treatment; changing therapy is justified by observations rather than the supplied label 'intolerant'.

Short-acting subcutaneous octreotide is the defensible best offered next drug under the stated sequence. Continued acarbose rewards attention to efficacy while ignoring reproducible harm; diazoxide tests premature movement to a later alternative. Exact guideline sequencing is not freshly verified offline, so this editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

Two consequential steps remain: infer drug intolerance despite efficacy, then choose the next treatment stage. A reader can reject continuation from the trajectory without specialized knowledge, but cannot distinguish the two replacement agents by wording alone.
The node supplies established PBH, implemented dietary care and the full medication course. It stands alone, follows the diet node coherently and is not answered by that node's explanation.

The concept is useful and testable postoperative metabolic management. The clear dechallenge/rechallenge makes this moderate, not hard; it does not establish a universal adverse-effect threshold or require another rechallenge.
suggestions: Keep the efficacy-versus-tolerability trajectory and the equally concrete next-drug choices. Retain specialist-directed framing in feedback and verify the exact sequencing during clinical sign-off.

record.title: Initial investigation of acute pain after Roux-en-Y bypass
fairness: Independent answer: CT with oral and intravenous contrast. The transition from intermittent cramps to persistent pain and retching after bypass raises a bowel/extraluminal concern; the resident then selects an investigation that covers reconstructed anatomy rather than just the accessible lumen.

Endoscopy and an upper-GI contrast study are relevant post-bypass investigations but are less comprehensive for this acute pattern. The stable circulation and absence of guarding make an investigation-stage question coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally good offered alternative identified.

Renal function and contrast-reaction history address suitability and do not uniquely reveal the key by word matching, since another offered study also uses contrast. Options are comparably concrete investigations without teaching qualifiers.

The historical-admission frame is explicit and does not suggest a patient with acute symptoms is being kept in routine clinic. This node stands alone and its explanation does not preteach the next node's exploration decision. Difficulty is moderate at most, not a stretch item.

record.title: Persistent post-bypass pain despite a negative CT
fairness: Independent answer: diagnostic surgical laparoscopy. The learner must recognize that the technically described negative CT and normal lactate do not eliminate a dangerous post-bypass internal hernia, then use persistent pain and increasing tenderness to choose exploration over more observation/imaging or a luminal test.

The repeat-CT option is a genuine management error to consider here, not simply a repeated-test wording cue: apparent reassuring imaging competes with worsening clinical findings. Endoscopy addresses a plausible luminal explanation but does not resolve the concerning trajectory.

No confident clinical error or equally defensible offered answer identified in this continued inpatient course. The explanation appropriately does not turn a negative CT into a guarantee or normal lactate into a rule-out.

The prior node explains initial CT selection without disclosing exploration. The current update restates acquisition, results and symptom trajectory, and the shared presentation supplies bypass anatomy and timing; the later decision is coherent and independently solvable within that presentation.

record.title: Choose reflux-monitoring modality and medication state in established GERD
fairness: On-treatment impedance-pH monitoring is the defensible best offered investigation: prior grade C esophagitis establishes GERD, while persistent symptoms during documented twice-daily PPI treatment leave their current reflux association unresolved.

Two consequential protocol decisions are required: distinguish established from unproven GERD to select medication state, then recognize why pH-only monitoring has insufficient scope for ongoing symptoms during acid suppression. The full balanced matrix prevents majority-component convergence.

Each choice is the same type of investigation with comparable wording. The task does not itself say 'on therapy' or 'nonacid', and the diagnosis-establishing endoscopy is legitimate necessary evidence rather than a diagnosis-task giveaway.

The later visit follows the initial medication-timing node coherently and supplies all decision-critical prior disease and current treatment observations when read alone. Earlier feedback teaches proper dosing but does not disclose the monitoring protocol.

The exact time on the revised regimen is not stated. That limits claims that medical treatment has definitively failed or surgery is indicated; it does not overturn the best monitoring modality/state among the offered tests. Preserve that distinction and do not invent a universal treatment-duration cutoff.
This is high-yield foregut/reflux workup with moderate difficulty. The guideline attribution is not newly verified offline, and this PASS does not approve an operative indication.
suggestions: Keep the established-GERD evidence and actual dosing/adherence record. If a future node asks whether to escalate treatment or operate, separately supply the supported treatment course and decision criteria rather than inheriting a claim of refractory disease from this test-selection item.

record.title: Separate symptomatic episodes from discordant overnight glucose readings
fairness: Sampling a typical spontaneous symptomatic episode is the best offered investigation. The nocturnal CGM readings conflict with contemporaneous finger-stick values and are not the symptomatic daytime events; the well-state clinic sample does not resolve the latter.

Two consequential steps are present: interpret measurement provenance and temporal mismatch, then choose the sampling context rather than a fast or glucose challenge. The normal observations have specific evidentiary roles rather than merely declaring a diagnosis excluded.

The three choices are comparable sampling strategies with no unique explanation, rhetorical absolute or majority-component key. 'Separately timed' helps orient the table but does not identify which test to order.

The opening node stands alone. Its explanation does not disclose the later diet or medication answers. The later case supplies an established diagnosis explicitly rather than requiring the learner to assume that this proposed test has already proved it.

This tests a high-yield diagnostic principle. No confident inaccuracy identified from the candidate; the exact current guideline position on provocative testing has not been independently reverified offline.
suggestions: Retain the episode/sample distinction and the caution that an isolated low does not establish etiology. Avoid expanding this into a second task about the full hypoglycemia laboratory panel.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: On admission, intermittent cramps had become continuous with repeated retching. His abdomen was tender without guarding; pulse was 96/min and blood pressure 122/76 mmHg. The record showed normal renal function and no prior contrast reaction.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial study best fits {patientName}'s recorded acute presentation after gastric bypass?

answerChoices.label: Upper endoscopy of the pouch and anastomosis
answerChoices.rationale: Endoscopy assesses the pouch and gastrojejunal lumen, but it does not survey the entire altered mesenteric and intestinal anatomy needed for this acute pain course.

answerChoices.label: Computed tomography with oral and intravenous contrast
answerChoices.rationale: Contrast-enhanced CT surveys the altered bowel limbs, mesentery and possible extraluminal complications in this stable acute presentation.

answerChoices.label: Water-soluble contrast examination of the upper gastrointestinal tract
answerChoices.rationale: A luminal contrast study can assess proximal passage or leakage, but it provides less complete evaluation of the bowel and mesentery for the current acute course.

decisionNodes.explanation: The change to persistent acute pain after RYGB requires assessment beyond the pouch lumen. Contrast-enhanced CT with oral contrast evaluates the reconstructed bowel pathways and extraluminal anatomy. This is a review of the hospital investigation, not a clinic CT order.
sourceLabels: World Society of Emergency Surgery / IFSO; World Journal of Emergency Surgery (2022)

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: CT was acquired with oral and intravenous contrast and reviewed with the bypass operative report. It showed no fixed transition, no free air and no reported mesenteric swirl. Despite fluids and repeated reassessment, continuous pain and retching persisted and focal tenderness increased. Lactate remained within that laboratory's interval.

answerChoices.label: Repeat contrast CT after another observation period
answerChoices.rationale: The first study was adequately acquired for the question. Another observation-and-scan cycle does not resolve the concerning persistent course and can delay recognition of an internal hernia.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Endoscopy is useful for a luminal source, but persistent acute symptoms after RYGB can arise from an internal hernia outside its field. The negative CT and normal lactate do not settle that risk.

answerChoices.label: Proceed to diagnostic surgical laparoscopy
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent acute pain and retching with increasing tenderness after RYGB justify prompt exploration despite inconclusive CT. A normal lactate is not evidence that the concerning course has resolved.

decisionNodes.explanation: A negative CT does not exclude an internal hernia after RYGB. The persistent acute symptoms and increasing tenderness justify prompt surgical exploration in the recorded hospital setting. Neither a normal lactate nor the absence of a reported swirl substitutes for clinical reassessment.

record.title: Source control after a sleeve leak with shock and peritonitis
fairness: Independent answer: urgent operative exploration with washout and drainage. The learner must integrate the distribution of fluid with new hypotension, tachycardia and diffuse guarding, then change from a potentially localized/endoscopic leak strategy to operative source control.

Percutaneous drainage and endoscopic treatment are credible approaches in other leak states; the current deterioration makes them inferior here. The shared resuscitation and antimicrobials prevent the key from winning merely by being the only complete treatment bundle.

The word 'Urgent' is appropriate to the actual operative option and is supported by necessary findings, not a gratuitous rhetorical cue. No confident clinical error or competing best answer identified. Preserve the instability findings rather than hide them for difficulty.

The progression from persistent symptoms to CT findings and deterioration is coherent. The preceding explanation does not select this route. The current update supplies sleeve anatomy, CT results and the decisive condition, so it remains solvable with the shared presentation even if the earlier answer is not recalled.

record.title: Function-preserving excision after representative lipomatous-tumor sampling
fairness: Marginal en bloc excision with neurovascular preservation is the best offered plan. The documented sampling includes the only nonfatty nodule and does not identify a dedifferentiated component; the symptomatic extremity lipomatous-tumor pattern supports a function-preserving local operation.

The learner must first interpret the representative fatty and nodule findings, then apply subtype-specific margin policy where a normal-tissue cuff would sacrifice the femoral nerve. The pathology detail changes the decision instead of merely naming ALT before a margin-recall task.

The nerve relationship is essential morbidity information, not an answer leak. Two options preserve the bundle, so avoiding nerve injury alone does not distinguish marginal surgery from preoperative radiation plus excision.

Targeted cores cannot guarantee absence of every unsampled malignant focus, but the wording says 'without an identified dedifferentiated component' rather than claiming absolute exclusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy is found in that limitation.

Wide excision/nerve sacrifice and adding radiotherapy are recognizable overtreatment errors for this presented pattern. The explanation's reference to a high-grade margin policy should not be read as a universal rule that a high-grade tumor requires nerve sacrifice.

This is high-yield subtype-specific surgical planning. Although the update refers to additional cores, the standalone exhibit provides both initial and targeted findings, so no prior sampling node is required.
suggestions: Clarify in feedback that high grade does not by itself mandate femoral-nerve sacrifice; resection of critical structures depends on actual involvement and the overall oncologic plan.
Preserve the targeted nodule result in any future multipart version, and re-review the preceding explanation so it does not announce this margin decision.

record.title: Calf biopsy target, corridor and method
fairness: The resident must recognize that the B corridor crosses an additional compartment despite its more intense enhancement, then combine the acceptable corridor with the preferred initial tissue-sampling method. Both decisions alter the plan.

All four options cross the same two methods with the same two targets, so component frequency and uniquely comprehensive wording do not select the answer. Greater enhancement provides a plausible competing attraction rather than identifying the key.

A posterior image-guided core of A is the single best offered initial plan under the supplied mapping. Both targets are solid enhancing intramass tissue, and the record supplies avoidance of visible neurovascular structures. Open biopsy is a recognizable escalation error rather than another equally preferred initial method.

The prior MRI explanation does not teach the corridor or method choice. The current update and table restate the tumor location, target viability and route anatomy sufficiently for this later node to stand alone.
The precise constructed procedural corridors still require clinician/anatomical sign-off; this offline review identifies no confident anatomical contradiction and does not certify procedural safety.

record.title: Desmoid surveillance after growth followed by functional recovery
fairness: Continued specialist active surveillance is the best offered plan for the supplied plateau, decreased pain, recovered usual workload, and nonthreatening anatomical relationship. Prior enlargement alone does not require escalation at the current visit.

The functional comparison is meaningful: working modified duties at the interim visit is not the same as tolerating the original workload. The learner must integrate the interval size trajectory with actual function, then decide whether treatment is currently justified.

The improving findings favor the answer clinically rather than through label matching. The three specific plans are at the same decision stage, with no unique rationale-bearing key, absolute, or convergence cue.

Initial growth and earlier symptomatic limitation make resection or systemic treatment credible temptations; they are not selected merely because the mass remains larger than baseline. The table's measurements are fictional observations, not invented treatment thresholds.

The exact duration of the plateau is not given. That limits any claim of durable stability, but the key is continued monitored surveillance, not discharge or a fixed long follow-up interval; no such durability claim is required.

Desmoid surveillance versus intervention is a high-yield contemporary management principle. This standalone node supplies the full longitudinal course and does not borrow an earlier treatment decision.
suggestions: Retain the actual usual-work comparison and the monitored nature of surveillance.
Do not turn the single plateau into a universal growth threshold or claim lasting remission. Any future interval-specific teaching point would need its own support.

record.title: Hereditary polyposis evaluation after a normal distal examination
fairness: Complete colonoscopy with APC-focused germline evaluation is the best offered plan. The mesenteric desmoid and father's early colectomy for numerous adenomas favor an APC-associated polyposis evaluation over the offered mismatch-repair pathway.

The second consequential inference is that a normal examination ending in the sigmoid does not clear the proximal colon. A hereditary direction and the extent of colorectal examination both matter to the proposed evaluation.

The balanced four-option matrix prevents 'Complete' or 'APC-focused' alone from identifying the key. The pedigree is clinical evidence, not a pre-answer named syndrome. No material nonmedical cue was found.

A negative tumor CTNNB1 result does not diagnose germline APC disease; the explanation appropriately describes raised concern rather than established FAP. APC-focused evaluation need not exclude broader genetics assessment when clinically indicated.
Desmoid/polyposis association and the limitations of incomplete colorectal examination are high-yield. The pattern is recognizable, so this is moderate rather than hard.
The standalone record includes the actual examination extent, family history, and absence of a known familial result. It does not depend on a preceding diagnosis question.
suggestions: Preserve the original procedure extent rather than replacing it with the interpretive label 'inadequate screening.'
Keep the explanation at the level of evaluation for suspected hereditary disease; do not equate CTNNB1-negative tumor testing with a proven germline diagnosis.

record.title: Escalation of progressive symptomatic mesenteric desmoid
fairness: The best offered direction is systemic treatment through sarcoma oncology. Repeated enlargement and worsening meal-limiting pain distinguish this from a stable surveillance course, while the bowel/mesenteric-root setting makes local therapy a consequential competing choice.

The two steps are recognizing clinically meaningful progression after surveillance/supportive care and selecting a systemic rather than upfront radiation approach for this anatomy. The absence of obstruction/ischemia is necessary urgency information; it does not disclose the drug.

Nirogacestat is presented as one adult systemic option, not as superior to every other desmoid drug. No definite clinical inaccuracy is identified, but current drug selection and eligibility were not externally verified in this offline review and still require clinician sign-off.

The three options are concrete treatment strategies. The oncology-referral wording is somewhat more specific than the other labels, but there is no meaningful length, convergence, absolute, or wording-match shortcut that selects the drug without clinical knowledge.
The high-yield objective is progression-driven escalation and treatment by anatomical site. Exact drug-name recall is more specialized; do not infer that it is itself a frequently tested board fact.
The standalone case supplies prior monitoring/analgesia, current trajectory, anatomy, and emergency negatives. It remains answerable without the hereditary-evaluation node.
suggestions: In feedback, replace the author-facing sentence 'The question compares systemic versus initial local treatment, not superiority among drugs' with concise clinical teaching about why this patient's progression and anatomy favor systemic care.
Retain the absence of obstruction/ischemia and the distinction between supportive care and prior tumor-directed systemic treatment.

record.title: Microscopic desmoid margin after grossly complete removal
fairness: The positive microscopic margin creates a genuine competing concern despite improving symptoms and no gross residual mass. The learner must distinguish microscopic margin involvement from persistent gross/progressive disease, then weigh the desmoid-specific significance against additional functional loss.
Surveillance is the best offered plan under this grossly complete, improving postoperative scenario. Re-excision and adjuvant RT represent plausible overapplication of malignant-sarcoma margin rules.

The explanation uses appropriately limited language: the margin can be accepted and does not automatically require treatment. It does not claim that imaging excludes microscopic disease or that RT is never appropriate.

This is a separate named patient and standalone postoperative record. The operative-extent node's explanation is not preceding feedback in this case, so it does not directly give away the answer within the encounter.
Exact postoperative desmoid margin/RT practice remains a clinician-review boundary; this offline editorial PASS is not independent verification of a universal R1 management rule.

record.title: Off-target forearm biopsy and repeat sampling
fairness: The benign pathology must first be restricted to the tissue actually sampled. The learner must then distinguish a correctable targeting failure from failure of a representative core that could justify escalation to open sampling.

The documented core throw and feasible repeat route are decision-critical observations. They do not say which biopsy method to select. Repeating the word intramass in the key is not a decisive nonmedical shortcut because both other procedures also explicitly sample the mass.

A corrected specialist image-guided core is the best offered plan. Planned incisional biopsy is possible in the broader workup but is not equally preferred merely because the first needle missed the lesion; aspiration is a credible architecture-versus-cytology error.

The standalone presentation, specimen report and needle-location exhibit contain the needed context. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; exact procedural preference remains subject to clinician approval.

record.title: Close negative anatomical margin after preoperative RT
fairness: The resident must classify the ink-negative intact epineurial boundary as a close negative margin, then interpret it in the context of completed preoperative RT before recommending further local treatment.

Surveillance is the best offered action; neither sacrificing an uninvolved nerve nor an automatic boost follows from this record. The options represent recognizable over-treatment errors rather than competing equally indicated treatments.
The negative findings are necessary to distinguish this scenario from residual disease and are not avoidable diagnosis disclosure. No option is uniquely long or assembled by majority components.
The standalone patient has an explicit preoperative-RT and postoperative-surgery chronology. It does not depend on the different thigh patient's RT-sequencing answer.
No confident inaccuracy is identified. The exact margin/boost application still requires named clinician approval; an editorial PASS does not establish a universal margin-width rule.

record.title: Retroperitoneal tumor sampling after fatty-component biopsy
fairness: The best offered plan is image-guided coaxial cores of region B. The existing fatty-component pathology establishes useful information, but its documented footprint does not establish the histology of the distinct enhancing solid nodule.

Two decisions remain: recognize possible heterogeneous tumor biology despite the well-differentiated biopsy label, then select representative sampling by a percutaneous rather than open route. Repeating A and using open biopsy are recognizable clinical errors.

The four labels form a balanced target-by-method matrix; neither B nor the percutaneous method appears only in the key. The access record is decision-critical feasibility information, not a key-only permission, because it applies to both targets. No material grammar, length, absolute, or diagnostic-label giveaway was found.

Representative biopsy and avoiding an unnecessary operative biopsy field in suspected retroperitoneal sarcoma are high-yield surgical principles. No definite clinical inaccuracy was identified in the supplied explanation.
The standalone case contains the prior result, target map, and access findings. It does not require an earlier scored biopsy decision.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between a supported fatty-component diagnosis and the unsampled nodule; do not turn possible higher-grade tissue into a declared diagnosis before sampling.
If recomposed with another sampling node, review prior feedback again: the MDM2 sampling item tests a closely overlapping limitation and could become rehearsed recall.

record.title: Histotype and organ preservation in retroperitoneal resection
fairness: Tumor/cava resection with preservation of kidney and colon is the best offered plan. The morphology, myoid panel, and caval involvement support leiomyosarcoma, while the organ interfaces do not supply an indication to remove either adjacent organ.

The two consequential steps are inferring the tumor family from the biopsy/venous context and applying its operative implications to the actual organ interfaces. The broad kidney-and-colon operation is the closest credible error through overgeneralization of retroperitoneal liposarcoma surgery.

The uninvolved interfaces understandably favor organ preservation, but they are necessary findings rather than disposable answer hints: histotype can affect how apparent interfaces are used in retroperitoneal operative planning. The diagnosis itself is not supplied in the visible pre-answer fields.

All options include tumor/cava removal and balance kidney and colon inclusion. There is no component-frequency convergence. The isolated kidney-only and colon-only additions are weaker distractors than the multivisceral plan, so this is moderate rather than hard.
No definite clinical inaccuracy is identified. Preservation is judged for the stated records, not as a promise that imaging always excludes operative adherence or microscopic invasion.

The named patient, pathology, vascular plan, and staging are present in this standalone node; no prior histologic answer is needed. Histotype-informed complete resection and avoiding unnecessary organ loss are testable surgical concepts.
suggestions: Preserve the histotype and organ-interface reasoning if editing the set. Any stronger distractor should represent a real operative error without adding an unsupported organ-sacrifice rule.
Keep the explanation conditional on the supplied anatomy and findings; do not generalize radiographic fat planes into a universal guarantee of a negative operative margin.

record.title: Positive-margin unplanned excision despite negative bed MRI
fairness: The resident must reconcile no discrete MRI mass with tumor at multiple inked margins, then choose feasible definitive bed clearance rather than treat imaging as proof of microscopic clearance.

Re-excision of the scar and tumor bed is the single best offered plan in this localized, operable situation. Definitive RT is a plausible alternative when re-excision is unsuitable; the supplied anatomy makes that distinction clinically relevant here.

The statement that major nerves and vessels need not be sacrificed is necessary to establish the comparative morbidity of re-excision. It does not resolve the key pathology-versus-imaging inference on its own.

The explanation appropriately leaves subsequent RT assessment dependent on the final local-risk context instead of claiming that re-excision necessarily completes all treatment. The standalone record has a coherent chronology.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of A through the posterior corridor
answerChoices.rationale: Both targets are enhancing intramass tissue. The planned core route through the tumor-bearing muscle avoids adding another compartment to the definitive surgical field. Greater enhancement at B does not resolve that tract problem.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided core biopsy of B through the lateral corridor
answerChoices.rationale: B is an attractive enhancing target, but this route crosses peroneal muscle in another compartment before reaching the gastrocnemius mass.

answerChoices.label: Open incisional biopsy of A through the posterior corridor
answerChoices.rationale: The corridor is favorable, but an initial feasible image-guided core is preferred to creating an open biopsy wound.

answerChoices.rationale: This combines escalation of the initial method with a route through another compartment.

Greater enhancement at B does not resolve that tract problem. concept.displayName: Specialist-planned biopsy of a suspicious soft-tissue mass
concept.learningObjective: Refer a suspicious extremity mass to an experienced sarcoma team for planned image-guided core biopsy that preserves the future surgical approach.

record.title: Calf biopsy target, corridor and method
fairness: The resident must recognize that the B corridor crosses an additional compartment despite its more intense enhancement, then combine the acceptable corridor with the preferred initial tissue-sampling method. Both decisions alter the plan.

All four options cross the same two methods with the same two targets, so component frequency and uniquely comprehensive wording do not select the answer. Greater enhancement provides a plausible competing attraction rather than identifying the key.

A posterior image-guided core of A is the single best offered initial plan under the supplied mapping. Both targets are solid enhancing intramass tissue, and the record supplies avoidance of visible neurovascular structures. Open biopsy is a recognizable escalation error rather than another equally preferred initial method.

The prior MRI explanation does not teach the corridor or method choice. The current update and table restate the tumor location, target viability and route anatomy sufficiently for this later node to stand alone.
The precise constructed procedural corridors still require clinician/anatomical sign-off; this offline review identifies no confident anatomical contradiction and does not certify procedural safety.

record.title: Off-target forearm biopsy and repeat sampling
fairness: The benign pathology must first be restricted to the tissue actually sampled. The learner must then distinguish a correctable targeting failure from failure of a representative core that could justify escalation to open sampling.

The documented core throw and feasible repeat route are decision-critical observations. They do not say which biopsy method to select. Repeating the word intramass in the key is not a decisive nonmedical shortcut because both other procedures also explicitly sample the mass.

A corrected specialist image-guided core is the best offered plan. Planned incisional biopsy is possible in the broader workup but is not equally preferred merely because the first needle missed the lesion; aspiration is a credible architecture-versus-cytology error.

The standalone presentation, specimen report and needle-location exhibit contain the needed context. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; exact procedural preference remains subject to clinician approval.

decisionNodes.stem: What further local treatment should be recommended from {patientName}’s postoperative records?

answerChoices.label: Begin surveillance after the completed local treatment
answerChoices.rationale: The record describes a close negative planned anatomical boundary, not demonstrated residual tumor. Its context does not establish a need to sacrifice the nerve or add an automatic radiation boost.

answerChoices.label: Re-excise the bed including the preserved nerve
answerChoices.rationale: Wider surgery would sacrifice an uninvolved major nerve merely to widen a negative epineurial boundary. The supplied record does not justify that functional cost.

answerChoices.label: Deliver an additional postoperative radiation boost
answerChoices.rationale: Preoperative RT has already been given. An automatic postoperative boost for a close or microscopic margin is not established and adds late toxicity.

record.title: Close negative anatomical margin after preoperative RT
fairness: The resident must classify the ink-negative intact epineurial boundary as a close negative margin, then interpret it in the context of completed preoperative RT before recommending further local treatment.

Surveillance is the best offered action; neither sacrificing an uninvolved nerve nor an automatic boost follows from this record. The options represent recognizable over-treatment errors rather than competing equally indicated treatments.
The negative findings are necessary to distinguish this scenario from residual disease and are not avoidable diagnosis disclosure. No option is uniquely long or assembled by majority components.
The standalone patient has an explicit preoperative-RT and postoperative-surgery chronology. It does not depend on the different thigh patient's RT-sequencing answer.
No confident inaccuracy is identified. The exact margin/boost application still requires named clinician approval; an editorial PASS does not establish a universal margin-width rule.

record.title: Positive-margin unplanned excision despite negative bed MRI
fairness: The resident must reconcile no discrete MRI mass with tumor at multiple inked margins, then choose feasible definitive bed clearance rather than treat imaging as proof of microscopic clearance.

Re-excision of the scar and tumor bed is the single best offered plan in this localized, operable situation. Definitive RT is a plausible alternative when re-excision is unsuitable; the supplied anatomy makes that distinction clinically relevant here.

The statement that major nerves and vessels need not be sacrificed is necessary to establish the comparative morbidity of re-excision. It does not resolve the key pathology-versus-imaging inference on its own.

The explanation appropriately leaves subsequent RT assessment dependent on the final local-risk context instead of claiming that re-excision necessarily completes all treatment. The standalone record has a coherent chronology.

record.title: Retroperitoneal tumor sampling after fatty-component biopsy
fairness: The best offered plan is image-guided coaxial cores of region B. The existing fatty-component pathology establishes useful information, but its documented footprint does not establish the histology of the distinct enhancing solid nodule.

Two decisions remain: recognize possible heterogeneous tumor biology despite the well-differentiated biopsy label, then select representative sampling by a percutaneous rather than open route. Repeating A and using open biopsy are recognizable clinical errors.

The four labels form a balanced target-by-method matrix; neither B nor the percutaneous method appears only in the key. The access record is decision-critical feasibility information, not a key-only permission, because it applies to both targets. No material grammar, length, absolute, or diagnostic-label giveaway was found.

Representative biopsy and avoiding an unnecessary operative biopsy field in suspected retroperitoneal sarcoma are high-yield surgical principles. No definite clinical inaccuracy was identified in the supplied explanation.
The standalone case contains the prior result, target map, and access findings. It does not require an earlier scored biopsy decision.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between a supported fatty-component diagnosis and the unsampled nodule; do not turn possible higher-grade tissue into a declared diagnosis before sampling.
If recomposed with another sampling node, review prior feedback again: the MDM2 sampling item tests a closely overlapping limitation and could become rehearsed recall.

record.title: Histotype and organ preservation in retroperitoneal resection
fairness: Tumor/cava resection with preservation of kidney and colon is the best offered plan. The morphology, myoid panel, and caval involvement support leiomyosarcoma, while the organ interfaces do not supply an indication to remove either adjacent organ.

The two consequential steps are inferring the tumor family from the biopsy/venous context and applying its operative implications to the actual organ interfaces. The broad kidney-and-colon operation is the closest credible error through overgeneralization of retroperitoneal liposarcoma surgery.

The uninvolved interfaces understandably favor organ preservation, but they are necessary findings rather than disposable answer hints: histotype can affect how apparent interfaces are used in retroperitoneal operative planning. The diagnosis itself is not supplied in the visible pre-answer fields.

All options include tumor/cava removal and balance kidney and colon inclusion. There is no component-frequency convergence. The isolated kidney-only and colon-only additions are weaker distractors than the multivisceral plan, so this is moderate rather than hard.
No definite clinical inaccuracy is identified. Preservation is judged for the stated records, not as a promise that imaging always excludes operative adherence or microscopic invasion.

The named patient, pathology, vascular plan, and staging are present in this standalone node; no prior histologic answer is needed. Histotype-informed complete resection and avoiding unnecessary organ loss are testable surgical concepts.
suggestions: Preserve the histotype and organ-interface reasoning if editing the set. Any stronger distractor should represent a real operative error without adding an unsupported organ-sacrifice rule.
Keep the explanation conditional on the supplied anatomy and findings; do not generalize radiographic fat planes into a universal guarantee of a negative operative margin.

concept.displayName: Initial active surveillance for selected desmoid tumors
concept.learningObjective: Choose specialist active surveillance as the initial strategy for newly diagnosed, stable or minimally symptomatic desmoid disease without critical threat or meaningful functional deterioration.

record.title: Desmoid surveillance after growth followed by functional recovery
fairness: Continued specialist active surveillance is the best offered plan for the supplied plateau, decreased pain, recovered usual workload, and nonthreatening anatomical relationship. Prior enlargement alone does not require escalation at the current visit.

The functional comparison is meaningful: working modified duties at the interim visit is not the same as tolerating the original workload. The learner must integrate the interval size trajectory with actual function, then decide whether treatment is currently justified.

The improving findings favor the answer clinically rather than through label matching. The three specific plans are at the same decision stage, with no unique rationale-bearing key, absolute, or convergence cue.

Initial growth and earlier symptomatic limitation make resection or systemic treatment credible temptations; they are not selected merely because the mass remains larger than baseline. The table's measurements are fictional observations, not invented treatment thresholds.

The exact duration of the plateau is not given. That limits any claim of durable stability, but the key is continued monitored surveillance, not discharge or a fixed long follow-up interval; no such durability claim is required.

Desmoid surveillance versus intervention is a high-yield contemporary management principle. This standalone node supplies the full longitudinal course and does not borrow an earlier treatment decision.
suggestions: Retain the actual usual-work comparison and the monitored nature of surveillance.
Do not turn the single plateau into a universal growth threshold or claim lasting remission. Any future interval-specific teaching point would need its own support.

concept.displayName: Distinguish a desmoid microscopic margin from a mandate for repeat surgery or RT.
concept.learningObjective: Distinguish a desmoid microscopic margin from a mandate for repeat surgery or RT.

record.title: Microscopic desmoid margin after grossly complete removal
fairness: The positive microscopic margin creates a genuine competing concern despite improving symptoms and no gross residual mass. The learner must distinguish microscopic margin involvement from persistent gross/progressive disease, then weigh the desmoid-specific significance against additional functional loss.
Surveillance is the best offered plan under this grossly complete, improving postoperative scenario. Re-excision and adjuvant RT represent plausible overapplication of malignant-sarcoma margin rules.

The explanation uses appropriately limited language: the margin can be accepted and does not automatically require treatment. It does not claim that imaging excludes microscopic disease or that RT is never appropriate.

This is a separate named patient and standalone postoperative record. The operative-extent node's explanation is not preceding feedback in this case, so it does not directly give away the answer within the encounter.
Exact postoperative desmoid margin/RT practice remains a clinician-review boundary; this offline editorial PASS is not independent verification of a universal R1 management rule.

concept.learningObjective: Recognize the limits of a normal distal examination when planning colorectal and hereditary evaluation for possible APC-associated disease.

record.title: Hereditary polyposis evaluation after a normal distal examination
fairness: Complete colonoscopy with APC-focused germline evaluation is the best offered plan. The mesenteric desmoid and father's early colectomy for numerous adenomas favor an APC-associated polyposis evaluation over the offered mismatch-repair pathway.

The second consequential inference is that a normal examination ending in the sigmoid does not clear the proximal colon. A hereditary direction and the extent of colorectal examination both matter to the proposed evaluation.

The balanced four-option matrix prevents 'Complete' or 'APC-focused' alone from identifying the key. The pedigree is clinical evidence, not a pre-answer named syndrome. No material nonmedical cue was found.

A negative tumor CTNNB1 result does not diagnose germline APC disease; the explanation appropriately describes raised concern rather than established FAP. APC-focused evaluation need not exclude broader genetics assessment when clinically indicated.
Desmoid/polyposis association and the limitations of incomplete colorectal examination are high-yield. The pattern is recognizable, so this is moderate rather than hard.
The standalone record includes the actual examination extent, family history, and absence of a known familial result. It does not depend on a preceding diagnosis question.
suggestions: Preserve the original procedure extent rather than replacing it with the interpretive label 'inadequate screening.'
Keep the explanation at the level of evaluation for suspected hereditary disease; do not equate CTNNB1-negative tumor testing with a proven germline diagnosis.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The latest specialist records show enlargement on successive studies and pain that now limits meals despite supportive treatment. Care to date has consisted of clinical/MRI monitoring and analgesia.
decisionNodes.stem: Which current management plan best fits {patientName}’s mesenteric desmoid course?

answerChoices.label: Begin nirogacestat through sarcoma oncology
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent symptomatic progression warrants reconsidering surveillance. For mesenteric disease around critical bowel/vessel anatomy, a systemic pathway is standard; nirogacestat is one supported adult option. The question compares systemic versus initial local treatment, not superiority among drugs.

answerChoices.label: Deliver external-beam radiotherapy to the mesenteric tumor
answerChoices.rationale: RT can be a selected desmoid treatment, but this untreated progressive mesenteric disease has an established systemic pathway. Its bowel/vessel setting does not make upfront radiation automatically preferable before medical options.

answerChoices.label: Continue the existing clinical/MRI surveillance plan
answerChoices.rationale: The repeated growth and increasing meal-limiting symptoms are not a stable surveillance course. Continuing the same plan would leave the current clinical deterioration unaddressed.

record.title: Escalation of progressive symptomatic mesenteric desmoid
fairness: The best offered direction is systemic treatment through sarcoma oncology. Repeated enlargement and worsening meal-limiting pain distinguish this from a stable surveillance course, while the bowel/mesenteric-root setting makes local therapy a consequential competing choice.

The two steps are recognizing clinically meaningful progression after surveillance/supportive care and selecting a systemic rather than upfront radiation approach for this anatomy. The absence of obstruction/ischemia is necessary urgency information; it does not disclose the drug.

Nirogacestat is presented as one adult systemic option, not as superior to every other desmoid drug. No definite clinical inaccuracy is identified, but current drug selection and eligibility were not externally verified in this offline review and still require clinician sign-off.

The three options are concrete treatment strategies. The oncology-referral wording is somewhat more specific than the other labels, but there is no meaningful length, convergence, absolute, or wording-match shortcut that selects the drug without clinical knowledge.
The high-yield objective is progression-driven escalation and treatment by anatomical site. Exact drug-name recall is more specialized; do not infer that it is itself a frequently tested board fact.
The standalone case supplies prior monitoring/analgesia, current trajectory, anatomy, and emergency negatives. It remains answerable without the hereditary-evaluation node.
suggestions: In feedback, replace the author-facing sentence 'The question compares systemic versus initial local treatment, not superiority among drugs' with concise clinical teaching about why this patient's progression and anatomy favor systemic care.
Retain the absence of obstruction/ischemia and the distinction between supportive care and prior tumor-directed systemic treatment.

record.title: Function-preserving excision after representative lipomatous-tumor sampling
fairness: Marginal en bloc excision with neurovascular preservation is the best offered plan. The documented sampling includes the only nonfatty nodule and does not identify a dedifferentiated component; the symptomatic extremity lipomatous-tumor pattern supports a function-preserving local operation.

The learner must first interpret the representative fatty and nodule findings, then apply subtype-specific margin policy where a normal-tissue cuff would sacrifice the femoral nerve. The pathology detail changes the decision instead of merely naming ALT before a margin-recall task.

The nerve relationship is essential morbidity information, not an answer leak. Two options preserve the bundle, so avoiding nerve injury alone does not distinguish marginal surgery from preoperative radiation plus excision.

Targeted cores cannot guarantee absence of every unsampled malignant focus, but the wording says 'without an identified dedifferentiated component' rather than claiming absolute exclusion. No confident clinical inaccuracy is found in that limitation.

Wide excision/nerve sacrifice and adding radiotherapy are recognizable overtreatment errors for this presented pattern. The explanation's reference to a high-grade margin policy should not be read as a universal rule that a high-grade tumor requires nerve sacrifice.

This is high-yield subtype-specific surgical planning. Although the update refers to additional cores, the standalone exhibit provides both initial and targeted findings, so no prior sampling node is required.
suggestions: Clarify in feedback that high grade does not by itself mandate femoral-nerve sacrifice; resection of critical structures depends on actual involvement and the overall oncologic plan.
Preserve the targeted nodule result in any future multipart version, and re-review the preceding explanation so it does not announce this margin decision.
