record.title: Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms with negative plasma CMV testing
fairness: Ileocolonoscopy with mucosal biopsy best distinguishes the represented mucosal differential, including tissue-invasive CMV and medication injury. Repeated negative blood testing does not settle tissue disease. A cellular-immunity assay does not provide a competing tissue diagnosis.

The resident must reject false reassurance from blood testing and choose a test that distinguishes remaining mucosal causes. This is a useful transplant infection decision; the two other blood-focused choices make it moderate rather than hard.

No direct lexical cue names the biopsy. The repeated plasma assay is a weaker distractor because it has already been performed, but it still represents a recognizable mistaken reliance on blood surveillance. Do not count its repetition as an independent hard discriminator.

The standalone update includes persistent symptoms, prior tests, medication and structural context. 'Antiviral treatment records' in the presentation anticipates the broader record but neither establishes the cause of this episode nor supplies the investigation.
suggestions: For a future harder variant, compare tissue evaluation with a genuinely plausible competing diagnostic or medication strategy; do not add more negative tests just to lengthen the stem.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional medication change best fits {patientName}'s new marrow findings?

answerChoices.label: Substitute febuxostat
answerChoices.rationale: Febuxostat also inhibits xanthine oxidase and is not a safe way to preserve the same azathioprine regimen.

answerChoices.label: Stop allopurinol
answerChoices.rationale: The new thiopurine interaction with marrow toxicity requires immediate medication review; withholding the added inhibitor prevents further unreviewed exposure.

answerChoices.label: Reduce tacrolimus
answerChoices.rationale: Measured tacrolimus exposure is unchanged, and lowering it does not address thiopurine accumulation.

decisionNodes.explanation: Allopurinol inhibits a pathway that inactivates azathioprine metabolites. The new marrow findings make this a consequential medication interaction. record.title: Cytopenias after adding allopurinol to azathioprine
fairness: Stopping allopurinol is the best listed additional medication change while the service addresses cytopenias and the azathioprine regimen. Substitution with febuxostat preserves the important xanthine-oxidase interaction concern; reducing tacrolimus does not address the represented temporal pattern.

The resident identifies the interaction from chronology and then avoids a same-class substitution error. The febuxostat alternative gives this high-yield drug interaction more than simple culprit recognition.

The task's 'additional' wording is justified by the shared active assessment of azathioprine; it does not mean stopping allopurinol is the complete cytopenia management plan. No option is a uniquely cautious composite answer.

The standalone update explicitly supplies the regimen, added medicine and blood-count changes; 'A later record' is understandable without the former pregnancy companion. The explanation appropriately acknowledges management-strategy differences without inventing a dose.

The represented biopsy, recovering function and appropriate exposure support continuing the selected CNI-based maintenance plan. New toxicity or deterioration would require reassessment.

record.title: Tacrolimus during recovering delayed graft function
fairness: Continuing the represented tacrolimus regimen is the best listed plan given improving output/creatinine, tissue-supported tubular injury and verified target-range exposure. Earlier dialysis alone does not establish ongoing CNI toxicity or justify a routine switch to sirolimus.

The resident interprets the recovery trajectory against the earlier dialysis requirement, then decides whether the existing regimen needs alteration. This is a practical high-yield distinction between delayed function and an indication to withdraw immunosuppression.

Continue/withhold/replace options are parallel specific plans. The target-range result is relevant but is not presented as universally excluding CNI injury. No reliable nonmedical cue selects the key.
The case is now standalone and includes the biopsy and trajectory it requires; 'subsequent biopsy' does not leave a decision-critical prior result missing.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During the outside kidney-transplant admission, creatinine remained above the established baseline after correction of volume status; graft flow and drainage were adequate. The core contains interstitial mononuclear inflammation with cells crossing tubular epithelium. Arteries are represented, with no inflammatory cells beneath their endothelial lining. Polyomavirus staining and plasma BK testing are negative. There is no glomerular or peritubular capillary inflammation or endothelial C4d staining, and donor-specific HLA antibodies are not detected. No antirejection treatment has been given.
decisionNodes.stem: Which initial antirejection treatment best fits {patientName}'s persistent kidney-allograft dysfunction and represented biopsy?

answerChoices.label: Intravenous antithymocyte globulin therapy
answerChoices.rationale: The tissue does not show the represented vascular severity or a failed steroid course that would support this escalation.

answerChoices.label: Intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent dysfunction with this cellular distribution, negative BK assessment and no represented arteritis supports initial corticosteroid treatment.

answerChoices.label: Plasma exchange with intravenous immunoglobulin therapy
answerChoices.rationale: The represented antibody, capillary and complement findings do not support the humoral process targeted by this backbone.

decisionNodes.explanation: The interstitial and tubular pattern, considered with the viral assessment, supports a cellular process. The sampled arteries lack intimal inflammation, and this is an untreated episode rather than steroid failure. Initial corticosteroid treatment is the best listed plan; lymphocyte depletion belongs to a different severity or response boundary. No numeric Banff grade is inferred.

question.explanation: The interstitial and tubular pattern, considered with the viral assessment, supports a cellular process. The sampled arteries lack intimal inflammation, and this is an untreated episode rather than steroid failure. record.title: Initial therapy for untreated cellular graft injury
fairness: Intravenous methylprednisolone is the best listed initial treatment for the represented untreated interstitial/tubular cellular process without the described arterial, viral or humoral component. The explicit arterial sampling repairs an important severity ambiguity without inventing a Banff grade.
The resident interprets the biopsy and competing infection/humoral findings, then distinguishes initial steroid therapy from lymphocyte-depleting rescue. These are consequential high-yield decisions.

The negatives are extensive and lower difficulty, but they establish relevant treatment boundaries; there is no key-only wording overlap or option-length advantage. The task prespecifies antirejection treatment appropriately for choosing among three such regimens.

The current update retains persistent dysfunction and the treatment-naive stage, so the standalone node no longer needs a preceding biopsy-selection question. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; exact pathology/severity ranking still needs clinician sign-off.
suggestions: Consider tightening the report wording without removing the represented arterial assessment, infection studies or initial-treatment boundary.

record.title: Renewed graft dysfunction after BK treatment
fairness: Repeat allograft biopsy is the best listed cause-defining plan before increasing or further decreasing maintenance therapy. Prior biopsy-proven BK and subsequent plasma clearance do not identify the cause of renewed dysfunction.

The resident must interpret the discordance between viral and renal trajectories, then avoid opposite empiric immunosuppression changes with different hazards. The prior initial improvement is useful chronology, not decorative detail.

The biopsy choice is the only investigation, but this does not automatically invalidate the option set: the case supplies a real unresolved discrepancy that determines whether an empiric drug change is justified. 'Graft-assessment plan' mildly favors evaluation; it is not a deterministic match because the other plans also include follow-up creatinine.

The standalone node includes the prior biopsy, treatment, response and new deterioration. The earlier BK case need not be seen. This is high-yield graft dysfunction reasoning with no asserted universal BK threshold.
suggestions: Use a neutral lead-in such as 'Which next plan best fits the renewed graft dysfunction?' to avoid even the mild investigation bias from 'graft-assessment plan'.

record.title: Renewed dysfunction after correction of a tacrolimus interaction
fairness: Allograft tissue is the best listed next step after the earlier exposure problem improves and renal dysfunction subsequently recurs despite valid target-range levels and the represented initial assessment. Neither further reduction nor restoration of the earlier dose follows from creatinine alone.

The resident must separate the earlier drug-interaction episode from the current unexplained course, then choose tissue assessment rather than another unsupported dose-direction change. This meets two-step reasoning and tests a high-yield anchoring error.

The different plan types are justified by a genuine unresolved causal discrepancy. The task does not name biopsy, and the explanation expressly avoids claiming that a target trough excludes all CNI injury or that dose reduction proves rejection.

The standalone chronology is coherent and complete. The interaction facts support the earlier episode rather than diagnose the renewed decline. This substantially overlaps the general renal-biopsy construct, which is a coverage consideration rather than a fairness failure.
suggestions: Keep the initial response followed by renewed deterioration; shortening this to a single high tacrolimus concentration would change the decision.

record.title: Tacrolimus dosing after a mistimed concentration
fairness: Continuing the monitored current dose while obtaining a valid predose level is the best listed plan given a postdose sample, unchanged renal function, no represented toxicity symptoms and no other medication change. The flagged value does not establish an excessive trough.

The resident interprets sampling validity and then uses the stable clinical course to choose continuation rather than precautionary dose reduction or withholding. The added treatment decision is consequential; it is not merely choosing the definition of a trough.

The shared repeat-level clause in all three choices prevents monitoring wording from identifying the answer. The explicitly stated postdose timing is necessary data, not an unfair disclosure of the dose decision.

The standalone update supplies timing, clinical trajectory and the imminent dosing decision. This is a common medication-monitoring pitfall. Its difficulty is toward the easier end of moderate; no numerical toxicity threshold is asserted.
suggestions: Preserve the stable-function and symptom context so the answer is not generalized to an ill patient merely because one specimen was mistimed.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During the outside admission, gastrointestinal biopsies demonstrated CMV cytopathic changes and positive CMV immunohistochemistry. Intravenous ganciclovir was started during repeated vomiting and profuse diarrhea. Nursing records now show full meals and scheduled oral medicines taken without vomiting; stools have decreased to two loose bowel movements daily and abdominal pain has resolved. Plasma CMV DNA is falling but remains quantifiable above the laboratory's treatment endpoint. Kidney function is unchanged, the treatment dose has been checked. The hospital is preparing discharge.

answerChoices.rationale: Clinical improvement and demonstrated oral tolerance permit oral continuation while active treatment is still needed.

answerChoices.rationale: Ongoing detectable DNA requires continued treatment, but does not by itself require continued IV delivery after clinical improvement and oral tolerance.

answerChoices.rationale: The current CMV episode has not reached its treatment endpoint. Prevention dosing is a different phase and cannot substitute for the represented active-treatment course.

decisionNodes.explanation: Route and treatment phase are different decisions. The observed improvement and oral intake support oral valganciclovir, which consensus guidance prefers when feasible for non-life-threatening disease. Quantifiable DNA above the local endpoint still calls for treatment dosing. It does not mandate continued IV delivery or justify prevention dosing. A decision about later secondary prophylaxis would be separate and is not routine.

record.title: CMV discharge therapy: route and treatment phase
fairness: Oral valganciclovir at renal-adjusted treatment dosing is the best listed discharge plan with improving gastrointestinal symptoms, demonstrated oral intake and persistent quantifiable CMV above the stated endpoint. Continued treatment does not itself require IV delivery.

Two consequential distinctions remain: infer adequate oral delivery from the clinical response, then distinguish unfinished treatment from prevention. The balanced four-cell matrix does not select the key by majority-component convergence.

'Scheduled oral medicines taken without vomiting' supports two oral options, while the unfinished virologic course supports two treatment-dose options. Neither phrase uniquely identifies the answer without integrating both observations. The intake observations are decision-critical, not gratuitous permission.

The standalone update contains the diagnosis, initial severe delivery problem, improvement and remaining treatment indication. The task is complete. No universal viral-load endpoint is invented; clinician review should retain the represented clinical improvement when accepting the route switch.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 61-year-old woman with a kidney transplant, attends clinic after an outside admission for persistent diarrhea. The founder reviews the diagnostic and antiviral treatment records.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Outside biopsies established gastrointestinal CMV disease. She is improving on oral valganciclovir, but plasma CMV DNA remains quantifiable above the service's treatment endpoint. The treatment dose is appropriate for unchanged kidney function. Absolute neutrophil counts fall from 1.0 to 0.8 × 10^9/L while she also receives mycophenolate, tacrolimus and prednisone. She is afebrile, graft function is at baseline, no rejection episode has occurred, and the transplant service considers her immunologic risk low. Blood-count support and close reassessment are being arranged.
decisionNodes.stem: Which interim medication plan best fits {patientName}'s neutrophil trajectory during the unfinished CMV treatment course?

answerChoices.label: Temporarily hold mycophenolate; retain renal-adjusted valganciclovir
answerChoices.rationale: The neutrophil decline warrants medication review; modifying the other marrow suppressant preserves correctly dosed treatment for still-active CMV.

answerChoices.label: Retain mycophenolate; lower the valganciclovir treatment dose
answerChoices.rationale: The renal dose is already correct. Neutropenia by itself is not a recommended reason to underdose the active antiviral while leaving the competing marrow suppressant unchanged.

answerChoices.label: Retain mycophenolate; replace valganciclovir with letermovir
answerChoices.rationale: A prophylactic alternative does not provide the represented active-disease treatment strategy; modifying other marrow suppressants is available in this low-risk graft context.

decisionNodes.explanation: The constructed neutrophil counts represent clinically meaningful neutropenia, not an unspecified falling white-cell trend. Guidance supports trying to preserve renal-adjusted ganciclovir exposure while addressing other marrow suppressants and considering count support. A temporary mycophenolate hold is the best listed interim plan in this low-risk graft setting; its timing, duration and restoration require transplant reassessment. This does not make mycophenolate the proven sole cause.

record.title: Medication adjustment during CMV-associated treatment neutropenia
fairness: Temporarily holding mycophenolate while retaining renal-adjusted valganciclovir is the best listed interim plan for the specified neutropenia during unfinished treatment, with low immunologic risk and count support/reassessment being arranged.

The resident interprets the neutrophil trajectory in a multiple-drug setting, then preserves antiviral treatment exposure while addressing another marrow suppressant. Lowering an otherwise appropriate treatment dose or treating active disease with letermovir are not equally supported alternatives.

The count trend supplies a meaningful problem rather than merely 'falling white cells'. No exact universal hold threshold is inferred from these constructed values. The explanation appropriately avoids asserting that mycophenolate is the proven sole cause.

The specific medication plans are comparably framed. 'Low' immunologic risk and 'appropriate' renal dosing are supplied judgments that narrow the choice but are necessary fairness boundaries here, not a nonmedical key match.

The standalone node includes current infection status, regimen, renal function and graft-risk context; it does not rely on the preceding CMV route question. This is high-yield competing drug-toxicity and treatment-efficacy reasoning.
suggestions: Keep the temporary/interim wording and explicit reassessment; do not turn this option into an automatic mycophenolate-stop rule for every declining count.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During the outside admission, kidney-allograft creatinine continued rising after a completed corticosteroid course. A repeat core now shows inflammatory cells in glomerular and peritubular capillaries with capillary C4d deposition; circulating donor-specific HLA antibodies are detected. The represented tubules and arteries lack cellular inflammatory injury, and there are no chronic glomerular double contours. Polyomavirus staining and plasma BK testing are negative. The transplant service is optimizing baseline maintenance therapy.
decisionNodes.stem: Which additional treatment backbone best fits {patientName}'s current graft findings after the completed steroid course?

answerChoices.label: Rabbit antithymocyte globulin therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Failure to improve after steroids is not by itself evidence of refractory cellular rejection; the current distribution and antibodies point to a humoral process.

answerChoices.label: Plasma exchange with intravenous immunoglobulin
answerChoices.rationale: The microvascular, complement and donor-specific antibody findings support an acute active humoral process for which this is a consensus backbone, with limited comparative efficacy evidence.

answerChoices.label: Stepwise reduction of maintenance immunosuppression
answerChoices.rationale: Reduction is important for BK disease in the appropriate context, but the represented viral assessment is negative and the microvascular antibody findings require a different strategy.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the new specimen before treating steroid nonresponse as cellular rescue failure. Capillary inflammation, C4d and donor-specific antibodies support an active antibody-mediated process; the represented tissue lacks a cellular component and chronic glomerular remodeling. Plasma exchange with IVIG is a consensus backbone for acute active AMR, with weak comparative evidence. It is not an optimal-regimen claim and does not extrapolate to chronic active AMR.

record.title: Treatment of active humoral injury after steroid nonresponse
fairness: Plasma exchange with IVIG is the best listed additional treatment backbone for the represented microvascular inflammation, C4d and donor-specific antibodies, without the described cellular or chronic glomerular component. The explanation appropriately labels the comparative evidence as weak.

The resident must reinterpret the repeat tissue rather than infer refractory cellular rejection from steroid failure, then choose mechanism-directed treatment. ATG is a credible anchoring error; maintenance reduction is an infection-pathway error.

The capillary findings and antibodies are necessary clinical observations, not a diagnosis label or direct phrase match to plasma exchange. Multiple negatives make the item moderate rather than hard but keep the competing treatment boundaries fair.
The standalone update supplies the prior course, current biopsy and background maintenance optimization. It does not depend on the earlier cellular rescue case.

Absence of glomerular double contours alone should not be taught as excluding every possible chronic AMR lesion. The text is limited to the represented tissue rather than a complete Banff classification; no confident key-changing inaccuracy is identified within this option set.
suggestions: Preserve the weak-evidence and acute-active scope qualifications; do not extend this backbone claim to all chronic active AMR.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The outside record concerns a deceased-donor kidney transplant. Dialysis was needed after implantation. A core on postoperative day 3 showed acute tubular injury without rejection. It is now postoperative day 11: urine output remains low, creatinine has not fallen between dialysis sessions, and dialysis is still required. Volume status has been corrected, Doppler studies continue to show patent vessels with adequate drainage, and valid tacrolimus predose levels are within the selected target. No fever or new infectious symptoms are documented. Supportive care continues with each proposed plan.
decisionNodes.stem: Which next graft-assessment plan best fits {patientName}'s postoperative course through day 11?

answerChoices.label: Repeat kidney-allograft core tissue sampling
answerChoices.rationale: The earlier sample establishes what was present then; continuing delayed function warrants reassessment for a new or previously unrepresented parenchymal process.

answerChoices.label: Continue supportive care with graft-function monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: Supportive care remains necessary, but an old tubular-injury sample does not establish the current cause of persistent nonrecovery.

answerChoices.label: Give intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy
answerChoices.rationale: Continuing delayed function does not establish rejection, and the cause can be assessed with tissue before directing antirejection therapy.

decisionNodes.explanation: The day-3 core is evidence about that time point. By day 11 there is still no functional recovery, so its tubular-injury finding should not substitute for current parenchymal assessment. KDIGO suggests interval biopsies during delayed function, albeit with low-quality evidence; the constructed chronology illustrates that reassessment rather than establishing a universal biopsy day. Continue necessary supportive care while the cause is determined.

concept.displayName: Reassess persistent delayed graft function with serial tissue sampling despite an earlier acute tubular injury core.
concept.learningObjective: Reassess persistent delayed graft function with serial tissue sampling despite an earlier acute tubular injury core.
concept.historyPolicy: Preserve old concepts, exact versions, frozen encounters and FSRS cards. No transfer of history to changed meanings.

record.title: Persistent delayed graft function after an earlier tubular-injury biopsy
fairness: Repeat allograft sampling is the best listed next assessment for persistent dialysis dependence/nonrecovery after an earlier tubular-injury specimen and the represented reassessment of reversible contributors. The earlier biopsy does not establish the current cause.

The resident interprets the age and limited temporal scope of tissue evidence, then decides to reassess rather than anchor on tubular injury or treat presumed rejection empirically. This is a high-yield delayed-function decision.

The supportive-care sentence applies to all options, preventing the biopsy answer from being the only comprehensive plan. 'Graft-assessment plan' mildly favors investigation, but monitoring is also an assessment strategy and the unresolved course justifies comparing assessment with empiric therapy.

The day-3/day-11 sequence is explicit and standalone. The explanation treats the dates as a constructed example and acknowledges low-quality interval-biopsy evidence rather than declaring a universal mandatory biopsy day.

Individual biopsy timing can vary with risk and prior findings; this offline review does not independently verify current interval guidance. Within the represented persistent nonrecovery and offered choices, no competing option is equally compelling.
suggestions: A neutral 'Which next plan best fits the postoperative course?' would remove the mild assessment-language bias without changing the clinical information.

record.title: Choose method and timing for a child's familial APC test
fairness: Exon-dosage testing now is the best listed plan: the old method does not resolve the familial deletion, and an asymptomatic 12-year-old is not equivalent to a child facing only adult-onset actionable risk. No definite clinical error identified offline.

Method and timing are independently consequential. A resident can choose the correct method but incorrectly defer testing, or choose timely testing with the wrong method. Each component appears twice, so neither lexical matching nor majority-component convergence uniquely selects the key.

The explicit assay limitation is necessary evidence rather than a complete answer: it still leaves the clinically important now-versus-adulthood choice. Childhood actionability and an uninformative negative are high-yield principles.

The standalone presentation identifies the mother and the son's age and sex; no preceding family-workup node is required. PASS is editorial only; the exact clinical version still needs clinician review.

record.title: Bevacizumab restart with persistent postoperative wound opening
clarityIssues: The current postoperative decision is clear. No material ambiguity identified.
fairness: Withholding is the best offered plan: the elapsed interval and actual wound status are separate conditions, and the unhealed wound remains consequential despite passage of time.
The restart and dose-reduction alternatives represent recognizable attempts to treat elapsed time or dose as sufficient. The feedback appropriately avoids clearing other chemotherapy.
The exact label interval quoted in feedback was not independently verified because network access is prohibited; clinician/source confirmation remains required before clinical approval.
This first node does not teach the later perforation-specific discontinuation decision.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between interval and adequate healing, and retain the limitation on restarting after a wound complication.
Preserve the draft clinical-review status; PASS does not validate the quoted label against a current source.

record.title: Initial treatment of pembrolizumab-associated inflammatory colitis
clarityIssues: 'Attends the clinic after discharge' and 'initial ... treatment' create a small retrospective tense mismatch; the task is otherwise complete.
fairness: Withholding pembrolizumab and starting systemic corticosteroids is the best offered treatment for the represented persistent inflammatory illness after the negative initial infectious evaluation.

The learner must interpret exposure, symptoms and workup, then choose initial therapy rather than symptomatic continuation or immediate biologic escalation. Absence of deep ulcers and no steroid course help distinguish the closest treatment alternative.

No exact toxicity grade, steroid dose or universal biologic preference is asserted. Initial treatment still requires clinical review of the exact case; no current guideline verification was performed offline.
The first node establishes a coherent starting treatment stage and does not disclose the later infection-reassessment answer.
suggestions: Make the task explicitly retrospective: ask what initial treatment should have been recommended at that documented assessment.
Retain decision-critical findings and avoid adding unsupported grading cutoffs or dose rules.

record.title: Investigate maternal risk after a negative paternal family-target test
fairness: The affected maternal aunt's constitutional panel is the best offered first investigation. The adequate paternal-target negative does not establish the cause of cancers on the maternal side. The mother's unmatched tumor and the unaffected patient's blood are credible but less informative alternatives for this stated inherited-risk goal.

The consequential choices are the informative family member and the type of evidence: a deceased affected relative's tumor is tempting, while the living affected relative supplies constitutional DNA. The paternal negative establishes context; it should not be counted as an additional third reasoning step.

The options do not have a unique majority-component intersection: both blood choices are constitutional, but choosing the affected aunt still requires interpreting the family history. No answer-specific feasibility statement disqualifies the other available specimens.

Branch-specific interpretation of a true negative and affected-relative-first testing are high yield. No definite clinical inaccuracy identified offline. The standalone family record is coherent and does not require earlier feedback; editorial PASS is not clinical approval.
suggestions: Optional readability edit for a future version: replace 'her sister' with 'maternal aunt' and 'the consultand' with the patient's name. These are not blocking ambiguities in the current complete record.

record.title: Determine future rasburicase exposure after a suspected oxidant reaction
fairness: Permanent avoidance is the best listed plan. The oxygen-resistant cyanosis, abnormal blood color and preserved arterial oxygen tension strongly support methemoglobinemia; a prior reassuring G6PD screen does not negate the actual reaction. No definite clinical error identified offline.

The learner must recognize the reaction from observations and then distinguish an event-based contraindication from a screening-based temporary hold. Repeat G6PD testing is a plausible but insufficient condition for deciding future exposure; monitoring is not a remedy for the demonstrated adverse reaction.

'Permanently' is a substantive safety disposition, not an unjustified rhetorical absolute here. The classic findings are diagnostically informative, but the diagnosis is not supplied before the choice and the normal screening result creates a consequential competing interpretation.

This is a high-yield drug-toxicity and contraindication principle. The task supplies the drug context and asks about the future record after completed hospital treatment; the standalone case needs no earlier urate node. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Reassess infection before escalating treatment of refractory colitis
fairness: Flexible sigmoidoscopy with tissue CMV assessment is the best offered additional investigation. The change during corticosteroid exposure warrants renewed infection assessment, and a negative plasma PCR does not settle tissue-invasive colonic disease. No definite clinical inaccuracy identified offline; this does not independently verify diagnostic performance or a treatment-escalation threshold.

Two consequential interpretations remain: the earlier negative workup does not close the later infectious differential, and the current negative blood test does not substitute for the relevant tissue assessment. Repeat noninvasive testing is a credible temptation, while calprotectin assesses inflammation rather than establishing its infectious cause.

The repeated CMV wording is not unique to the key, and the blood result is necessary to the tested limitation rather than an answer disclosure. Stool testing may also be clinically indicated; the stem fairly asks for the best additional investigation, not a complete mutually exclusive care package.

This is a high-yield treatment-toxicity/infection distinction. The retrospective hospital task, ongoing shared care and absence of free air keep the setting coherent after discharge; it stands alone without the preserved checkpoint-colitis node. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Breast risk management after a true negative and separate VUS
clarityIssues: The management task is clear. Current update and exhibit duplicate most findings; compress the presentation without deleting the family-risk context.
fairness: Routine age-based screening is the best offered plan under the represented history: the validated familial negative and nonactionable VUS must both be interpreted before choosing management.
Carrier surveillance and risk-reducing surgery are meaningful overinterpretation errors; no independent high-risk indication is supplied.

The sequence follows coherently and the current node restates the familial result, separate VUS and relevant other risk history. Earlier feedback scaffolds the VUS principle but does not supply the final risk-management decision.
PASS is an editorial judgment on the supplied text, not clinical approval or verification of a specific screening schedule.
suggestions: Remove redundant prose/exhibit repetition while retaining the evidence supporting a true negative and the absence of another represented high-risk indication.
Retain needs_clinician_review until Melissa approves the exact version.

record.title: Choose method and timing for a child's familial APC test
fairness: Exon-dosage testing now is the best listed plan: the old method does not resolve the familial deletion, and an asymptomatic 12-year-old is not equivalent to a child facing only adult-onset actionable risk. No definite clinical error identified offline.

Method and timing are independently consequential. A resident can choose the correct method but incorrectly defer testing, or choose timely testing with the wrong method. Each component appears twice, so neither lexical matching nor majority-component convergence uniquely selects the key.

The explicit assay limitation is necessary evidence rather than a complete answer: it still leaves the clinically important now-versus-adulthood choice. Childhood actionability and an uninformative negative are high-yield principles.

The standalone presentation identifies the mother and the son's age and sex; no preceding family-workup node is required. PASS is editorial only; the exact clinical version still needs clinician review.

record.title: Investigate maternal risk after a negative paternal family-target test
fairness: The affected maternal aunt's constitutional panel is the best offered first investigation. The adequate paternal-target negative does not establish the cause of cancers on the maternal side. The mother's unmatched tumor and the unaffected patient's blood are credible but less informative alternatives for this stated inherited-risk goal.

The consequential choices are the informative family member and the type of evidence: a deceased affected relative's tumor is tempting, while the living affected relative supplies constitutional DNA. The paternal negative establishes context; it should not be counted as an additional third reasoning step.

The options do not have a unique majority-component intersection: both blood choices are constitutional, but choosing the affected aunt still requires interpreting the family history. No answer-specific feasibility statement disqualifies the other available specimens.

Branch-specific interpretation of a true negative and affected-relative-first testing are high yield. No definite clinical inaccuracy identified offline. The standalone family record is coherent and does not require earlier feedback; editorial PASS is not clinical approval.
suggestions: Optional readability edit for a future version: replace 'her sister' with 'maternal aunt' and 'the consultand' with the patient's name. These are not blocking ambiguities in the current complete record.

record.title: Bevacizumab restart with persistent postoperative wound opening
clarityIssues: The current postoperative decision is clear. No material ambiguity identified.
fairness: Withholding is the best offered plan: the elapsed interval and actual wound status are separate conditions, and the unhealed wound remains consequential despite passage of time.
The restart and dose-reduction alternatives represent recognizable attempts to treat elapsed time or dose as sufficient. The feedback appropriately avoids clearing other chemotherapy.
The exact label interval quoted in feedback was not independently verified because network access is prohibited; clinician/source confirmation remains required before clinical approval.
This first node does not teach the later perforation-specific discontinuation decision.
suggestions: Keep the distinction between interval and adequate healing, and retain the limitation on restarting after a wound complication.
Preserve the draft clinical-review status; PASS does not validate the quoted label against a current source.

record.title: Initial treatment of pembrolizumab-associated inflammatory colitis
clarityIssues: 'Attends the clinic after discharge' and 'initial ... treatment' create a small retrospective tense mismatch; the task is otherwise complete.
fairness: Withholding pembrolizumab and starting systemic corticosteroids is the best offered treatment for the represented persistent inflammatory illness after the negative initial infectious evaluation.

The learner must interpret exposure, symptoms and workup, then choose initial therapy rather than symptomatic continuation or immediate biologic escalation. Absence of deep ulcers and no steroid course help distinguish the closest treatment alternative.

No exact toxicity grade, steroid dose or universal biologic preference is asserted. Initial treatment still requires clinical review of the exact case; no current guideline verification was performed offline.
The first node establishes a coherent starting treatment stage and does not disclose the later infection-reassessment answer.
suggestions: Make the task explicitly retrospective: ask what initial treatment should have been recommended at that documented assessment.
Retain decision-critical findings and avoid adding unsupported grading cutoffs or dose rules.

record.title: Reassess infection before escalating treatment of refractory colitis
fairness: Flexible sigmoidoscopy with tissue CMV assessment is the best offered additional investigation. The change during corticosteroid exposure warrants renewed infection assessment, and a negative plasma PCR does not settle tissue-invasive colonic disease. No definite clinical inaccuracy identified offline; this does not independently verify diagnostic performance or a treatment-escalation threshold.

Two consequential interpretations remain: the earlier negative workup does not close the later infectious differential, and the current negative blood test does not substitute for the relevant tissue assessment. Repeat noninvasive testing is a credible temptation, while calprotectin assesses inflammation rather than establishing its infectious cause.

The repeated CMV wording is not unique to the key, and the blood result is necessary to the tested limitation rather than an answer disclosure. Stool testing may also be clinically indicated; the stem fairly asks for the best additional investigation, not a complete mutually exclusive care package.

This is a high-yield treatment-toxicity/infection distinction. The retrospective hospital task, ongoing shared care and absence of free air keep the setting coherent after discharge; it stands alone without the preserved checkpoint-colitis node. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Determine future rasburicase exposure after a suspected oxidant reaction
fairness: Permanent avoidance is the best listed plan. The oxygen-resistant cyanosis, abnormal blood color and preserved arterial oxygen tension strongly support methemoglobinemia; a prior reassuring G6PD screen does not negate the actual reaction. No definite clinical error identified offline.

The learner must recognize the reaction from observations and then distinguish an event-based contraindication from a screening-based temporary hold. Repeat G6PD testing is a plausible but insufficient condition for deciding future exposure; monitoring is not a remedy for the demonstrated adverse reaction.

'Permanently' is a substantive safety disposition, not an unjustified rhetorical absolute here. The classic findings are diagnostically informative, but the diagnosis is not supplied before the choice and the normal screening result creates a consequential competing interpretation.

This is a high-yield drug-toxicity and contraindication principle. The task supplies the drug context and asks about the future record after completed hospital treatment; the standalone case needs no earlier urate node. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Discordant size and attenuation during imatinib treatment
fairness: Continuing the current imatinib regimen is the best offered answer when the marked attenuation reduction on matched imaging is considered with the absence of a new enhancing nodule or new lesion. Size enlargement creates a real competing interpretation that could otherwise prompt escalation or a change to sunitinib.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret the discordant size/density findings rather than treating diameter as the entire response assessment, then decide whether the findings justify changing systemic therapy. The exhibit is essential; removing its response data prevents a defensible treatment choice.

Matching the acquisition phase and lesion region makes the attenuation comparison interpretable. The observations concerning hemorrhage and peritumoral fluid address alternative explanations rather than explicitly declaring a response. No arbitrary numerical threshold is supplied or required by the task.

The options are parallel, concrete systemic-treatment actions. The first two repeat 'current imatinib regimen,' so this overlap does not uniquely cue the key. No decisive nonmedical shortcut, diagnosis-label giveaway or option-length cue was identified.

The explanation says the findings 'can reflect imatinib effect' and retains specialist response review. That qualification matters: this record should not teach that every enlarging, less-dense GIST is responding. I identify no confident clinical inaccuracy, but this offline PASS is not independent verification of a universal response criterion.

Recognition of non-size response findings in treated GIST is a high-yield surgical-oncology concept. The substantial size increase makes the wrong treatment changes credible; predicted difficulty is moderate.
The independent case states the pretreatment diagnosis, mutation, reason for treatment, current therapy and comparison scan. It stands alone without the neoadjuvant question or its explanation.

record.title: Lymphatic invasion after apparently complete endoscopic resection
fairness: Lymphatic tumor involvement overrides the otherwise reassuring mucosal depth, small size and clear margins. In the stated fit patient, gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy is the single best offered plan. Repeating local excision does not address the relevant risk.

The microscopic description requires interpretation followed by distinguishing local clearance from potential nodal disease. Surveillance remains a meaningful temptation because the other reported features favor endoscopic curability.

Lymphatic spaces and lymphadenectomy share a word root, but that relationship alone cannot distinguish appropriate nodal treatment from management of a fully excised primary; this is necessary clinical evidence rather than a decisive nonmedical cue.
Self-contained presentation and complete task; no preceding answer is needed. High-yield gastric endoscopic-curability boundary. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Initial treatment of a KIT exon 11 cardia GIST
fairness: Preoperative imatinib with resection reassessment is the single best offered plan. The learner must interpret the tumor phenotype and molecular result, then integrate the morbidity of the proposed total gastrectomy to choose treatment before surgery.

Immediate gastrectomy is a genuine competing definitive treatment for localized GIST, but the cardia anatomy creates a reason to seek tumor response first. Avapritinib represents a molecular-treatment selection error rather than a wording caricature. The three options are specific plans at the same decision stage.

The absence of active bleeding or obstruction keeps an urgent intervention from displacing elective planning; absence of metastatic disease defines the treatment setting. These necessary constraints are not interpretive teaching sentences.

Both preoperative options share the reassessment wording, so that phrasing does not uniquely identify the key. No persuasive key-only overlap, length outlier, convergence or absolute-language cue was found.

The explanation appropriately avoids promising that imatinib will eliminate the need for total gastrectomy or implying that every large GIST requires neoadjuvant treatment. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in this offline review.

Genotype-informed GIST treatment and choosing neoadjuvant treatment to reduce surgical morbidity are high-yield surgical concepts. Difficulty is predicted moderate, not hard: the molecular and anatomical discriminators are fairly explicit.

This singleton supplies its own pathology, operative proposal and extent. It does not depend on the separate tissue-acquisition question or its feedback; the presentation, age/sex, short complaint and complete task are coherent.

record.title: Operation for a localized peripheral gastric GIST
fairness: The immunophenotype supports GIST, and the peripheral 3.2-cm fundic anatomy supports full-thickness wedge resection rather than total gastrectomy/D2 or submucosal shelling out. Histology and anatomy must both inform the operative choice.

The distractors represent confusing GIST with gastric adenocarcinoma and confusing local resection with enucleation. They are easier than the closest specialist alternatives, but remain recognizable resident errors for a high-yield surgical principle.

The presentation explicitly frames retrospective review of a tumor and its later resection, so the initial operation question and subsequent margin review are coherent. The first item supplies its own pathology and anatomy.

No decisive wording-only cue or confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Negative nodes do not alone establish that lymphadenectomy is unnecessary; the learner still needs the tumor-type distinction.

record.title: Imatinib after complete resection of previously metastatic GIST
fairness: Continuing effective, tolerated imatinib is the single best offered plan. Biopsy-confirmed liver metastasis establishes the prior metastatic setting; complete resection and currently clear imaging do not by themselves convert that history into the finite adjuvant-treatment setting of initially localized disease.

The two consequential steps are to determine the treatment context from the original disease despite current absence of visible tumor, then choose maintenance rather than a localized-adjuvant endpoint or recurrence-triggered restart. Complete removal without rupture is relevant counterpressure, not decorative detail.

A finite adjuvant course is a credible category error after an apparently complete operation. Stopping and restarting at measurable recurrence is also a recognizable error prompted by the patient's clear scans. Neither is made wrong through explanatory wording in its option.

All options are concrete continuation/stopping policies. The key is not uniquely elaborate or generic, and the two stopping options have different timing rather than being synonymous. The patient's question motivates the decision without supplying the answer.
No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The explanation correctly ties continuation to effective, tolerated therapy and does not supply an invented duration or dose.

Treatment continuity in previously metastatic GIST is high-yield. The resection history adds meaningful discrimination beyond simply recalling treatment of unresected metastatic disease; predicted difficulty is moderate.

This singleton includes the original metastatic proof, treatment response, operation and present follow-up. The lack of a separate Current update is not a continuity gap because the exhibit provides the chronology. Named age/sex, complaint and task are coherent.

record.title: Additional staging of diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma
fairness: Laparoscopy with washings is the single best offered procedure for this diffuse, locally advanced pattern despite CT without visible metastases. EUS addresses locoregional detail, and PET/CT does not settle occult peritoneal involvement. The necessary negative CT is data, not an unfair exclusion.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret the diffuse poorly cohesive cancer and extramural findings, then choose the staging method that can change the proposed treatment sequence. This is a high-yield gastric-cancer staging decision.
The first node is self-contained. Its explanation prepares the importance of peritoneal staging without giving the later positive-cytology treatment answer.

The 17 kept records, 28 retirement proposals, recorded holds and parked alternatives were noted but not adjudicated. Clinical judgments are offline assessments of the supplied visible fields, not fresh source verification or clinical sign-off. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified exam frequencies. Runtime rendering, waits and source-ledger accuracy were not tested.

record.title: Treatment sequence after positive peritoneal cytology
fairness: Concordant malignant cells establish peritoneal involvement despite a negative visual survey. No treatment has begun and no bleeding or obstructive indication for palliation is supplied; systemic treatment followed by reassessment is the best offered sequence.

The real competing error is proceeding with gastrectomy because no macroscopic deposits were seen. Interpreting the discordant staging observations and changing treatment intent/sequence are two consequential steps.

Chronology follows the first node coherently. The shared presentation, current update and cytology exhibit supply the facts needed without remembering the earlier CT. Prior feedback does not specify this answer.

The explanation appropriately leaves later surgery conditional; it does not promise conversion to resectability or prescribe an unsupported regimen. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in this offline review.

record.title: Microscopic GIST margin versus rupture and recurrence risk
fairness: The supplied gastric site, 3.2-cm size, low mitotic count, intact removal and absence of gross residual disease distinguish a microscopic positive edge from rupture or a high-risk residual-disease situation. With completion total gastrectomy required, surveillance is the best offered plan.

Both major completion surgery and automatic adjuvant imatinib are credible responses to a positive margin that the learner must reconsider using tumor risk and re-excision burden. These are genuinely consequential linked interpretations.

The postoperative narrowing is a new operative consequence, not a contradiction of the earlier tumor not encircling the cardia. The second node repeats the tumor type, size, mitoses and margin/rupture findings and can be answered independently.

Earlier advice to obtain complete removal does not tell the learner how to manage a microscopic edge afterward. The explanation appropriately avoids claiming every R1 GIST needs neither re-excision nor treatment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Adjuvant boundary after resection of high-risk D842V GIST
fairness: Size and mitotic activity create a real temptation to recommend adjuvant treatment, but D842V makes routine imatinib inappropriate and metastatic-drug efficacy does not establish an adjuvant avapritinib standard. Surveillance is the defensible offered plan after intact complete resection.

The learner must first interpret recurrence risk, then apply mutation-specific sensitivity and the difference between metastatic and adjuvant evidence. Removing either risk or genotype changes the meaningful comparison.
The repeated phrase "after complete resection" is shared across all choices and does not uniquely cue the key. Surveillance is a named plan rather than a vague individualized-management answer.

Self-contained and high yield. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, but the absence of an established adjuvant targeted-drug indication is time-sensitive and not freshly source-verified under the no-network restriction. This PASS remains an editorial assessment requiring clinician sign-off.

record.title: Adjuvant treatment after upfront R0 D2 gastrectomy
fairness: Among the offered choices, CAPOX is defensible after upfront clear-margin D2 resection of stage III disease in this recovered patient. The extent of dissection and absence of preoperative treatment make the radiation and perioperative-treatment extrapolation errors consequential.

Retained mismatch-repair proteins, renal function and neuropathy assessment address relevant treatment modifiers. The question supplies final stage rather than asking the learner to reconstruct it from an unspecified positive-node count; that is fair for this management objective.
The repeated CAPOX component does not uniquely identify the key: deciding whether to add nivolumab still requires knowledge. All options are comparably specific postoperative regimens.

Self-contained and high yield. No confident inaccuracy identified, but the time-sensitive immunotherapy/adjuvant boundary has not been freshly verified under the no-network constraint; editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Lymphatic invasion after apparently complete endoscopic resection
fairness: Lymphatic tumor involvement overrides the otherwise reassuring mucosal depth, small size and clear margins. In the stated fit patient, gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy is the single best offered plan. Repeating local excision does not address the relevant risk.

The microscopic description requires interpretation followed by distinguishing local clearance from potential nodal disease. Surveillance remains a meaningful temptation because the other reported features favor endoscopic curability.

Lymphatic spaces and lymphadenectomy share a word root, but that relationship alone cannot distinguish appropriate nodal treatment from management of a fully excised primary; this is necessary clinical evidence rather than a decisive nonmedical cue.
Self-contained presentation and complete task; no preceding answer is needed. High-yield gastric endoscopic-curability boundary. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX chemotherapy
answerChoices.rationale: Capecitabine and oxaliplatin are supported after curative D2 surgery for stage II/III disease. This is postoperative treatment after upfront surgery, not selection of a new perioperative regimen.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant capecitabine chemoradiation
answerChoices.rationale: The completed R0 D2 record lacks the margin or inadequate-dissection boundary that would make a postoperative local-control strategy more compelling.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant CAPOX plus nivolumab
answerChoices.rationale: The adjuvant nivolumab trial after upfront D2 surgery did not establish added benefit. A newer perioperative immunotherapy approval is not interchangeable with this postoperative-only plan.

record.title: Adjuvant treatment after upfront R0 D2 gastrectomy
fairness: Among the offered choices, CAPOX is defensible after upfront clear-margin D2 resection of stage III disease in this recovered patient. The extent of dissection and absence of preoperative treatment make the radiation and perioperative-treatment extrapolation errors consequential.

Retained mismatch-repair proteins, renal function and neuropathy assessment address relevant treatment modifiers. The question supplies final stage rather than asking the learner to reconstruct it from an unspecified positive-node count; that is fair for this management objective.
The repeated CAPOX component does not uniquely identify the key: deciding whether to add nivolumab still requires knowledge. All options are comparably specific postoperative regimens.

Self-contained and high yield. No confident inaccuracy identified, but the time-sensitive immunotherapy/adjuvant boundary has not been freshly verified under the no-network constraint; editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Operation for a localized peripheral gastric GIST
fairness: The immunophenotype supports GIST, and the peripheral 3.2-cm fundic anatomy supports full-thickness wedge resection rather than total gastrectomy/D2 or submucosal shelling out. Histology and anatomy must both inform the operative choice.

The distractors represent confusing GIST with gastric adenocarcinoma and confusing local resection with enucleation. They are easier than the closest specialist alternatives, but remain recognizable resident errors for a high-yield surgical principle.

The presentation explicitly frames retrospective review of a tumor and its later resection, so the initial operation question and subsequent margin review are coherent. The first item supplies its own pathology and anatomy.

No decisive wording-only cue or confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Negative nodes do not alone establish that lymphadenectomy is unnecessary; the learner still needs the tumor-type distinction.

record.title: Microscopic GIST margin versus rupture and recurrence risk
fairness: The supplied gastric site, 3.2-cm size, low mitotic count, intact removal and absence of gross residual disease distinguish a microscopic positive edge from rupture or a high-risk residual-disease situation. With completion total gastrectomy required, surveillance is the best offered plan.

Both major completion surgery and automatic adjuvant imatinib are credible responses to a positive margin that the learner must reconsider using tumor risk and re-excision burden. These are genuinely consequential linked interpretations.

The postoperative narrowing is a new operative consequence, not a contradiction of the earlier tumor not encircling the cardia. The second node repeats the tumor type, size, mitoses and margin/rupture findings and can be answered independently.

Earlier advice to obtain complete removal does not tell the learner how to manage a microscopic edge afterward. The explanation appropriately avoids claiming every R1 GIST needs neither re-excision nor treatment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

decisionNodes.stem: Which postoperative plan should be discussed for {patientName}'s completely resected gastric tumor?

answerChoices.label: CT surveillance after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: The adverse risk features justify close sarcoma follow-up, but do not make an imatinib-resistant driver sensitive. Metastatic avapritinib activity does not establish routine adjuvant benefit after complete resection.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant imatinib after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: Size and mitotic activity cannot overcome primary D842V resistance. Adjuvant imatinib is not indicated for this molecular subtype.

answerChoices.label: Adjuvant avapritinib after complete resection
answerChoices.rationale: Selecting an active drug from the metastatic setting does not establish an adjuvant indication in a patient with complete local removal. A clinical trial is a separate discussion.

decisionNodes.explanation: High recurrence risk is not a substitute for a supported adjuvant drug. D842V excludes routine adjuvant imatinib, and the established avapritinib indication concerns unresectable or metastatic disease. Use risk-based surveillance and sarcoma review rather than invent an adjuvant standard.

record.title: Adjuvant boundary after resection of high-risk D842V GIST
fairness: Size and mitotic activity create a real temptation to recommend adjuvant treatment, but D842V makes routine imatinib inappropriate and metastatic-drug efficacy does not establish an adjuvant avapritinib standard. Surveillance is the defensible offered plan after intact complete resection.

The learner must first interpret recurrence risk, then apply mutation-specific sensitivity and the difference between metastatic and adjuvant evidence. Removing either risk or genotype changes the meaningful comparison.
The repeated phrase "after complete resection" is shared across all choices and does not uniquely cue the key. Surveillance is a named plan rather than a vague individualized-management answer.

Self-contained and high yield. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, but the absence of an established adjuvant targeted-drug indication is time-sensitive and not freshly source-verified under the no-network restriction. This PASS remains an editorial assessment requiring clinician sign-off.

record.title: Initial treatment of a KIT exon 11 cardia GIST
fairness: Preoperative imatinib with resection reassessment is the single best offered plan. The learner must interpret the tumor phenotype and molecular result, then integrate the morbidity of the proposed total gastrectomy to choose treatment before surgery.

Immediate gastrectomy is a genuine competing definitive treatment for localized GIST, but the cardia anatomy creates a reason to seek tumor response first. Avapritinib represents a molecular-treatment selection error rather than a wording caricature. The three options are specific plans at the same decision stage.

The absence of active bleeding or obstruction keeps an urgent intervention from displacing elective planning; absence of metastatic disease defines the treatment setting. These necessary constraints are not interpretive teaching sentences.

Both preoperative options share the reassessment wording, so that phrasing does not uniquely identify the key. No persuasive key-only overlap, length outlier, convergence or absolute-language cue was found.

The explanation appropriately avoids promising that imatinib will eliminate the need for total gastrectomy or implying that every large GIST requires neoadjuvant treatment. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in this offline review.

Genotype-informed GIST treatment and choosing neoadjuvant treatment to reduce surgical morbidity are high-yield surgical concepts. Difficulty is predicted moderate, not hard: the molecular and anatomical discriminators are fairly explicit.

This singleton supplies its own pathology, operative proposal and extent. It does not depend on the separate tissue-acquisition question or its feedback; the presentation, age/sex, short complaint and complete task are coherent.

decisionNodes.stem: Which systemic-treatment plan best fits {patientName}'s first response assessment for gastric GIST?

answerChoices.label: Continue the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: A substantial fall in attenuation on comparable scans can represent GIST response despite increased size. The lack of a new enhancing nodule or additional lesion supports continuing while the specialist team follows the response, rather than declaring resistance from diameter alone.

answerChoices.label: Escalate the current imatinib regimen
answerChoices.rationale: Size has increased, but the density change is a competing treatment-effect signal. Escalation for presumed resistance should not follow a diameter-only progression call before integrated GIST response review.

answerChoices.label: Replace imatinib with sunitinib
answerChoices.rationale: A second-line drug presumes failure or intolerance. The supplied discordant scan does not establish failure, and dose-limiting toxicity is absent.

decisionNodes.explanation: The larger diameter cannot be ignored, but it cannot be interpreted alone. On matched contrast imaging, the marked attenuation decrease without a new enhancing nodule can reflect imatinib effect even as a GIST enlarges. Continue the current regimen with specialist response review rather than escalate or switch on size alone. This is not a claim that every enlarging low-density lesion is responding.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Pretreatment tissue and plan
items.value: Core biopsy showed DOG1-positive GIST with a KIT exon 11 deletion. The cardia location prompted preoperative imatinib before the proposed total gastrectomy.

items.label: Matched contrast CT measurements
items.value: The same acquisition phase and lesion region were used. Maximum diameter changed from 8.0 to 10.8 cm; mean attenuation changed from 72 to 34 HU.

items.label: Other imaging observations
items.value: No new enhancing intratumoral nodule or additional lesion is present. There is no internal high-attenuation blood product or peritumoral fluid.

record.title: Discordant size and attenuation during imatinib treatment
fairness: Continuing the current imatinib regimen is the best offered answer when the marked attenuation reduction on matched imaging is considered with the absence of a new enhancing nodule or new lesion. Size enlargement creates a real competing interpretation that could otherwise prompt escalation or a change to sunitinib.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret the discordant size/density findings rather than treating diameter as the entire response assessment, then decide whether the findings justify changing systemic therapy. The exhibit is essential; removing its response data prevents a defensible treatment choice.

Matching the acquisition phase and lesion region makes the attenuation comparison interpretable. The observations concerning hemorrhage and peritumoral fluid address alternative explanations rather than explicitly declaring a response. No arbitrary numerical threshold is supplied or required by the task.

The options are parallel, concrete systemic-treatment actions. The first two repeat 'current imatinib regimen,' so this overlap does not uniquely cue the key. No decisive nonmedical shortcut, diagnosis-label giveaway or option-length cue was identified.

The explanation says the findings 'can reflect imatinib effect' and retains specialist response review. That qualification matters: this record should not teach that every enlarging, less-dense GIST is responding. I identify no confident clinical inaccuracy, but this offline PASS is not independent verification of a universal response criterion.

Recognition of non-size response findings in treated GIST is a high-yield surgical-oncology concept. The substantial size increase makes the wrong treatment changes credible; predicted difficulty is moderate.
The independent case states the pretreatment diagnosis, mutation, reason for treatment, current therapy and comparison scan. It stands alone without the neoadjuvant question or its explanation.

answerChoices.label: Continue imatinib during scan-negative follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The liver biopsy established metastatic GIST before treatment. Resection and a clear current scan do not convert ongoing effective metastatic therapy into a finite adjuvant course; continue while effective and tolerated.

answerChoices.label: Set an adjuvant-course endpoint and then stop imatinib
answerChoices.rationale: This applies a finite localized-adjuvant framework to previously biopsy-proven metastatic disease. The original liver metastasis remains consequential after all visible sites have been removed.

answerChoices.label: Stop imatinib now and restart at measurable recurrence
answerChoices.rationale: A monitored stop-and-restart policy is not equivalent to maintaining effective treatment in metastatic GIST. A current clear scan does not establish that interruption is safe.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret the pretreatment liver biopsy before assigning the current treatment phase. This remains previously metastatic GIST despite complete resection and clear scans. Effective, tolerated imatinib continues; neither a finite localized-adjuvant endpoint nor scan-triggered stop-and-restart follows from radiographic clearance.

items.value: A gastric GIST and biopsy-confirmed liver metastasis both carried a KIT exon 11 alteration.

items.label: Current follow-up

record.title: Imatinib after complete resection of previously metastatic GIST
fairness: Continuing effective, tolerated imatinib is the single best offered plan. Biopsy-confirmed liver metastasis establishes the prior metastatic setting; complete resection and currently clear imaging do not by themselves convert that history into the finite adjuvant-treatment setting of initially localized disease.

The two consequential steps are to determine the treatment context from the original disease despite current absence of visible tumor, then choose maintenance rather than a localized-adjuvant endpoint or recurrence-triggered restart. Complete removal without rupture is relevant counterpressure, not decorative detail.

A finite adjuvant course is a credible category error after an apparently complete operation. Stopping and restarting at measurable recurrence is also a recognizable error prompted by the patient's clear scans. Neither is made wrong through explanatory wording in its option.

All options are concrete continuation/stopping policies. The key is not uniquely elaborate or generic, and the two stopping options have different timing rather than being synonymous. The patient's question motivates the decision without supplying the answer.
No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified. The explanation correctly ties continuation to effective, tolerated therapy and does not supply an invented duration or dose.

Treatment continuity in previously metastatic GIST is high-yield. The resection history adds meaningful discrimination beyond simply recalling treatment of unresected metastatic disease; predicted difficulty is moderate.

This singleton includes the original metastatic proof, treatment response, operation and present follow-up. The lack of a separate Current update is not a continuity gap because the exhibit provides the chronology. Named age/sex, complaint and task are coherent.
