record.title: Hospital record review — initial splenic abscess source control
fairness: The resident must interpret a stable, localized, unruptured infection and the liquid, unseptated cavity, then choose source control while accounting for substantial pulmonary operative risk. Drainage, splenectomy and continued antibiotic management are recognizable competing treatment strategies.

An image-guided catheter drainage attempt is the best offered initial plan. The CT observations support accessibility without explicitly calling the collection drainable, and the explanation properly retains antibiotics rather than treating drainage as their replacement.

The anatomy and respiratory history favor the key, but they do so clinically, not through answer-label repetition or a teaching sentence announcing eligibility. The item does not require an invented antibiotic-failure duration. Splenectomy remains a credible treatment rather than an absurd distractor, and the explanation appropriately avoids claiming every later collection is drainable.

No confident clinical error is identified. Size, exact access route and procedural feasibility are not fully specified, so this should remain an initial image-guided drainage assessment/attempt, not a guarantee of technical success. The visible record does not establish a precise size cutoff or a universally mandatory approach.

The historical decision point is explicitly identified, so the clinic setting does not imply that the patient currently has untreated sepsis. All required initial data are present in this standalone node; no later treatment or prior scored answer is needed.
suggestions: Optional shortening: remove the presentation's reference to 'subsequent hospital records' because this standalone task only uses the initial decision point.

Keep culture-directed antibiotics as shared ongoing care when comparing source-control plans. Preserve the explanation's limited claim of a drainage attempt and avoid deriving an exact size or duration rule from this record.

record.title: Painful back lump — change in procedural phase
fairness: The longstanding pore-bearing lesion and the new tense, tender, fluctuant inflammatory episode support acute drainage rather than proceeding with the previously booked complete excision. The diagnosis is not supplied as a label, and the prior elective indication makes excision a real competing plan. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The consequential reasoning is to interpret the changed state of the longstanding lesion and let that change the procedural phase. Aspiration is a weaker competitor, but it is a specific alternative decompression procedure rather than a generic reassurance or knowingly untreated lesion.

The explanation correctly distinguishes debris on ultrasound from proof of infection. It also presents inflamed-tissue dissection as less favorable, not an absolute prohibition on all excision in every inflamed cyst. This avoids a false binary based on imaging debris.

All three labels are parallel procedures on the same lesion, without a uniquely complete key, explanatory option wording or nonmedical phrase match. The stem supplies the elective plan and new findings directly; no earlier question is needed.

Recognizing when an acute change alters definitive cyst management is a high-yield surgical decision. The familiar pattern and weaker aspiration competitor keep the difficulty moderate rather than hard.

record.title: Foot admission review - setting and source control
fairness: The deep plantar cavity between tendons and worsening function support hospital-capable drainage/debridement with systemic treatment. Improving redness, no fever and a susceptible surface isolate do not establish source control.
The balanced four-option matrix requires source-control selection and setting selection. Each component appears twice, so component-frequency convergence does not identify the key.
The historical hospital frame identifies whose decision is reviewed but does not itself establish that admission was appropriate; anatomy must justify the plan.
The operative-specimen follow-up is coherent. This offline editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Persistent axillary drainage — procedure selection
fairness: The supplied findings support a persistent superficial communicating tract despite improvement in new inflammatory nodules. Choosing deroofing requires distinguishing that structural problem from an acute collection and then matching procedural extent to the localized burden. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The established HS diagnosis is appropriate background for this management task and does not identify the procedure by itself. Probe passage is an observed anatomical finding, not a diagnosis-label shortcut. All options name axillary procedures with comparable specificity.

Incision and drainage is less suitable for the described non-distended communicating structure. Regional excision is a real chronic-disease option, but the localized mapped finding and freely mobile surrounding skin favor the offered lesion-directed procedure. This ranking does not imply that every excisional technique is inappropriate for localized HS; limited excision is not one of the offered choices.

The case supplies its own treatment response and procedural mapping. It stands alone without an earlier staging or treatment answer. Matching acute versus chronic structural HS disease to procedural scope is high-yield, with moderate rather than hard discrimination here.

record.title: Hospital infection review - initial exploration
fairness: Progression during treatment, deep symptoms beyond erythema and fascial fluid support urgent exploration despite absent gas, a low laboratory score and maintained blood pressure.
The learner weighs conflicting evidence, then selects action over imaging or observation. MRI and monitored treatment are credible errors from overreliance on reassuring findings.
The explanation appropriately says negative findings do not reliably exclude necrotizing infection; it does not claim every fascial-fluid finding proves necrosis.
Subsequent operative and wound updates are coherent. This offline editorial PASS is not clinical approval or fresh guideline verification.
suggestions: For precision in a future version, name the laboratory instrument instead of laboratory risk score; no invented numeric cutoff is needed.

record.title: Recurrent cleft disease — elective wound strategy
fairness: The candidate explicitly separates resolved acute inflammation from the elective wound decision and states that excision is planned. Off-midline closure is a defensible best choice among the offered wound strategies given recurrence after midline repair and the stated prolonged open-wound care constraint. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The care constraint legitimately favors a closed strategy, but does not distinguish the two closed options without clinical knowledge. It is decision-critical patient context rather than an unfair key-only permission. The prior midline failure is relevant history, not proof that closure in general has failed.

Open secondary healing remains a legitimate alternative in general; the explanation correctly ranks it for this patient's support situation and acknowledges that closure can still require substantial wound care. It does not promise uncomplicated healing.

The two consequential considerations are wound-care feasibility and the relative suitability of closure location in recurrent disease. The competing strategies are specific, parallel and at the same decision stage. This is moderate, high-yield application rather than a guarantee about operative outcomes.
All earlier drainage, operative history and current resolution are restated in the candidate. The elective task stands alone and does not depend on answering the separate acute-drainage item.

record.title: Recurrent back swelling — radiolucent foreign-body assessment
fairness: The candidate supports targeted ultrasonography as the best next investigation: recurrence after drainage raises a residual local-source problem; the penetrating material and adequate negative radiographs must then be interpreted before choosing a superficial localization method. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The negative radiograph does not exclude the relevant material. Correct-site coverage is necessary to distinguish repeating an inadequately targeted study from changing modalities. CT remains a real anatomical alternative, but the superficial focus supports ultrasound first in the described situation.

The prior drainage note is evidence about an unresolved source, not the name of the keyed test. No key-only word match, conspicuous label-length advantage, convergence or rhetorical absolute identifies ultrasound without clinical knowledge.

The repeat-radiography distractor is weaker for a resident who knows the material limitation, so this is moderate rather than hard. Retained foreign material in recurrent local infection is a useful, commonly taught surgical concept.
The case is self-contained: the prior procedure and imaging results are supplied directly, without requiring an earlier question or explanation.

case.presentation: Marcus Reed, a 62-year-old man, attends clinic after a foot-infection admission. The founder reviews the referring hospital's initial records. Oral treatment had reduced the visible redness around a plantar ulcer, but drainage and difficulty bearing weight increased. Imaging described a cavity beneath the plantar fascia extending between flexor tendons; the surface swab was susceptible to the oral drug. He was afebrile with palpable pedal pulses.

A firm focus remains beneath the skin while the surrounding redness has diminished.

record.title: Recurrent back swelling — radiolucent foreign-body assessment
fairness: The candidate supports targeted ultrasonography as the best next investigation: recurrence after drainage raises a residual local-source problem; the penetrating material and adequate negative radiographs must then be interpreted before choosing a superficial localization method. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The negative radiograph does not exclude the relevant material. Correct-site coverage is necessary to distinguish repeating an inadequately targeted study from changing modalities. CT remains a real anatomical alternative, but the superficial focus supports ultrasound first in the described situation.

The prior drainage note is evidence about an unresolved source, not the name of the keyed test. No key-only word match, conspicuous label-length advantage, convergence or rhetorical absolute identifies ultrasound without clinical knowledge.

The repeat-radiography distractor is weaker for a resident who knows the material limitation, so this is moderate rather than hard. Retained foreign material in recurrent local infection is a useful, commonly taught surgical concept.
The case is self-contained: the prior procedure and imaging results are supplied directly, without requiring an earlier question or explanation.

case.presentation: Priya Ellis, a 34-year-old woman with hidradenitis suppurativa, returns to clinic after medical treatment reduced the formation of new tender nodules. Drainage repeatedly returns from the same two axillary openings. Between them, a narrow band is palpable beneath mobile skin. During procedural mapping a probe passed between the openings in the superficial plane, with scant fluid released. The rest of the axillary skin moves freely during arm elevation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which procedure is the best next option for Priya Ellis's persistent axillary problem?

answerChoices.label: Axillary tunnel deroofing
answerChoices.rationale: The response separates reduced new inflammatory lesions from a persisting superficial communicating structure. Deroofing addresses that recurrent structure; repeating acute decompression does not remove it, while regional excision exceeds the documented localized burden.

answerChoices.label: Axillary incision and drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Prior episodes may have improved after drainage, but the remaining problem is repeated output from a communicating structure rather than a newly distended acute pocket.

answerChoices.label: Axillary regional excision
answerChoices.rationale: Excision is a legitimate chronic HS treatment. For this mapped localized structure with freely moving surrounding skin, a lesion-directed deroofing option has a more appropriate scope among the offered procedures.

record.title: Persistent axillary drainage — procedure selection
fairness: The supplied findings support a persistent superficial communicating tract despite improvement in new inflammatory nodules. Choosing deroofing requires distinguishing that structural problem from an acute collection and then matching procedural extent to the localized burden. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The established HS diagnosis is appropriate background for this management task and does not identify the procedure by itself. Probe passage is an observed anatomical finding, not a diagnosis-label shortcut. All options name axillary procedures with comparable specificity.

Incision and drainage is less suitable for the described non-distended communicating structure. Regional excision is a real chronic-disease option, but the localized mapped finding and freely mobile surrounding skin favor the offered lesion-directed procedure. This ranking does not imply that every excisional technique is inappropriate for localized HS; limited excision is not one of the offered choices.

The case supplies its own treatment response and procedural mapping. It stands alone without an earlier staging or treatment answer. Matching acute versus chronic structural HS disease to procedural scope is high-yield, with moderate rather than hard discrimination here.

case.presentation: Jordan Hale, a 25-year-old man, attends an elective clinic consultation after drainage of an upper-cleft abscess. The tense swelling, warmth and acute pain have resolved. His earlier operations included pit excision followed by excision with a primary midline closure; drainage subsequently reopened along that scar. Current mapping shows connected lateral tracts and the scarred midline. Excision is planned. He can manage the expected care of a closed wound but lacks help for prolonged daily deep open-cavity dressing care; wound complications could still change that burden.

answerChoices.label: Excision with off-midline closure
answerChoices.rationale: The care constraint favors a planned closed-wound strategy over prolonged open-cavity healing, and off-midline closure is favored over another primary midline repair. It does not guarantee uncomplicated healing or eliminate dressing needs.

answerChoices.label: Excision with primary midline closure
answerChoices.rationale: A closed repair fits the dressing constraint, but repeating a primary midline strategy is less favorable than off-midline closure for the represented recurrent pilonidal disease.

answerChoices.label: Excision with open secondary healing
answerChoices.rationale: Open healing is a legitimate strategy, but its expected ongoing cavity-care burden conflicts with the documented support constraint.

record.title: Recurrent cleft disease — elective wound strategy
fairness: The candidate explicitly separates resolved acute inflammation from the elective wound decision and states that excision is planned. Off-midline closure is a defensible best choice among the offered wound strategies given recurrence after midline repair and the stated prolonged open-wound care constraint. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The care constraint legitimately favors a closed strategy, but does not distinguish the two closed options without clinical knowledge. It is decision-critical patient context rather than an unfair key-only permission. The prior midline failure is relevant history, not proof that closure in general has failed.

Open secondary healing remains a legitimate alternative in general; the explanation correctly ranks it for this patient's support situation and acknowledges that closure can still require substantial wound care. It does not promise uncomplicated healing.

The two consequential considerations are wound-care feasibility and the relative suitability of closure location in recurrent disease. The competing strategies are specific, parallel and at the same decision stage. This is moderate, high-yield application rather than a guarantee about operative outcomes.
All earlier drainage, operative history and current resolution are restated in the candidate. The elective task stands alone and does not depend on answering the separate acute-drainage item.

Ultrasound describes a superficial debris-containing cavity separate from deeper structures.

decisionNodes.stem: Which procedural plan should be selected for Robert Lewis's current back lesion?

answerChoices.label: Incision and drainage of the back lump
answerChoices.rationale: The longstanding pore-bearing lesion has changed into an acutely inflamed, tense fluid focus. The procedural choice rests on that new examination, not on ultrasound debris proving infection. Acute drainage addresses the current pressure burden while dissection through inflamed tissue is less favorable than in the earlier quiet state.

answerChoices.label: Complete excision of the back lump
answerChoices.rationale: The prior booking remains a tempting plan for the underlying lesion, but the new warmth, erythema, tension and fluctuance change the current procedural phase and make intact dissection less favorable.

answerChoices.label: Needle aspiration of the back lump
answerChoices.rationale: Aspiration may seem a smaller way to preserve the booked plan, but is less dependable than incision and drainage for the offered symptomatic cutaneous collection.

record.title: Painful back lump — change in procedural phase
fairness: The longstanding pore-bearing lesion and the new tense, tender, fluctuant inflammatory episode support acute drainage rather than proceeding with the previously booked complete excision. The diagnosis is not supplied as a label, and the prior elective indication makes excision a real competing plan. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The consequential reasoning is to interpret the changed state of the longstanding lesion and let that change the procedural phase. Aspiration is a weaker competitor, but it is a specific alternative decompression procedure rather than a generic reassurance or knowingly untreated lesion.

The explanation correctly distinguishes debris on ultrasound from proof of infection. It also presents inflamed-tissue dissection as less favorable, not an absolute prohibition on all excision in every inflamed cyst. This avoids a false binary based on imaging debris.

All three labels are parallel procedures on the same lesion, without a uniquely complete key, explanatory option wording or nonmedical phrase match. The stem supplies the elective plan and new findings directly; no earlier question is needed.

Recognizing when an acute change alters definitive cyst management is a high-yield surgical decision. The familiar pattern and weaker aspiration competitor keep the difficulty moderate rather than hard.

record.title: An incidental lesion outside operative permission
fairness: The best offered plan is to document the lesion and obtain the patient's separate decision after recovery. The unrelated, nonbleeding lesion does not supply a reason to bypass that opportunity.

Two consequential steps are present: recognize that a shoulder biopsy is outside the right-groin consent and does not need to be done during the present anesthetic, then choose later patient decision-making over immediate proxy permission.
The agent option is a plausible timing/authority error, and same-anesthetic permission is a familiar scope error. Necessary scope and urgency facts are not gratuitous cues.

The case stands alone, has a consistent patient frame, and asks a complete permission task. No confident clinical inaccuracy or decisive wording-only shortcut identified. This does not assert that the lesion is benign or requires no follow-up.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between the consent decision and the separate clinical assessment of whether biopsy is indicated.
Keep any future revision explicit about urgency and the ability to wait for the patient's own participation.

record.title: Support-dependent physiology and an agreed recovery endpoint
fairness: The best answer is to retain temporary airway permission at that handover: the pressure improves when new vasopressor support is restored, so reassuring readings do not demonstrate the stated pre-anesthetic condition.

Two consequential steps are present: interpret the dose-response evidence as persistent support dependence, then apply the patient's specific reinstatement endpoint. The competing errors are using awake appearance or repeated supported readings as sufficient recovery.
The endpoint is supplied as this patient's agreement, not a universal physiological cutoff. The explanation preserves that boundary and keeps the compression refusal separate.

Standalone presentation and update provide the baseline, current support, permission scope and task. No consequential wording-only cue or confident clinical inaccuracy identified. PASS is editorial and does not resolve source or clinician-review holds.
suggestions: Preserve the patient-specific endpoint, baseline oxygen requirement and response during infusion reduction.
If later paired with another node, recheck whether preceding feedback teaches this exact support-versus-measurement distinction.

record.title: Suspected falsification versus routine correction
fairness: The protocol, original log, enrollment chronology and instruction to reclassify post-treatment complications support referral for a research-integrity assessment beyond a routine data correction.

Two consequential steps are present: reconcile the records to identify a substantive classification discrepancy with evidence of directed alteration, then select the appropriate escalation rather than treating it as routine cleaning or a statistical-definition question.
The alternatives are credible neighboring workflows, and all concern the present response. The key's preservation step is not an omission cue because the records are already retained.

The explanation appropriately reserves the misconduct determination to the institution rather than declaring intent or guilt established. The standalone case and task are coherent; no confident clinical inaccuracy or decisive wording-only cue identified.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between grounds for referring a concern and a final finding of misconduct.
Keep the concrete record chronology if the item is shortened; it is what makes escalation more than a generic honesty answer.

record.title: A new operative proposal after sedation
fairness: The best offered process is to seek the patient's decision after recovery for the newly proposed, nonurgent left repair. Prior informed permission remains relevant to the unchanged right-sided plan.

Two consequential steps are required: separate preserved earlier consent from the new proposal, then use reversible inability and the absence of urgent left-sided findings to rank waiting over the available agent.
The agent is verified and favors repair, making that a credible competitor rather than an automatically unauthorized relative. The same-operation scope expansion is also a credible error.

Standalone chronology is clear and the task specifically concerns the left side. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the explanation does not claim that sedation invalidates all earlier consent or that agents can never decide during temporary incapacity.
suggestions: Preserve the explicit prior informed discussion, unchanged right-sided plan, new left-sided scope and nonurgent findings.
Retain the distinction from consent-scope if both remain in the bank; do not count their similar answer pattern as independent evidence of difficulty.

record.title: Support-dependent physiology and an agreed recovery endpoint
fairness: The best answer is to retain temporary airway permission at that handover: the pressure improves when new vasopressor support is restored, so reassuring readings do not demonstrate the stated pre-anesthetic condition.

Two consequential steps are present: interpret the dose-response evidence as persistent support dependence, then apply the patient's specific reinstatement endpoint. The competing errors are using awake appearance or repeated supported readings as sufficient recovery.
The endpoint is supplied as this patient's agreement, not a universal physiological cutoff. The explanation preserves that boundary and keeps the compression refusal separate.

Standalone presentation and update provide the baseline, current support, permission scope and task. No consequential wording-only cue or confident clinical inaccuracy identified. PASS is editorial and does not resolve source or clinician-review holds.
suggestions: Preserve the patient-specific endpoint, baseline oxygen requirement and response during infusion reduction.
If later paired with another node, recheck whether preceding feedback teaches this exact support-versus-measurement distinction.

concept.learningObjective: Preserve the patient’s later nonurgent biopsy decision.
concept.historyMigration: None. Existing definitions, cards and frozen encounters retain their exact identities.

record.title: An incidental lesion outside operative permission
fairness: The best offered plan is to document the lesion and obtain the patient's separate decision after recovery. The unrelated, nonbleeding lesion does not supply a reason to bypass that opportunity.

Two consequential steps are present: recognize that a shoulder biopsy is outside the right-groin consent and does not need to be done during the present anesthetic, then choose later patient decision-making over immediate proxy permission.
The agent option is a plausible timing/authority error, and same-anesthetic permission is a familiar scope error. Necessary scope and urgency facts are not gratuitous cues.

The case stands alone, has a consistent patient frame, and asks a complete permission task. No confident clinical inaccuracy or decisive wording-only shortcut identified. This does not assert that the lesion is benign or requires no follow-up.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between the consent decision and the separate clinical assessment of whether biopsy is indicated.
Keep any future revision explicit about urgency and the ability to wait for the patient's own participation.

concept.displayName: reversible delay
concept.learningObjective: Wait for recoverable patient capacity for the new nonurgent decision rather than expand the old permission.
concept.historyMigration: None. Existing definitions, cards and frozen encounters retain their exact identities.

record.title: A new operative proposal after sedation
fairness: The best offered process is to seek the patient's decision after recovery for the newly proposed, nonurgent left repair. Prior informed permission remains relevant to the unchanged right-sided plan.

Two consequential steps are required: separate preserved earlier consent from the new proposal, then use reversible inability and the absence of urgent left-sided findings to rank waiting over the available agent.
The agent is verified and favors repair, making that a credible competitor rather than an automatically unauthorized relative. The same-operation scope expansion is also a credible error.

Standalone chronology is clear and the task specifically concerns the left side. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; the explanation does not claim that sedation invalidates all earlier consent or that agents can never decide during temporary incapacity.
suggestions: Preserve the explicit prior informed discussion, unchanged right-sided plan, new left-sided scope and nonurgent findings.
Retain the distinction from consent-scope if both remain in the bank; do not count their similar answer pattern as independent evidence of difficulty.

record.title: Suspected falsification versus routine correction
fairness: The protocol, original log, enrollment chronology and instruction to reclassify post-treatment complications support referral for a research-integrity assessment beyond a routine data correction.

Two consequential steps are present: reconcile the records to identify a substantive classification discrepancy with evidence of directed alteration, then select the appropriate escalation rather than treating it as routine cleaning or a statistical-definition question.
The alternatives are credible neighboring workflows, and all concern the present response. The key's preservation step is not an omission cue because the records are already retained.

The explanation appropriately reserves the misconduct determination to the institution rather than declaring intent or guilt established. The standalone case and task are coherent; no confident clinical inaccuracy or decisive wording-only cue identified.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between grounds for referring a concern and a final finding of misconduct.
Keep the concrete record chronology if the item is shortened; it is what makes escalation more than a generic honesty answer.

record.title: Route-specific midazolam planning with cobicistat
clarityIssues: 'That earlier record documents the increments and responses' adds little because the actual increments and responses are not displayed and no calculation uses them.
fairness: Omitting oral midazolam and starting with smaller IV increments is the best offered revision. The learner must recognize the newly relevant interaction, then apply its different implications to oral exposure and monitored repeated IV administration.

The four combinations balance both component frequencies, so convergence cannot reconstruct the key. The common IV monitoring/titration conditions apply to every IV plan rather than making only the key safe by wording.

The prior dosing record predates cobicistat, providing a real reason not to simply reuse it. No exact dose reduction is invented; the explanation retains the need for individualized titration and the qualification that reduction is considered especially with repeated use.

Self-contained. Perioperative drug interactions and altered sedative exposure are high-yield, although the precise boosted-antiretroviral route distinction is more specialized than basic benzodiazepine reversal.
suggestions: Delete the unused sentence announcing the earlier record's increments and responses; retain that the copied IV increments predate cobicistat.
Keep all IV options under the same monitoring conditions and retain balanced paired components. Do not imply that every form of midazolam is categorically contraindicated.

record.title: Seizure treatment during local-anesthetic toxicity with hypotension
clarityIssues: Minor tense friction: 'reviews ... after recovery' shifts to 'Generalized convulsions now continue.' The task makes the historical decision understandable, but a recorded-checkpoint transition would read more naturally.
fairness: Midazolam is the best offered agent for ongoing seizures in this toxicity context with persistent circulatory depression. Propofol and thiopental are real anticonvulsant/anesthetic alternatives whose hemodynamic effects matter; their use is not falsely described as universally prohibited.

Two consequential considerations remain: identify the toxic exposure pattern and select seizure suppression in the setting of hypotension. Ventilation, lipid therapy and circulatory support are already underway, so an omitted primary resuscitation action does not compete with the requested drug choice.
The three labels use identical grammar and specificity. Neither the drug name nor its class is supplied in the stem, and no nonmedical key cue was found.
The node is self-contained. Recognition and management of local-anesthetic systemic toxicity are high-yield; the hemodynamic constraint makes this more than naming its antidote.
suggestions: Optional clarity polish: introduce the last sentence with 'At the recorded treatment checkpoint' instead of 'now.'
Retain the explanation's qualification that midazolam still needs titration and respiratory support; do not convert the alternative-agent caution into an absolute.

record.title: Adjunct treatment for recurrent broad-complex rhythm during bupivacaine toxicity
clarityIssues: The prose repeats nearly all of the electrical exhibit. 'Reasonable' also sets a looser comparison than a single-best-answer task needs. Neither issue prevents solving this offered set.
fairness: Sodium bicarbonate is a defensible best adjunct among these three options for the represented local-anesthetic sodium-channel toxicity with broad complexes. The pulse, poor perfusion, already-delivered synchronized cardioversion and continuing resuscitation prevent the drug question from replacing urgent electrical treatment.

The uniform rhythm and absence of a rotating axis distinguish a torsades-oriented magnesium choice; lidocaine introduces another local anesthetic. These are medical discriminators, not word-matching cues for a reader without medical knowledge.

The inference combines toxicologic context with electrical findings and then selects an adjunct at the specified treatment stage. This is more specialized than the commonly tested initial LAST response, so the particular bicarbonate decision should not be represented as a core high-frequency general-surgery examination concept.

Uncertainty: the exact AHA recommendation strength and applicability were not independently source-verified in this offline review. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified, but the explanation's limited-evidence qualifier must remain for clinician review.
Self-contained: seizure treatment, lipid administration and the recurrent rhythm are supplied locally. No preceding seizure-node answer is needed.
suggestions: Prefer 'Which additional medication is most appropriate ...' while preserving the explicit adjunctive treatment stage.
Let the exhibit carry the electrical observations and remove their duplicate prose. Retain the pulse, perfusion and treatment chronology.
Consider a lower-priority advanced item designation; retain core LAST coverage elsewhere.

record.title: MH family risk and timing of prepared anesthesia
fairness: Review-wide scope: all 15 current proposed executable nodes were reviewed independently from their after/candidate visible fields; those fields match the current proposedCases. Prior PASS labels and author reasoning were not evidence of quality. The six Keep records, 69 retirement proposals, historical/parked attempts and held records are noted but not adjudicated. None of the 15 current cases has multiple nodes. No network or fresh source verification was used; editorial PASS is not clinical approval, and all drafts remain needs_clinician_review.

Proceed with the proposed nontriggering anesthetic and arrange specialist assessment is the best offered recommendation. Prior uneventful exposure and an uninformative panel do not negate the affected first-degree relative; that risk must then be separated from a requirement to finish definitive testing before prepared anesthesia.

The readiness details are decision-critical rather than an assertion that the patient is cleared. The three options have comparable length and address the same scheduling/preparation decision; no decisive nonmedical wording shortcut was found.

Self-contained: the anesthetic regimen, family testing context and preparation are present without a prior node. MH susceptibility and trigger avoidance are high-yield; this tests their application rather than drug-list recall.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between maintaining MH precautions and completing susceptibility testing. Do not shorten the negative-panel description to a definitive negative familial test.
Clinical sign-off should confirm that the summarized facility readiness supports the intended setting; this offline review does not certify operational readiness or exact rescue provisions.

record.title: Conflicting recovery assessments after rocuronium
clarityIssues: 'An eye muscle' is less precise than naming the monitored muscle, although the checked adductor-pollicis result is sufficient to resolve the offered decision.
fairness: Addressing residual rocuronium and reassessing is the best offered plan. The checked adductor-pollicis ratio conflicts with reassuring clinical strength and the eye-site result; the learner must decide which evidence establishes recovery and then act before extubation.

Fentanyl makes naloxone a recognizable competing drug, but opioid reversal does not correct the represented peripheral transmission deficit. Head lift and a reassuring eye-site ratio are credible extubation errors rather than arbitrary distractors.
No option is uniquely long or comprehensive. The extubation distractor repeats observations, but understanding why those observations are inadequate still requires medical knowledge.
Self-contained and high-yield: residual neuromuscular block and the limitations of clinical recovery tests are practical perioperative safety concepts.
suggestions: Name the monitored eye muscle if supported by the underlying record, without adding a pre-answer statement about which site is preferred.
Retain quantitative reassessment and the explanation's reminder that other extubation requirements still apply.

record.title: Normalized acceleromyography and reversal in severe renal impairment
fairness: The stated raw measurement and baseline give a normalized ratio of 1.02/1.20 = 0.85. The device behavior is explicit, so the learner need not guess whether normalization or capping was already performed.

Neostigmine/glycopyrrolate with quantitative reassessment is the best offered plan: residual block remains, while severe renal impairment makes routine sugammadex selection less appropriate. This combines monitor interpretation with a patient-specific reversal choice; both change the action.
The options are concrete and comparably scoped. Clinical strength competes credibly with the monitor evidence, and the renal condition does not identify an answer without pharmacologic knowledge.
The explanation says sugammadex is 'not recommended,' not absolutely impossible in every circumstance. No new renal cutoff or dosing rule is needed to solve the offered set.
Self-contained. Residual-block prevention and reversal selection are high-yield; baseline normalization is a legitimate advanced technical discriminator rather than ambiguity.
suggestions: Preserve the explicit raw-display and baseline information and the worked normalization in feedback.
Keep clinical sign-off focused on the exact monitoring method and renal-context antagonist ranking; do not generalize the key to every device or every degree of renal dysfunction.

record.title: Naloxone delivery after repeated respiratory relapses

cues.phrase: IV access, infusion equipment and continuous bedside monitoring are available.
cues.why: Minor priming: 'infusion equipment' repeats the key's delivery method. It does not establish that an infusion is preferable to usable IV boluses; that ranking still depends on the repeated unsupported-breathing gaps.

fairness: A respiratory-response-adjusted IV infusion is the best offered maintenance strategy given repeated return of hypoventilation requiring assisted ventilation between effective rescues. IV boluses remain clinically useful, so the explanation correctly favors rather than universally mandates infusion.

Two steps are consequential: use repeated reversal responses to identify an ongoing reversible opioid component, then use the relapse trajectory to choose sustained titratable delivery. Pain and respiratory support remain relevant to the treatment target.

The options are parallel delivery plans. IM dosing is less attractive with IV access and a need for close titration, but the credible IV-bolus alternative prevents the equipment sentence from resolving the question by itself.

Self-contained and coherent with the separate recurrence and endpoint vignettes. High-yield postoperative respiratory-depression management; no invented recurrence count or time threshold is asserted.
suggestions: Trim the equipment inventory if the monitored hospital setting already establishes the offered treatments' feasibility. Retain the relapse/support trajectory.
If these separate cases are ever recombined, review the first node's feedback against this task; do not place an infusion recommendation in earlier feedback.

record.title: Early naloxone-infusion endpoint with residual dozing
fairness: Maintaining the present rate is the best offered immediate adjustment: spontaneous ventilation and responsiveness have improved, pain is tolerable, and this is only the first early reassessment after repeated relapses.

The resident must distinguish an adequate respiratory endpoint from complete wakefulness, then decide whether the recent relapse history permits stopping treatment. Increasing for dozing and stopping after an initial success are different credible errors.
The task clearly asks for an immediate infusion adjustment, not discharge eligibility or a later weaning plan. The options are parallel and there is no unique wording match or length cue.
Self-contained: the repeated rescues and current response are restated without requiring the delivery-plan node. This is high-yield opioid-reversal titration and monitoring.
suggestions: Preserve both the current respiratory observations and the early timing relative to recurrent hypoventilation; removing either would weaken the ranking.
If recombined with the delivery-plan case, keep the prior explanation from prescribing this exact maintenance decision. Do not add an unsupported fixed observation or infusion duration.

decisionNodes.stem: Which drug should {patientName}'s outside team select for the ongoing convulsions while ventilation and circulatory support continue?

answerChoices.label: Titrated intravenous midazolam
answerChoices.rationale: A benzodiazepine is preferred for seizures in local-anesthetic toxicity. Titrate with airway and circulatory support; it can also depress breathing.

answerChoices.label: Titrated intravenous propofol
answerChoices.rationale: Propofol can suppress seizures, but it can aggravate cardiovascular depression. Persistent hypotension favors a benzodiazepine when available. Small incremental propofol remains a fallback in some guidance, not an absolute contraindication.

answerChoices.label: Titrated intravenous thiopental
answerChoices.rationale: Historical guidance includes small incremental thiopental, but current AHA/ASRA guidance prefers benzodiazepines for this toxicity. The present circulatory compromise does not justify choosing a less-supported anesthetic alternative first.

decisionNodes.explanation: The recorded convulsions follow systemic local-anesthetic toxicity and occur during persistent circulatory depression. Current guidance favors a benzodiazepine. Midazolam still requires titration and respiratory support; the comparison does not assume that every sedative is hemodynamically harmless or that small propofol/thiopental increments are never used.

record.title: Seizure treatment during local-anesthetic toxicity with hypotension
clarityIssues: Minor tense friction: 'reviews ... after recovery' shifts to 'Generalized convulsions now continue.' The task makes the historical decision understandable, but a recorded-checkpoint transition would read more naturally.
fairness: Midazolam is the best offered agent for ongoing seizures in this toxicity context with persistent circulatory depression. Propofol and thiopental are real anticonvulsant/anesthetic alternatives whose hemodynamic effects matter; their use is not falsely described as universally prohibited.

Two consequential considerations remain: identify the toxic exposure pattern and select seizure suppression in the setting of hypotension. Ventilation, lipid therapy and circulatory support are already underway, so an omitted primary resuscitation action does not compete with the requested drug choice.
The three labels use identical grammar and specificity. Neither the drug name nor its class is supplied in the stem, and no nonmedical key cue was found.
The node is self-contained. Recognition and management of local-anesthetic systemic toxicity are high-yield; the hemodynamic constraint makes this more than naming its antidote.
suggestions: Optional clarity polish: introduce the last sentence with 'At the recorded treatment checkpoint' instead of 'now.'
Retain the explanation's qualification that midazolam still needs titration and respiratory support; do not convert the alternative-agent caution into an absolute.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 46-year-old woman, reviews an outside operative record in clinic after recovery. Bupivacaine infiltration was followed by auditory symptoms, confusion, convulsions and cardiovascular collapse. Injection stopped, lipid emulsion began, ventilation was secured and midazolam stopped the convulsions. At the recorded decision a rapid rhythm has uniform broad QRS complexes, a palpable pulse and poor perfusion. Synchronized cardioversion was delivered, but the same rhythm recurred; electrical treatment and circulatory support continue.

decisionNodes.stem: Which additional toxicology-directed medication is reasonable for {patientName}'s recurrent rhythm while electrical treatment, lipid therapy and resuscitation continue?

answerChoices.label: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
answerChoices.rationale: AHA describes bicarbonate as a reasonable adjunct for life-threatening wide-complex tachycardia from local-anesthetic toxicity. This addresses the exposure/conduction problem during, not instead of, electrical and supportive treatment.

answerChoices.label: Intravenous lidocaine
answerChoices.rationale: Lidocaine is familiar from other ventricular-arrhythmia care, but adding another local anesthetic is avoided during local-anesthetic systemic toxicity.

answerChoices.label: Intravenous magnesium sulfate
answerChoices.rationale: The described uniform rhythm does not show the polymorphic twisting pattern associated with torsades; magnesium does not address the demonstrated local-anesthetic sodium-channel toxicity as directly.

The broad uniform complexes and recurrent poor perfusion support a toxicity-directed bicarbonate adjunct rather than another local anesthetic or a torsades-directed choice. AHA calls bicarbonate reasonable on limited evidence; it is not a universal first-line rhythm drug. Cardioversion and ongoing resuscitation are already being provided.

record.title: Adjunct treatment for recurrent broad-complex rhythm during bupivacaine toxicity
clarityIssues: The prose repeats nearly all of the electrical exhibit. 'Reasonable' also sets a looser comparison than a single-best-answer task needs. Neither issue prevents solving this offered set.
fairness: Sodium bicarbonate is a defensible best adjunct among these three options for the represented local-anesthetic sodium-channel toxicity with broad complexes. The pulse, poor perfusion, already-delivered synchronized cardioversion and continuing resuscitation prevent the drug question from replacing urgent electrical treatment.

The uniform rhythm and absence of a rotating axis distinguish a torsades-oriented magnesium choice; lidocaine introduces another local anesthetic. These are medical discriminators, not word-matching cues for a reader without medical knowledge.

The inference combines toxicologic context with electrical findings and then selects an adjunct at the specified treatment stage. This is more specialized than the commonly tested initial LAST response, so the particular bicarbonate decision should not be represented as a core high-frequency general-surgery examination concept.

Uncertainty: the exact AHA recommendation strength and applicability were not independently source-verified in this offline review. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified, but the explanation's limited-evidence qualifier must remain for clinician review.
Self-contained: seizure treatment, lipid administration and the recurrent rhythm are supplied locally. No preceding seizure-node answer is needed.
suggestions: Prefer 'Which additional medication is most appropriate ...' while preserving the explicit adjunctive treatment stage.

record.title: Conflicting recovery assessments after rocuronium
clarityIssues: 'An eye muscle' is less precise than naming the monitored muscle, although the checked adductor-pollicis result is sufficient to resolve the offered decision.
fairness: Addressing residual rocuronium and reassessing is the best offered plan. The checked adductor-pollicis ratio conflicts with reassuring clinical strength and the eye-site result; the learner must decide which evidence establishes recovery and then act before extubation.

Fentanyl makes naloxone a recognizable competing drug, but opioid reversal does not correct the represented peripheral transmission deficit. Head lift and a reassuring eye-site ratio are credible extubation errors rather than arbitrary distractors.
No option is uniquely long or comprehensive. The extubation distractor repeats observations, but understanding why those observations are inadequate still requires medical knowledge.
Self-contained and high-yield: residual neuromuscular block and the limitations of clinical recovery tests are practical perioperative safety concepts.
suggestions: Name the monitored eye muscle if supported by the underlying record, without adding a pre-answer statement about which site is preferred.
Retain quantitative reassessment and the explanation's reminder that other extubation requirements still apply.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 69-year-old woman, reviews an outside anesthetic in clinic. Vecuronium was used. She is awake, follows commands and breathes adequately with the tracheal tube still in place. The calibrated adductor-pollicis acceleromyograph recorded a pre-block train-of-four ratio of 1.20 and now repeatedly displays 1.02. The device displays raw T4/T1 without baseline normalization or capping; thumb movement is unobstructed. Severe chronic renal impairment is documented.

answerChoices.label: Give neostigmine/glycopyrrolate and reassess quantitative recovery
answerChoices.rationale: Normalizing the current raw ratio gives 1.02/1.20 = 0.85, below adequate recovery. This is minimal residual vecuronium block, for which neostigmine with an antimuscarinic is appropriate. Severe renal impairment makes the sugammadex alternative inconsistent with its labeling.

answerChoices.label: Omit blocker antagonism and complete extubation assessment
answerChoices.rationale: The raw display above 1.0 is not normalized recovery. Clinical strength does not correct the measured residual block.

answerChoices.label: Give sugammadex and reassess quantitative recovery
answerChoices.rationale: Sugammadex targets vecuronium, but it is not recommended in severe renal impairment. The represented minimal block provides an alternative antagonist approach.

record.title: Normalized acceleromyography and reversal in severe renal impairment
fairness: The stated raw measurement and baseline give a normalized ratio of 1.02/1.20 = 0.85. The device behavior is explicit, so the learner need not guess whether normalization or capping was already performed.

Neostigmine/glycopyrrolate with quantitative reassessment is the best offered plan: residual block remains, while severe renal impairment makes routine sugammadex selection less appropriate. This combines monitor interpretation with a patient-specific reversal choice; both change the action.
The options are concrete and comparably scoped. Clinical strength competes credibly with the monitor evidence, and the renal condition does not identify an answer without pharmacologic knowledge.
The explanation says sugammadex is 'not recommended,' not absolutely impossible in every circumstance. No new renal cutoff or dosing rule is needed to solve the offered set.
Self-contained. Residual-block prevention and reversal selection are high-yield; baseline normalization is a legitimate advanced technical discriminator rather than ambiguity.
suggestions: Preserve the explicit raw-display and baseline information and the worked normalization in feedback.
Keep clinical sign-off focused on the exact monitoring method and renal-context antagonist ranking; do not generalize the key to every device or every degree of renal dysfunction.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 57-year-old man, reviews an outside hospital recovery record in clinic. Fentanyl, midazolam and rocuronium were used; checked hand transmission returned to baseline after motor reversal. Each of several titrated IV naloxone rescues restores regular deeper breaths. Between the most recent rescues he again becomes poorly responsive with shallow breaths and rising expired CO2, requiring assisted ventilation while another dose is prepared. No further opioid was given. When breathing improves he reports tolerable incisional pain. IV access, infusion equipment and continuous bedside monitoring are available.

answerChoices.label: Use an IV infusion adjusted to respiratory response
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated IV rescue is producing only temporary breathing improvement with renewed ventilatory support between doses. A response-adjusted infusion can sustain titratable antagonism. Continue bedside respiratory assessment and preserve analgesia where possible.

concept.displayName: Repeated respiratory recurrence during opioid reversal
concept.learningObjective: Reproducible short respiratory responses coexist with painful over-reversal after a larger peak. Choose titratable ongoing antagonism rather than repeatedly increase or reproduce bolus peaks.
concept.conceptVersionReason: Applies the same clinical rule to meaningful observations; stable history retained.

record.title: Naloxone delivery after repeated respiratory relapses

cues.phrase: IV access, infusion equipment and continuous bedside monitoring are available.
cues.why: Minor priming: 'infusion equipment' repeats the key's delivery method. It does not establish that an infusion is preferable to usable IV boluses; that ranking still depends on the repeated unsupported-breathing gaps.

fairness: A respiratory-response-adjusted IV infusion is the best offered maintenance strategy given repeated return of hypoventilation requiring assisted ventilation between effective rescues. IV boluses remain clinically useful, so the explanation correctly favors rather than universally mandates infusion.

Two steps are consequential: use repeated reversal responses to identify an ongoing reversible opioid component, then use the relapse trajectory to choose sustained titratable delivery. Pain and respiratory support remain relevant to the treatment target.

The options are parallel delivery plans. IM dosing is less attractive with IV access and a need for close titration, but the credible IV-bolus alternative prevents the equipment sentence from resolving the question by itself.

Self-contained and coherent with the separate recurrence and endpoint vignettes. High-yield postoperative respiratory-depression management; no invented recurrence count or time threshold is asserted.
suggestions: Trim the equipment inventory if the monitored hospital setting already establishes the offered treatments' feasibility. Retain the relapse/support trajectory.
If these separate cases are ever recombined, review the first node's feedback against this task; do not place an infusion recommendation in earlier feedback.

decisionNodes.stem: Which immediate infusion adjustment best fits {patientName}'s first early reassessment after titration?

answerChoices.label: Maintain the present naloxone infusion rate
answerChoices.rationale: Breathing and responsive alertness have just reached the intended endpoint with tolerable pain. The early success does not yet demonstrate resolution of the recurrent drug effect. Continue reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Increase the present naloxone infusion rate
answerChoices.rationale: Dozing between prompts is not itself evidence of an inadequate reversal endpoint when breathing is adequate and he responds promptly. Extra antagonism may unnecessarily remove analgesia.

answerChoices.label: Discontinue the naloxone infusion
answerChoices.rationale: This is the first early post-titration success after repeated respiratory recurrences, not a sustained demonstration of drug-effect resolution. Stopping now risks losing the just-restored endpoint.

concept.learningObjective: Separate adequate respiratory reversal from complete opioid/analgesic reversal.

record.title: Early naloxone-infusion endpoint with residual dozing
fairness: Maintaining the present rate is the best offered immediate adjustment: spontaneous ventilation and responsiveness have improved, pain is tolerable, and this is only the first early reassessment after repeated relapses.

The resident must distinguish an adequate respiratory endpoint from complete wakefulness, then decide whether the recent relapse history permits stopping treatment. Increasing for dozing and stopping after an initial success are different credible errors.
The task clearly asks for an immediate infusion adjustment, not discharge eligibility or a later weaning plan. The options are parallel and there is no unique wording match or length cue.
Self-contained: the repeated rescues and current response are restated without requiring the delivery-plan node. This is high-yield opioid-reversal titration and monitoring.
suggestions: Preserve both the current respiratory observations and the early timing relative to recurrent hypoventilation; removing either would weaken the ranking.
If recombined with the delivery-plan case, keep the prior explanation from prescribing this exact maintenance decision. Do not add an unsupported fixed observation or infusion duration.

answerChoices.label: Omit oral midazolam; start with smaller IV increments

For repeated parenteral midazolam, close monitoring and dose-reduction consideration are required; smaller initial increments followed by response titration are a concrete lower-exposure plan rather than copying pre-interaction dosing.

answerChoices.label: Retain oral midazolam; start with smaller IV increments
answerChoices.rationale: Reducing parenteral exposure does not remove the oral-midazolam contraindication under the current regimen.

answerChoices.label: Omit oral midazolam; start with the copied IV increments

record.title: Route-specific midazolam planning with cobicistat
clarityIssues: 'That earlier record documents the increments and responses' adds little because the actual increments and responses are not displayed and no calculation uses them.
fairness: Omitting oral midazolam and starting with smaller IV increments is the best offered revision. The learner must recognize the newly relevant interaction, then apply its different implications to oral exposure and monitored repeated IV administration.

The four combinations balance both component frequencies, so convergence cannot reconstruct the key. The common IV monitoring/titration conditions apply to every IV plan rather than making only the key safe by wording.

The prior dosing record predates cobicistat, providing a real reason not to simply reuse it. No exact dose reduction is invented; the explanation retains the need for individualized titration and the qualification that reduction is considered especially with repeated use.

Self-contained. Perioperative drug interactions and altered sedative exposure are high-yield, although the precise boosted-antiretroviral route distinction is more specialized than basic benzodiazepine reversal.
suggestions: Delete the unused sentence announcing the earlier record's increments and responses; retain that the copied IV increments predate cobicistat.
Keep all IV options under the same monitoring conditions and retain balanced paired components. Do not imply that every form of midazolam is categorically contraindicated.

record.title: N01 — Treat a reached but uncaptured distal duct stone
fairness: Transoral duct incision and stone extraction is the defensible best offered intervention for a fixed distal submandibular duct stone that was reached but could not be captured. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The absence of an offered intraductal fragmentation technique does not create two correct offered answers.

The learner must interpret the outside failure as a capture/impaction problem rather than inability to reach the stone, then combine that with distal localization to choose an accessible extraction route over external fragmentation or gland excision. These findings change the action.

The known stone diagnosis appropriately establishes the treatment problem. The options are parallel specific procedures, and no wording-only overlap, absolute, convergence pattern or teaching sentence uniquely selects the key. Distal location is necessary anatomical evidence, not a defect to delete.

Location-dependent management of salivary obstruction is high yield. The current standalone case is coherent and complete; it does not require the parked N02 follow-up, which is excluded from this review.
suggestions: Retain the reached-but-not-captured distinction and distal localization. A generic statement that sialendoscopy failed would lose the deciding information.
Preserve this exact clinical version pending clinician sign-off. Do not infer approval of an unreviewed residual-stone follow-up from this PASS.

record.title: N05 — Reconstruct a divided facial nerve without tension
fairness: An interposition cable graft is the defensible best offered reconstruction when viable tumor-free proximal and distal facial stumps are available but approximation requires sustained traction despite mobilization. Direct repair and donor-nerve transfer each address a different anatomical situation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The two decisive interpretations are that native proximal input is available, making a facial-to-facial reconstruction appropriate, and that the gap cannot be closed without tension, favoring a graft over direct coaptation. Changing either observation would change the ranking of a credible competitor.

The key is not uniquely lengthy, explanatory or cautious. Both stumps and traction are necessary operative findings, not diagnoses that simply repeat an answer label. No reliable nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

The retrospective task clearly asks what should have been done during the recorded operation, not how to treat the patient at the later clinic visit. The mechanism of the documented nerve discontinuity need not be inferred to select the repair. This case stands alone; it is not a continuation of N06's preserved operative account.

Tension-free nerve repair and selection by proximal stump availability are high-yield surgical principles. Specialist details of graft selection and reconstruction are outside this narrow question; the explanation appropriately acknowledges that boundary.
suggestions: Preserve both viable stump availability and failure of tension-free approximation after mobilization; neither can be omitted without changing the best repair.

Optionally shorten the feedback by removing its opening discussion of observation for transient weakness, which is not an offered competitor. Prioritize the comparison among the three actual reconstructions.
Keep this standalone reconstruction case distinct from the separate held question about sacrificing a functioning grossly invaded nerve. PASS does not resolve that held clinical issue.

record.title: N06 — Adjuvant treatment for microscopic perineural involvement
fairness: Postoperative radiotherapy discussion is the defensible best offered plan for perineural invasion despite favorable grade, negative nodes and clear margins. Surveillance is a credible temptation from those favorable features; adding cisplatin is not established routine treatment in this setting. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Exact adjuvant decisions still require clinician review.

The learner identifies microscopic perineural involvement from the small-nerve sheath observation, then weighs that adverse feature against the otherwise favorable pathology to choose adjuvant treatment without unsupported systemic intensification. The new pathological observation changes the decision.

The options are similarly specific postoperative strategies. The diagnosis in the presentation appropriately establishes a management task; it does not disclose the adverse feature or treatment. No reliable length, overlap, absolute, teaching-sentence or convergence shortcut uniquely identifies the key.

Perineural invasion as an adverse oncological finding is high yield. The update follows the recorded operation coherently and distinguishes small-nerve microscopic disease from gross main-facial-nerve invasion. The case stands alone and does not require an earlier nerve-preservation answer or N05's separate reconstruction scenario.
suggestions: Preserve the competing favorable pathological features and the distinction between small-nerve involvement and the main facial nerve.
Keep the recommendation framed as postoperative team discussion, as written. This editorial PASS does not approve an exact radiation field, dose or treatment course and is not clinical sign-off.

record.title: R03 — Obtain nodal architecture despite a better needle target
fairness: Excision of the accessible superficial node is the defensible best offered way to obtain architecture for this unresolved suspected T-cell lymphoid process. There is no confident clinical inaccuracy in that ranking. Exact subtype-specific recommendations remain subject to clinician review; this is not a universal prohibition on needle diagnosis of lymphoma.

The meaningful competition is between correcting a genuine necrotic-center targeting problem with viable peripheral cores and obtaining the nodal organization needed for classification. The learner must distinguish cell yield from architectural adequacy, then select a feasible specimen acquisition. These are consequential steps rather than two synonyms for lymphoma.

The hematopathology statement about nodal organization is a legitimate description of the unresolved diagnostic requirement. It does not name a biopsy method, and viable peripheral cores are a credible temptation. Surgical anatomy makes excision feasible without gratuitous permission statements. Mobility is correctly attributed to examination.

No reliable wording-only key was found: all options are concrete biopsy plans; none is an explanatory critique, absolute, uniquely cautious answer or simple repetition of an already failed identical procedure. The longer core/FNA labels do not identify the key by length.
Lymphoma specimen adequacy and architectural assessment are high yield. This standalone case includes the prior sampling and its limitations, and needs no earlier node or feedback.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between poor central cell yield and the separate architectural requirement, including the genuinely available viable peripheral target.

Keep the conclusion specific to the supplied suspected process and accessible node; do not expand the feedback into a universal rule that core specimens can never classify lymphoma. Editorial PASS is not clinical sign-off.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 66-year-old man, attends clinic with enlarging cervical nodes. Aspirate flow cytometry from the larger node found an aberrant T-cell population. Core passes through its center yielded mainly necrosis and fragmented atypical lymphoid cells. Hematopathology cannot classify the process without nodal organization. A smaller superficial node is mobile on examination; ultrasound shows a fat plane separating it from the carotid and jugular vessels. Viable peripheral tissue in the larger node is also accessible to an image-guided needle.

decisionNodes.stem: Which biopsy should be requested next to classify {patientName}'s cervical lymphoid process?

answerChoices.label: Excisional biopsy of the accessible superficial node
answerChoices.rationale: The suspected T-cell lymphoid process still needs intact nodal organization for classification. The clinically accessible node offers surgical architectural assessment.

answerChoices.label: Core biopsies of viable peripheral tissue in the larger node
answerChoices.rationale: Changing from the necrotic center to viable peripheral tissue could improve yield, but does not provide the intact organization sought when surgical tissue is feasible for this T-cell differential.

answerChoices.label: FNA of the superficial node with cell block and flow cytometry
answerChoices.rationale: Ancillary cytology may characterize cells, but does not supply the nodal organization missing from the classification workup.

Needle approaches remain alternatives when surgical sampling is not feasible.

question.explanation: Cell detection and lymphoma classification are different endpoints. Better targeting could recover more viable cells from the larger node, but the suspected T-cell process still requires assessment of nodal organization. concept.displayName: Obtain nodal architecture for T-cell classification
concept.learningObjective: Distinguish improved viable needle yield from a required architectural classification endpoint and select surgical tissue when feasible.

record.title: R03 — Obtain nodal architecture despite a better needle target
fairness: Excision of the accessible superficial node is the defensible best offered way to obtain architecture for this unresolved suspected T-cell lymphoid process. There is no confident clinical inaccuracy in that ranking. Exact subtype-specific recommendations remain subject to clinician review; this is not a universal prohibition on needle diagnosis of lymphoma.

The meaningful competition is between correcting a genuine necrotic-center targeting problem with viable peripheral cores and obtaining the nodal organization needed for classification. The learner must distinguish cell yield from architectural adequacy, then select a feasible specimen acquisition. These are consequential steps rather than two synonyms for lymphoma.

The hematopathology statement about nodal organization is a legitimate description of the unresolved diagnostic requirement. It does not name a biopsy method, and viable peripheral cores are a credible temptation. Surgical anatomy makes excision feasible without gratuitous permission statements. Mobility is correctly attributed to examination.

No reliable wording-only key was found: all options are concrete biopsy plans; none is an explanatory critique, absolute, uniquely cautious answer or simple repetition of an already failed identical procedure. The longer core/FNA labels do not identify the key by length.
Lymphoma specimen adequacy and architectural assessment are high yield. This standalone case includes the prior sampling and its limitations, and needs no earlier node or feedback.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between poor central cell yield and the separate architectural requirement, including the genuinely available viable peripheral target.

Keep the conclusion specific to the supplied suspected process and accessible node; do not expand the feedback into a universal rule that core specimens can never classify lymphoma. Editorial PASS is not clinical sign-off.

record.title: N01 — Treat a reached but uncaptured distal duct stone
fairness: Transoral duct incision and stone extraction is the defensible best offered intervention for a fixed distal submandibular duct stone that was reached but could not be captured. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The absence of an offered intraductal fragmentation technique does not create two correct offered answers.

The learner must interpret the outside failure as a capture/impaction problem rather than inability to reach the stone, then combine that with distal localization to choose an accessible extraction route over external fragmentation or gland excision. These findings change the action.

The known stone diagnosis appropriately establishes the treatment problem. The options are parallel specific procedures, and no wording-only overlap, absolute, convergence pattern or teaching sentence uniquely selects the key. Distal location is necessary anatomical evidence, not a defect to delete.

Location-dependent management of salivary obstruction is high yield. The current standalone case is coherent and complete; it does not require the parked N02 follow-up, which is excluded from this review.
suggestions: Retain the reached-but-not-captured distinction and distal localization. A generic statement that sialendoscopy failed would lose the deciding information.
Preserve this exact clinical version pending clinician sign-off. Do not infer approval of an unreviewed residual-stone follow-up from this PASS.

case.presentation: {patientName}, a 54-year-old woman, attends clinic to review an outside operation for a small low-grade parotid mucoepidermoid carcinoma. Before surgery, facial movement was symmetric. The operative note describes a plane between tumor and facial branches, without encasement or gross entry into the nerve. During dissection, the note then describes separated proximal and distal ends of an extratemporal facial-nerve segment with no connecting fibers. Both ends are viable and free of tumor. After mobilization they meet only with sustained traction.

decisionNodes.stem: During {patientName}'s recorded parotid operation, which immediate facial-nerve reconstruction best fits these findings?

answerChoices.label: Interposition cable graft between the facial nerve stumps
answerChoices.rationale: The identified viable proximal and distal facial stumps permit facial-to-facial reconstruction, but a graft is needed to bridge a repair that otherwise requires sustained traction.

answerChoices.label: Direct end-to-end repair between the facial nerve stumps
answerChoices.rationale: Direct repair is attractive with both stumps present, but the described sustained traction does not meet the requirement for a tension-free repair.

answerChoices.label: Hypoglossal-to-facial nerve anastomosis to the distal stump
answerChoices.rationale: A viable proximal facial stump is available for reconstruction. A donor-nerve plan does not resolve the case as well as bridging the gap between the available facial stumps.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is a documented nerve discontinuity, so observation for transient weakness does not restore its continuity. Both viable facial stumps are available, but direct approximation requires sustained traction. An interposition cable graft preserves a facial-to-facial reconstruction without a tense direct repair. A donor-nerve strategy is considered when a suitable proximal facial stump is unavailable; the exact reconstruction needs specialist judgment.

concept.displayName: Choose tension-free facial-nerve reconstruction
concept.learningObjective: Use viable proximal/distal stump availability and approximation tension to select immediate reconstruction after an iatrogenic nerve discontinuity.

record.title: N05 — Reconstruct a divided facial nerve without tension
fairness: An interposition cable graft is the defensible best offered reconstruction when viable tumor-free proximal and distal facial stumps are available but approximation requires sustained traction despite mobilization. Direct repair and donor-nerve transfer each address a different anatomical situation. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The two decisive interpretations are that native proximal input is available, making a facial-to-facial reconstruction appropriate, and that the gap cannot be closed without tension, favoring a graft over direct coaptation. Changing either observation would change the ranking of a credible competitor.

The key is not uniquely lengthy, explanatory or cautious. Both stumps and traction are necessary operative findings, not diagnoses that simply repeat an answer label. No reliable nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

The retrospective task clearly asks what should have been done during the recorded operation, not how to treat the patient at the later clinic visit. The mechanism of the documented nerve discontinuity need not be inferred to select the repair. This case stands alone; it is not a continuation of N06's preserved operative account.

Tension-free nerve repair and selection by proximal stump availability are high-yield surgical principles. Specialist details of graft selection and reconstruction are outside this narrow question; the explanation appropriately acknowledges that boundary.
suggestions: Preserve both viable stump availability and failure of tension-free approximation after mobilization; neither can be omitted without changing the best repair.

Optionally shorten the feedback by removing its opening discussion of observation for transient weakness, which is not an offered competitor. Prioritize the comparison among the three actual reconstructions.
Keep this standalone reconstruction case distinct from the separate held question about sacrificing a functioning grossly invaded nerve. PASS does not resolve that held clinical issue.

record.title: N06 — Adjuvant treatment for microscopic perineural involvement
fairness: Postoperative radiotherapy discussion is the defensible best offered plan for perineural invasion despite favorable grade, negative nodes and clear margins. Surveillance is a credible temptation from those favorable features; adding cisplatin is not established routine treatment in this setting. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. Exact adjuvant decisions still require clinician review.

The learner identifies microscopic perineural involvement from the small-nerve sheath observation, then weighs that adverse feature against the otherwise favorable pathology to choose adjuvant treatment without unsupported systemic intensification. The new pathological observation changes the decision.

The options are similarly specific postoperative strategies. The diagnosis in the presentation appropriately establishes a management task; it does not disclose the adverse feature or treatment. No reliable length, overlap, absolute, teaching-sentence or convergence shortcut uniquely identifies the key.

Perineural invasion as an adverse oncological finding is high yield. The update follows the recorded operation coherently and distinguishes small-nerve microscopic disease from gross main-facial-nerve invasion. The case stands alone and does not require an earlier nerve-preservation answer or N05's separate reconstruction scenario.
suggestions: Preserve the competing favorable pathological features and the distinction between small-nerve involvement and the main facial nerve.
Keep the recommendation framed as postoperative team discussion, as written. This editorial PASS does not approve an exact radiation field, dose or treatment course and is not clinical sign-off.
