MRI surveillance of the operative region

record.title: Foot-drop localization despite pre-existing lumbar narrowing

cues.phrase: no electrodiagnostic localization is available
cues.why: This named omission favors an electrodiagnostic option, but it does not uniquely identify the key because both fibular and tibial study options remain. The motor map still has to be interpreted. This is a nonblocking cue, not a sufficient nonmedical answer shortcut.

fairness: Fibular nerve conduction and needle EMG is the best offered investigation: dorsiflexion/eversion weakness with preserved inversion and hip abduction favors a fibular distribution over assigning causation to the old foraminal image.
Localization changes the study choice before a lumbar intervention is considered. Repeat spine imaging is a plausible anchoring error; a tibial-directed study mismatches the principal deficit.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified if 'needle EMG' denotes an appropriate differential localization examination. The feedback should not imply that testing only fibular-innervated muscles definitively excludes a root lesion, or that an old image proves incidental disease.
All relevant postoperative context, examination and prior imaging are restated in the singleton. Peripheral-versus-root localization of foot drop is a high-yield application.
suggestions: Optional cue reduction: remove the named electrodiagnostic omission while preserving the old image and current motor map.

Clarify in feedback that a differential needle examination may sample appropriate nonfibular muscles; retain the distinction between a favored localization and a proven operative mechanism. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Persistent knee infection despite active antibiotics
fairness: Repeat arthroscopic knee debridement is the best offered next treatment: persistent purulence, reaccumulation and worsening motion pain indicate unresolved local infection despite an active delivered antibiotic regimen.

The resident must distinguish failed source control from antimicrobial inadequacy before selecting the treatment. Broader antibiotics are a credible error when inflammatory findings worsen; susceptibility and administration records are necessary to rank that alternative.
The explanation correctly avoids making an isolated CRP increase an operative threshold. No confident clinical inaccuracy or second equally defensible best answer is apparent among these choices.

Earlier washout, current findings and treatment verification are fully restated in the singleton. This is a high-yield surgical source-control decision, not a requirement to remember an earlier answer.
suggestions: Preserve the combination of worsening local findings and verified active treatment. Do not simplify the trigger to CRP alone.
Optional precision: align the explanation's 'debridement assessment' language with whether the task scores referral or the next operative treatment. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Joint sampling and antibiotic sequence in a stable patient
fairness: Aspirating the knee before empiric antibiotics is the single best offered sequence for this concerning native-joint presentation with preserved systemic physiology and blood cultures already collected.

The meaningful second decision is treatment order: antibiotics are appropriate, but the physiological state determines whether obtaining the joint specimen first is reasonable. The antibiotic-first option is a credible sequencing error rather than an absurd treatment.

Normal blood pressure, mentation and perfusion are necessary decision information, not gratuitous distractor exclusions. The explanation appropriately changes the priority when sepsis makes delay unsafe.

The retrospective clinic frame, age/sex, knee findings and task stand alone. The phrase 'next dated' is unnecessary continuity language but does not omit information needed to answer. No exact waiting interval is taught.
suggestions: Optional tightening: replace the generic 'next dated outside-hospital record' update with a short initial-assessment label.
Preserve the stability-dependent sequence and avoid expanding the feedback into permission to delay antibiotics for an unspecified prolonged period. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Progressive thenar motor loss despite sensory improvement
fairness: Hand-surgical assessment for carpal tunnel release is the single best offered referral: the motor examination and selective distal physiology localize the consequential deficit, and progressive weakness despite sensory benefit changes the escalation decision.

The old cervical abnormality and improved tingling are credible competing considerations. Normal sampled proximal recruitment does not exclude every root disorder; the explanation appropriately avoids that claim.

Palmar abduction is described explicitly, avoiding confusion with thumb extension. The independent case contains the relevant injection response, motor course and studies, so 'At a later hand review' does not require a preceding node.
Entrapment localization and escalation for progressive motor loss are high-yield principles. Difficulty is a qualitative prediction, not measured exam performance.
suggestions: Optional tightening: let the raw sensory and motor trends establish their divergence instead of announcing it in the current update.
Keep the distinction between referral for surgical assessment and an unconditional instruction to operate. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Concordant infection at one spinal site and a distinct second lesion
fairness: Image-guided T8 lesion biopsy for culture and histology is the best offered plan: the bloodstream isolate and lumbar disc/endplate pattern support one diagnosis, while the separate destructive pedicle/vertebral lesion with a solid mass remains insufficiently explained.

Two consequential interpretations are required: deciding where bloodstream microbiology is sufficiently concordant, then deciding which separate lesion still requires tissue. Sampling L3-L4 and treating both sites empirically are credible different errors.
The explanation correctly does not equate preserved discs with proof of tumor or exclusion of infection. It preserves the uncertainty that makes culture plus histology appropriate.

The shared continuing treatment prevents a false choice between biopsy and treating bacteremia. Hemodynamic and neurological stability support the diagnostic framing. Both sites and the preceding microbiology are restated, so the case is independent of earlier spinal nodes.

Diagnostic anchoring, tissue diagnosis of a discordant destructive lesion and concordant S. aureus spinal infection are valuable, testable principles. The exact two-site scenario is a stretch application, not a claim of documented ABSITE frequency.
suggestions: Preserve the site-specific uncertainty and continuing bacteremia treatment in all options.
Optional clarity: phrase the surveillance option as deferring biopsy with interval imaging, since all plans already continue antimicrobial treatment. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Worsening bony MRI appearance during clinical improvement
fairness: Continuing planned pathogen-directed treatment is the single best offered response to improving pain, walking tolerance and inflammatory markers without a new neural or mechanical complication.

The worsening endplate/disc appearance supplies real conflicting evidence. Interpreting that discordance and then choosing whether to escalate treatment are consequential steps; antibiotic broadening and surgery represent recognizable overreactions to imaging.

The negative neurological and structural observations establish why continued treatment is reasonable. They are necessary safety information rather than a reason to remove those alternatives from all future cases.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation does not endorse stopping therapy or require radiographic normalization. The established diagnosis and complete course are included in the singleton. Interpreting response and source-control indications is high yield.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between bony imaging evolution and new epidural, neural or mechanical complications. Do not generalize this answer to every worsening MRI during infection.
Optional tightening: remove the generic 'next dated' update. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

answerChoices.label: Hand-surgical assessment for carpal tunnel release
answerChoices.rationale: Selective distal conduction abnormality and progressive palmar-abduction weakness make the motor course consequential even though tingling improved.

answerChoices.label: Spine-surgical assessment for cervical root decompression
answerChoices.rationale: The cervical image is a real competing record, but it is less concordant with the selective distal physiology and thenar deficit than the hand-level findings.

answerChoices.label: Hand-therapy review for continued conservative symptom care
answerChoices.rationale: Sensory improvement makes this tempting, but continued motor deterioration means symptom relief has not resolved the consequential deficit.

decisionNodes.explanation: Palmar abduction is specified so the observed deficit is not confused with thumb extension. The current motor trajectory and focal physiology outweigh sensory improvement and an uncorrelated cervical image for this referral decision. This is an assessment for release, not a rule that an old MRI excludes coexisting root disease.

items.label: Observed movement
items.value: With the palm flat, the thumb cannot abduct perpendicular to the palm against resistance. The thenar contour has flattened and buttoning has become harder.

items.label: Competing trends
items.value: A local corticosteroid injection substantially reduced the tingling, but thumb power has continued to fall. An older cervical MRI also describes right foraminal narrowing.

question.stem: Which referral plan should lead treatment of {patientName}'s progressive hand motor loss?

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Observed movement
items.value: With the palm flat, the thumb cannot abduct perpendicular to the palm against resistance. The thenar contour has flattened and buttoning has become harder.

items.label: Conduction and sampling
items.value: Median conduction is selectively slowed across the carpal segment relative to same-distance control nerves, with a reduced thenar motor response. Sampled proximal arm muscles retain normal voluntary recruitment.

items.label: Competing trends
items.value: A local corticosteroid injection substantially reduced the tingling, but thumb power has continued to fall. An older cervical MRI also describes right foraminal narrowing.

answerChoices.label: Hand-surgical assessment for carpal tunnel release
answerChoices.rationale: Selective distal conduction abnormality and progressive palmar-abduction weakness make the motor course consequential even though tingling improved.

answerChoices.label: Spine-surgical assessment for cervical root decompression
answerChoices.rationale: The cervical image is a real competing record, but it is less concordant with the selective distal physiology and thenar deficit than the hand-level findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The cervical image is a real competing record, but it is less concordant with the selective distal physiology and thenar deficit than the hand-level findings.

answerChoices.label: Hand-therapy review for continued conservative symptom care
answerChoices.rationale: Sensory improvement makes this tempting, but continued motor deterioration means symptom relief has not resolved the consequential deficit.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Sensory improvement makes this tempting, but continued motor deterioration means symptom relief has not resolved the consequential deficit.

question.explanation: Palmar abduction is specified so the observed deficit is not confused with thumb extension. The current motor trajectory and focal physiology outweigh sensory improvement and an uncorrelated cervical image for this referral decision. This is an assessment for release, not a rule that an old MRI excludes coexisting root disease.

concept.displayName: Prioritize progressive distal median motor loss despite sensory relief and a competing cervical image.
concept.learningObjective: Prioritize progressive distal median motor loss despite sensory relief and a competing cervical image.

record.title: Progressive thenar motor loss despite sensory improvement
fairness: Hand-surgical assessment for carpal tunnel release is the single best offered referral: the motor examination and selective distal physiology localize the consequential deficit, and progressive weakness despite sensory benefit changes the escalation decision.

The old cervical abnormality and improved tingling are credible competing considerations. Normal sampled proximal recruitment does not exclude every root disorder; the explanation appropriately avoids that claim.

Palmar abduction is described explicitly, avoiding confusion with thumb extension. The independent case contains the relevant injection response, motor course and studies, so 'At a later hand review' does not require a preceding node.
Entrapment localization and escalation for progressive motor loss are high-yield principles. Difficulty is a qualitative prediction, not measured exam performance.
suggestions: Optional tightening: let the raw sensory and motor trends establish their divergence instead of announcing it in the current update.
Keep the distinction between referral for surgical assessment and an unconditional instruction to operate. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

concept.displayName: Sequence diagnostic sampling and treatment for a hemodynamically stable acute native-joint presentation.
concept.learningObjective: Sequence diagnostic sampling and treatment for a hemodynamically stable acute native-joint presentation.

record.title: Joint sampling and antibiotic sequence in a stable patient
fairness: Aspirating the knee before empiric antibiotics is the single best offered sequence for this concerning native-joint presentation with preserved systemic physiology and blood cultures already collected.

The meaningful second decision is treatment order: antibiotics are appropriate, but the physiological state determines whether obtaining the joint specimen first is reasonable. The antibiotic-first option is a credible sequencing error rather than an absurd treatment.

Normal blood pressure, mentation and perfusion are necessary decision information, not gratuitous distractor exclusions. The explanation appropriately changes the priority when sepsis makes delay unsafe.

The retrospective clinic frame, age/sex, knee findings and task stand alone. The phrase 'next dated' is unnecessary continuity language but does not omit information needed to answer. No exact waiting interval is taught.
suggestions: Optional tightening: replace the generic 'next dated outside-hospital record' update with a short initial-assessment label.
Preserve the stability-dependent sequence and avoid expanding the feedback into permission to delay antibiotics for an unspecified prolonged period. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

concept.displayName: Recognize failed local source control despite active antimicrobial therapy.
concept.learningObjective: Recognize failed local source control despite active antimicrobial therapy.

record.title: Persistent knee infection despite active antibiotics
fairness: Repeat arthroscopic knee debridement is the best offered next treatment: persistent purulence, reaccumulation and worsening motion pain indicate unresolved local infection despite an active delivered antibiotic regimen.

The resident must distinguish failed source control from antimicrobial inadequacy before selecting the treatment. Broader antibiotics are a credible error when inflammatory findings worsen; susceptibility and administration records are necessary to rank that alternative.
The explanation correctly avoids making an isolated CRP increase an operative threshold. No confident clinical inaccuracy or second equally defensible best answer is apparent among these choices.

Earlier washout, current findings and treatment verification are fully restated in the singleton. This is a high-yield surgical source-control decision, not a requirement to remember an earlier answer.
suggestions: Preserve the combination of worsening local findings and verified active treatment. Do not simplify the trigger to CRP alone.

concept.displayName: Avoid declaring failure from persistent MRI abnormalities during clinical improvement.
concept.learningObjective: Avoid declaring failure from persistent MRI abnormalities during clinical improvement.

record.title: Worsening bony MRI appearance during clinical improvement
fairness: Continuing planned pathogen-directed treatment is the single best offered response to improving pain, walking tolerance and inflammatory markers without a new neural or mechanical complication.

The worsening endplate/disc appearance supplies real conflicting evidence. Interpreting that discordance and then choosing whether to escalate treatment are consequential steps; antibiotic broadening and surgery represent recognizable overreactions to imaging.

The negative neurological and structural observations establish why continued treatment is reasonable. They are necessary safety information rather than a reason to remove those alternatives from all future cases.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation does not endorse stopping therapy or require radiographic normalization. The established diagnosis and complete course are included in the singleton. Interpreting response and source-control indications is high yield.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between bony imaging evolution and new epidural, neural or mechanical complications. Do not generalize this answer to every worsening MRI during infection.
Optional tightening: remove the generic 'next dated' update. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

decisionNodes.stem: While continuing bloodstream-infection treatment, which next diagnostic plan best addresses {patientName}'s two spinal sites?

answerChoices.label: Image-guided T8 lesion biopsy for culture and histology
answerChoices.rationale: The bloodstream isolate fits the lumbar disc/endplate pattern, but it does not automatically explain a structurally different thoracic lesion. Tissue at the unresolved site can address infection and mimickers.

answerChoices.label: Image-guided L3-L4 biopsy for culture and histology
answerChoices.rationale: This could resample a site already concordant with the bloodstream evidence while leaving the distinct thoracic process unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Treatment of both sites with follow-up spinal imaging
answerChoices.rationale: This correctly preserves active bacteremia treatment but assumes the separate lesion shares the lumbar cause without resolving its different structural pattern.

decisionNodes.explanation: A convincing blood isolate can remove the need for a routine diagnostic biopsy of a matching spinal infection. That inference is site specific. A distinct lesion with a different structural pattern can merit its own culture and histology while treatment of proven bacteremia continues. Disc preservation does not prove a tumor or exclude infection; it contributes to unresolved concordance.

concept.displayName: Apply bloodstream concordance to the matching spinal site while recognizing that a separate discordant lesion may need its own tissue diagnosis.
concept.learningObjective: Apply bloodstream concordance to the matching spinal site while recognizing that a separate discordant lesion may need its own tissue diagnosis.

record.title: Concordant infection at one spinal site and a distinct second lesion
fairness: Image-guided T8 lesion biopsy for culture and histology is the best offered plan: the bloodstream isolate and lumbar disc/endplate pattern support one diagnosis, while the separate destructive pedicle/vertebral lesion with a solid mass remains insufficiently explained.

Two consequential interpretations are required: deciding where bloodstream microbiology is sufficiently concordant, then deciding which separate lesion still requires tissue. Sampling L3-L4 and treating both sites empirically are credible different errors.
The explanation correctly does not equate preserved discs with proof of tumor or exclusion of infection. It preserves the uncertainty that makes culture plus histology appropriate.

The shared continuing treatment prevents a false choice between biopsy and treating bacteremia. Hemodynamic and neurological stability support the diagnostic framing. Both sites and the preceding microbiology are restated, so the case is independent of earlier spinal nodes.

Diagnostic anchoring, tissue diagnosis of a discordant destructive lesion and concordant S. aureus spinal infection are valuable, testable principles. The exact two-site scenario is a stretch application, not a claim of documented ABSITE frequency.
suggestions: Preserve the site-specific uncertainty and continuing bacteremia treatment in all options.
Optional clarity: phrase the surveillance option as deferring biopsy with interval imaging, since all plans already continue antimicrobial treatment. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Foot-drop localization despite pre-existing lumbar narrowing

cues.phrase: no electrodiagnostic localization is available
cues.why: This named omission favors an electrodiagnostic option, but it does not uniquely identify the key because both fibular and tibial study options remain. The motor map still has to be interpreted. This is a nonblocking cue, not a sufficient nonmedical answer shortcut.

fairness: Fibular nerve conduction and needle EMG is the best offered investigation: dorsiflexion/eversion weakness with preserved inversion and hip abduction favors a fibular distribution over assigning causation to the old foraminal image.
Localization changes the study choice before a lumbar intervention is considered. Repeat spine imaging is a plausible anchoring error; a tibial-directed study mismatches the principal deficit.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified if 'needle EMG' denotes an appropriate differential localization examination. The feedback should not imply that testing only fibular-innervated muscles definitively excludes a root lesion, or that an old image proves incidental disease.
All relevant postoperative context, examination and prior imaging are restated in the singleton. Peripheral-versus-root localization of foot drop is a high-yield application.
suggestions: Optional cue reduction: remove the named electrodiagnostic omission while preserving the old image and current motor map.

Clarify in feedback that a differential needle examination may sample appropriate nonfibular muscles; retain the distinction between a favored localization and a proven operative mechanism. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

record.title: Observe the actual staffing groups rather than the convenient planned sample
fairness: The learner must reclassify B and C by actual confirmed staffing and recognize that apparently mixed planned labels among volunteers still yield only usual staff. Roster selection across confirmed groups best guarantees coverage of both actual contexts.

Sampling across earlier planned groups could happen to include both actual groups, but does not ensure it. The question asks for the best plan, not whether one lucky selection could work; the key is defensible.
The complete four-cell option matrix is parallel and avoids component convergence. The current/earlier distinction is necessary timing information rather than an unnecessary teaching conclusion.

The shared presentation defines the pause and the local update supplies the new observation tool, roster and sampling data. The node stands alone and follows the implementation rehearsal coherently; prior feedback does not teach its staffing/volunteer discriminator.

Representative implementation sampling is a useful systems-measurement concept. This is one coherent sampling decision, not a demand for a second statistical endpoint; no numerical inference or arbitrary sample threshold is required. PASS remains editorial only.

record.title: Choose the receiving-work adaptation from observed task costs
fairness: The learner must reconcile fewer clarification contacts with increased total work, then localize the added work to destination entry and choose an adaptation. Retrieval and reconciliation alternatives address real workflow components rather than unrelated actions.

Totals independently recompute to 60 versus 100 staff-minutes for the same twenty referrals. Only destination entry changes from 5 to 45. Direct transfer of reconciled fields is the best bounded test; it is not presented as proven benefit.

The shared review and agreement checks preserve an important safety boundary without uniquely naming the key. Options are comparable specific workflow adaptations. PDSA adaptation and balancing measures are high-yield systems concepts.
The employee-discussion frame appropriately needs no invented patient age or sex. This is an editorial PASS, not clinical approval.

record.title: Use a favorable local result without assuming transfer
fairness: The reader must interpret fewer unresolved questions with unchanged measured workload, then recognize that a different callback assignment needs a bounded test. All three options are plausible choices about continuation and spread.

Continuing usual-staff use while testing relief coverage is the best offered step. Pooled rollout obscures the changed context; repeating only the usual assignment leaves the next operational uncertainty unresolved.
The equal denominators and constructed-data caption are clear. The explanation appropriately stops short of causal proof or a universal adoption threshold. No confident factual error identified.
suggestions: Preserve the matched outcome/workload comparison, distinct callback assignments and limited-benefit interpretation. This is an editorial PASS of the supplied wording, not clinician approval.

record.title: Choose the next portal pilot from complete work and instruction records
fairness: The learner must first preserve the stated instruction-agreement goal, then compare total work across both teams. Prefilled instructions look most efficient but have only 16/20 complete outputs; walkthrough preserves content but shifts enough work to nursing to eliminate the total-work advantage.

Independent totals are paper 120, prefilled 60, access-card 100 and walkthrough 120 staff-minutes. Access-card versus paper is therefore the best bounded pilot under the stated goal. No unsupported probability, cost-effectiveness threshold or clinical efficacy claim is needed.

The three options have the same comparator and parallel form. The key requires combining rows; it is not the unique minimum in either staff-work row or the only version preserving source instructions.

The update explains the portal's paperwork function and labels the same-record replay as simulation. It follows the reporting node coherently and stands alone with its own baseline, goals and exhibit. Prior feedback does not supply the workload answer.
Balancing measures, workload shifted between teams and choosing a bounded PDSA test are high-yield systems concepts. PASS is an editorial judgment, not clinical sign-off.

record.title: Compare harm using a frame independent of reporting uptake
fairness: The records show both an unreported harm event and multiple reports of one event. The learner must recognize that report records do not provide a stable representation of harm, then choose ascertainment independent of reporting participation.

A common harm definition does not fix missing events, and active review restricted to reporters still excludes eligible nonreporters. Roster-based active review in both periods is the best offered comparison.

Options are comparable measurement plans. 'Same' appears in every plan; the key is not uniquely cautious or qualified. No event rate, trend magnitude or causal effect can be inferred from these illustrative rows, and the explanation does not claim one.
The later workload node introduces a distinct portal function and new data. This explanation does not give its answer; this node is also self-contained.
Distinguishing safety-report activity from harm ascertainment is high yield. This editorial PASS does not establish clinical approval or verified exam frequency.

record.title: Verify use rather than installation of a barrier
fairness: The reader must recognize that print completion includes potentially bypassing work and that falling voluntary reports do not establish use, then select direct evaluation of identity linkage. All choices cover both staffing groups, so staffing words do not uniquely identify the key.

Direct observation is best for the implementation-fidelity question raised by the update. It does not by itself prove lower patient harm; logs and reports remain useful supporting measures as the explanation states.

The node is coherent after the first pilot and is answerable independently with the shared presentation and current update. Earlier feedback names the redesign, but does not prescribe this evaluation or disclose the new preprinting behavior.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between printing and actual identity linkage, and the limited interpretation of reporting counts. Editorial PASS does not approve the underlying specimen protocol or clinical claims.

record.title: Choose the receiving-work adaptation from observed task costs
fairness: The learner must reconcile fewer clarification contacts with increased total work, then localize the added work to destination entry and choose an adaptation. Retrieval and reconciliation alternatives address real workflow components rather than unrelated actions.

Totals independently recompute to 60 versus 100 staff-minutes for the same twenty referrals. Only destination entry changes from 5 to 45. Direct transfer of reconciled fields is the best bounded test; it is not presented as proven benefit.

The shared review and agreement checks preserve an important safety boundary without uniquely naming the key. Options are comparable specific workflow adaptations. PDSA adaptation and balancing measures are high-yield systems concepts.
The employee-discussion frame appropriately needs no invented patient age or sex. This is an editorial PASS, not clinical approval.

record.title: Verify use rather than installation of a barrier
fairness: The reader must recognize that print completion includes potentially bypassing work and that falling voluntary reports do not establish use, then select direct evaluation of identity linkage. All choices cover both staffing groups, so staffing words do not uniquely identify the key.

Direct observation is best for the implementation-fidelity question raised by the update. It does not by itself prove lower patient harm; logs and reports remain useful supporting measures as the explanation states.

The node is coherent after the first pilot and is answerable independently with the shared presentation and current update. Earlier feedback names the redesign, but does not prescribe this evaluation or disclose the new preprinting behavior.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between printing and actual identity linkage, and the limited interpretation of reporting counts. Editorial PASS does not approve the underlying specimen protocol or clinical claims.

record.title: Compare harm using a frame independent of reporting uptake
fairness: The records show both an unreported harm event and multiple reports of one event. The learner must recognize that report records do not provide a stable representation of harm, then choose ascertainment independent of reporting participation.

A common harm definition does not fix missing events, and active review restricted to reporters still excludes eligible nonreporters. Roster-based active review in both periods is the best offered comparison.

Options are comparable measurement plans. 'Same' appears in every plan; the key is not uniquely cautious or qualified. No event rate, trend magnitude or causal effect can be inferred from these illustrative rows, and the explanation does not claim one.
The later workload node introduces a distinct portal function and new data. This explanation does not give its answer; this node is also self-contained.
Distinguishing safety-report activity from harm ascertainment is high yield. This editorial PASS does not establish clinical approval or verified exam frequency.

record.title: Choose the next portal pilot from complete work and instruction records
fairness: The learner must first preserve the stated instruction-agreement goal, then compare total work across both teams. Prefilled instructions look most efficient but have only 16/20 complete outputs; walkthrough preserves content but shifts enough work to nursing to eliminate the total-work advantage.

Independent totals are paper 120, prefilled 60, access-card 100 and walkthrough 120 staff-minutes. Access-card versus paper is therefore the best bounded pilot under the stated goal. No unsupported probability, cost-effectiveness threshold or clinical efficacy claim is needed.

The three options have the same comparator and parallel form. The key requires combining rows; it is not the unique minimum in either staff-work row or the only version preserving source instructions.

The update explains the portal's paperwork function and labels the same-record replay as simulation. It follows the reporting node coherently and stands alone with its own baseline, goals and exhibit. Prior feedback does not supply the workload answer.
Balancing measures, workload shifted between teams and choosing a bounded PDSA test are high-yield systems concepts. PASS is an editorial judgment, not clinical sign-off.

record.title: Suspected bladder leak after an underfilled routine CT
fairness: Retrograde CT cystography is the best offered study after intravenous-contrast imaging with a freely draining, collapsed bladder when a bladder defect is suspected.

The learner identifies why the existing study does not exclude a leak and selects a protocol that tests the relevant compartment. Excretory images are a credible urinary-imaging misconception but do not substitute for proper retrograde distension.

The raw catheter/acquisition observations are necessary data rather than an illegitimate answer explanation. The standalone record includes operation, symptoms and prior study. No fixed volume/wait or confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Symptomatic tubal ectopic pregnancy with active hepatitis
fairness: Laparoscopic treatment is the best offered pathway: persistent symptoms and a nonresolving hCG course weaken expectant management, while active hepatic disease makes systemic methotrexate unsuitable.
Both the ongoing ectopic course and treatment contraindication must be applied. A supplied diagnosis is legitimate for this distinct treatment decision.

Although the update says "next specialist scan," all necessary diagnostic findings, stability and treatment constraints are present within this standalone node. No prior answer is needed and no confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: New adnexal symptoms after confirmed intrauterine pregnancy
fairness: Same-day pelvic ultrasound and gynecology assessment is the best offered pathway. A genuine earlier intrauterine pregnancy does not explain new adnexal symptoms after assisted conception or exclude a concurrent adnexal process.

The learner must distinguish validity of the old intrauterine finding from its temporal/anatomical limits, then choose current assessment over marker surveillance or an initial nongynecologic imaging route.
The earlier complete examination preceded symptoms, making current pelvic imaging a meaningful reassessment. The standalone story is coherent. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Elective stone clearance during required uninterrupted anticoagulation
fairness: Retrograde ureteroscopy is the best offered procedure under the explicit requirement to continue anticoagulation after infection resolution; shock-wave and percutaneous antegrade approaches have different bleeding implications.

Required anticoagulation is a legitimate patient-specific constraint, not an unsupported availability cue. The learner applies the treated-infection state and bleeding constraint to choose a clearance route.

The later elective visit and infection resolution are explicit, so no earlier node is needed. Feedback retains individualized risk discussion and prescribes neither bridging nor an invented waiting interval.
No confident clinical error identified offline; suitability in an actual patient remains a clinician decision.

record.title: Infected obstructed collecting system: drainage before stone clearance
fairness: Urgent stent or nephrostomy drainage is the best offered strategy for combined obstruction and systemic infection despite antibiotics and resuscitation already underway.

The learner identifies the infected obstructed system and distinguishes source-control drainage from definitive stone fragmentation. Antibiotics-only observation and premature definitive instrumentation are consequential errors.

The standalone node supplies CT findings, infection observations, renal change and treatment already started. The drainage methods are appropriately alternatives rather than falsely ranked. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Persistent intermittent colic before planned ureteroscopy
fairness: Noncontrast CT is the best offered reassessment when no stone was recovered, baseline radiography did not depict it, and ultrasound does not locate it.

Improved symptoms and absent hydronephrosis must be interpreted without equating them with clearance; that inference changes whether an intervention has a target. Proceeding and canceling are distinct credible errors.
The standalone record identifies the trial of passage, conditional surgery and current stability. No confident clinical inaccuracy found.

record.title: Confirming stone passage after reported gritty material
fairness: Pain resolution, baseline creatinine and unrecovered gritty material do not demonstrate clearance of the imaged stone. Anatomical reassessment is the best offered plan before discharge or an unnecessary procedure.
Baseline radiographic visibility supports ultrasound plus abdominal radiography. The learner judges the strength of passage evidence and selects a suitable follow-up pathway.
The node stands alone without a universal follow-up interval or mandatory CT rule. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical cue identified.

record.title: Stone reassessment before ureteroscopy after pain resolves
fairness: Low-dose noncontrast CT is the best offered plan: symptom resolution without recovery of the stone does not establish passage, and ultrasound plus a baseline nonvisualizing radiograph do not settle the procedural target.
Interpreting symptom change and imaging limits, then deciding between reassessment, proceeding and canceling, requires two consequential steps. Both procedural errors are credible.

Negative pregnancy testing and stable infection/renal observations support the pathway. The standalone record contains the prior imaging and proposed procedure. No confident clinical error identified offline.

record.title: Stone reassessment after hydronephrosis resolves
fairness: Resolution of dilation and pain does not demonstrate passage of a stone neither recovered nor located on follow-up imaging. Noncontrast CT before proceeding with or canceling ureteroscopy is the best offered action.
The first inference distinguishes resolved secondary findings from demonstrated clearance; the second changes the procedural plan. Earlier plain-film nonvisualization supports modality selection.
The standalone history and safety observations are sufficient. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical wording shortcut identified.

record.title: Possible adnexal torsion despite arterial Doppler flow
fairness: Urgent gynecologic assessment for laparoscopy is the best offered plan for intermittent acute pain, vomiting, persistent tenderness and concerning ovarian morphology despite arterial flow.

The learner integrates morphology and clinical course without treating arterial waveforms as exclusion, then avoids delaying surgical assessment for more imaging. This is a high-yield two-step error test.

The constructed text ultrasound exhibit is present, explicitly labeled and observational rather than diagnostic. The node stands alone. No claim of proven nonviability or confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: Postoperative urine leak: selecting upper-tract CT acquisitions
fairness: Markedly higher drain than serum creatinine supports urinary fluid; flank pain and a retroperitoneal collection raise ureteral/upper-tract concern. The performed portal-venous series does not adequately assess excreted urine leakage.
CT urography is the best offered next protocol. Identifying the likely leak pathway and interpreting actual acquisition limitations are distinct consequential steps.

The acquisition log establishes what was performed, rather than merely describing an absent exported image. Cystography is a credible competing urinary-leak study; noncontrast CT would not show excreted contrast leakage.
The standalone record includes surgery, symptoms, chemistry and imaging history. No confident clinical inaccuracy or unsupported diagnostic cutoff identified.

record.title: Infected obstructed collecting system: drainage before stone clearance
fairness: Urgent stent or nephrostomy drainage is the best offered strategy for combined obstruction and systemic infection despite antibiotics and resuscitation already underway.

The learner identifies the infected obstructed system and distinguishes source-control drainage from definitive stone fragmentation. Antibiotics-only observation and premature definitive instrumentation are consequential errors.

The standalone node supplies CT findings, infection observations, renal change and treatment already started. The drainage methods are appropriately alternatives rather than falsely ranked. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: After drainage of an infected obstructed system, antibiotics are complete, fever has resolved, creatinine is back at baseline and culture is negative. Current CT shows a 9-mm proximal ureteral stone beside the stent. At a later elective urology visit he chooses active stone clearance. He takes warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve; INR is within his prescribed therapeutic range, and the treating cardiology team advises that anticoagulation cannot be interrupted for the proposed treatment.
decisionNodes.stem: Which stone-clearance procedure should the team choose for Evan Collins under this treatment plan?

answerChoices.label: Retrograde ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy
answerChoices.rationale: This is an acceptable stone-clearance option when necessary anticoagulation cannot be stopped, after discussion of its bleeding risks.

answerChoices.label: Shock-wave lithotripsy targeting the ureteral stone
answerChoices.rationale: Therapeutic anticoagulation makes this otherwise real stone technique unsuitable in the stated treatment plan.

answerChoices.label: Percutaneous antegrade ureteroscopic stone treatment
answerChoices.rationale: A percutaneous/antegrade route is unsuitable under the stated uncorrected anticoagulation constraint.

decisionNodes.explanation: The infection has been treated and active clearance is now selected. When required anticoagulation cannot be interrupted, retrograde ureteroscopy is an acceptable option with individualized bleeding-risk discussion; shock-wave and antegrade procedures do not fit the stated constraint. No warfarin interruption, bridging regimen or universal postinfection interval is prescribed.
sourceLabels: Canadian Urological Association Journal (2021)

record.title: Elective stone clearance during required uninterrupted anticoagulation
fairness: Retrograde ureteroscopy is the best offered procedure under the explicit requirement to continue anticoagulation after infection resolution; shock-wave and percutaneous antegrade approaches have different bleeding implications.

Required anticoagulation is a legitimate patient-specific constraint, not an unsupported availability cue. The learner applies the treated-infection state and bleeding constraint to choose a clearance route.

The later elective visit and infection resolution are explicit, so no earlier node is needed. Feedback retains individualized risk discussion and prescribes neither bridging nor an invented waiting interval.
No confident clinical error identified offline; suitability in an actual patient remains a clinician decision.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: The original CT showed a ureteral stone with upstream dilation, and the stone was also identifiable on the baseline abdominal radiograph. At the planned trial-of-passage review he reports that pain stopped after passing gritty material into the toilet. He did not recover material for inspection. Creatinine is at baseline and he is afebrile.
decisionNodes.stem: Which follow-up plan should the team choose for Mason Burke at this review?

answerChoices.label: Renal ultrasound and abdominal radiograph reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: These can reassess the known radiograph-visible stone and collecting system before deciding that the episode is finished.

answerChoices.label: Discharge to routine stone-prevention follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: Symptom relief and the unverified report do not establish clearance of the known obstructing stone.

answerChoices.label: Ureteroscopy to clear the previously documented stone
answerChoices.rationale: The available record does not establish whether an invasive target remains; current noninvasive reassessment can resolve that uncertainty first.

decisionNodes.explanation: Pain relief, baseline creatinine and a report of gritty material do not reliably establish that the documented obstructing stone has cleared. Anatomical reassessment can determine whether follow-up can end or further stone treatment is needed. An indeterminate study may require additional imaging; no universal interval is set.
sourceLabels: Canadian Urological Association Journal (2021)

record.title: Confirming stone passage after reported gritty material
fairness: Pain resolution, baseline creatinine and unrecovered gritty material do not demonstrate clearance of the imaged stone. Anatomical reassessment is the best offered plan before discharge or an unnecessary procedure.
Baseline radiographic visibility supports ultrasound plus abdominal radiography. The learner judges the strength of passage evidence and selects a suitable follow-up pathway.
The node stands alone without a universal follow-up interval or mandatory CT rule. No confident clinical inaccuracy or nonmedical cue identified.

record.title: Postoperative urine leak: selecting upper-tract CT acquisitions
fairness: Markedly higher drain than serum creatinine supports urinary fluid; flank pain and a retroperitoneal collection raise ureteral/upper-tract concern. The performed portal-venous series does not adequately assess excreted urine leakage.
CT urography is the best offered next protocol. Identifying the likely leak pathway and interpreting actual acquisition limitations are distinct consequential steps.

The acquisition log establishes what was performed, rather than merely describing an absent exported image. Cystography is a credible competing urinary-leak study; noncontrast CT would not show excreted contrast leakage.
The standalone record includes surgery, symptoms, chemistry and imaging history. No confident clinical inaccuracy or unsupported diagnostic cutoff identified.

record.title: Suspected bladder leak after an underfilled routine CT
fairness: Retrograde CT cystography is the best offered study after intravenous-contrast imaging with a freely draining, collapsed bladder when a bladder defect is suspected.

The learner identifies why the existing study does not exclude a leak and selects a protocol that tests the relevant compartment. Excretory images are a credible urinary-imaging misconception but do not substitute for proper retrograde distension.

The raw catheter/acquisition observations are necessary data rather than an illegitimate answer explanation. The standalone record includes operation, symptoms and prior study. No fixed volume/wait or confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The learner integrates morphology and clinical course without treating arterial waveforms as exclusion, then avoids delaying surgical assessment for more imaging. This is a high-yield two-step error test.

The constructed text ultrasound exhibit is present, explicitly labeled and observational rather than diagnostic. The node stands alone. No claim of proven nonviability or confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

record.title: NASCET measurement and the treatment boundary
fairness: The supplied diameters yield 1 - 3/5 = 40% by NASCET, while using the estimated original bulb yields 1 - 3/10 = 70%. The learner must choose the correct reference vessel and then apply the treatment boundary; both steps affect the plan.

Medical prevention and follow-up is the defensible best offered plan for the stated ordinary sub-50% lesion without recurrent symptoms. CEA and stenting represent errors in transferring the outside percentage into a treatment indication.

The choices are parallel care plans with medical prevention shared. The nonsurgical option is not automatically a cue: its distinction is the actual decision being tested, and the exhibit is needed to justify it.

The sequence is coherent and the preceding explanation does not teach the NASCET denominator. With the shared presentation, update and exhibit shown, the node can be answered independently of the prior selection.

High-yield clinical measurement and management concept; this is not a statistics item requiring the single-skill exception. PASS is an offline editorial assessment, not current-source verification or clinical approval.
suggestions: Optional consistency cleanup: the earlier CTA is 'above 70%' while this update calls the outside result '70%'. Use the same reported value or explicitly identify rounding; this does not change the present best answer.

Keep the explanation focused on why the reference diameter changes treatment. Do not imply that the old CTA's error was proven to be denominator choice when the earlier presentation attributes a limitation to calcific blooming.

record.title: Distal ICA collapse and the limits of ordinary stenosis rules
fairness: The threadlike distal ICA, delayed filling and comparison with both the opposite ICA and ipsilateral external carotid provide observations from which the learner must infer distal collapse. The diagnosis is not stated before the answer.

The second consequential step is recognizing that the usual severe-symptomatic-stenosis intervention rule does not transfer directly to this anatomy, while considering the absence of recurrent events on prevention.

The three options are parallel treatment plans with background prevention shared. The medical option's distinct action is the tested clinical distinction, not a unique explanatory qualifier or convergence cue.

Continued prevention and neurovascular follow-up is a defensible best offered plan for the described nonrecurrent presentation. The explanation explicitly attributes its management recommendation to ESVS and preserves ESO uncertainty; absence of an ESO recommendation does not by itself establish that either routine early procedure is equally correct.

The narrower guideline recommendation and its current status were not independently verified in this no-network review. This editorial PASS is conditional on clinical confirmation of that evidence boundary and does not certify consensus or approve the exact version clinically.
High-yield severe-stenosis exception, though more specialized than routine CEA selection. It is a complete single-node case; no preceding feedback supplies the diagnosis.
suggestions: Preserve the explicit evidence limitation and named-guideline attribution in feedback; do not expand this into a universal near-occlusion prohibition.
Retain separate clinician review for recurrent events despite treatment. Do not import a recurrent-case intervention rule into this nonrecurrent item.

record.title: Recurrent weakness
fairness: The chronology distinguishes the earlier team's attribution from the current evidence. The INR observations require interpretation; the presentation does not label anticoagulation therapeutic. Recurrent left-arm events and right cortical infarcts make the severe right carotid lesion consequential despite the competing AF history.

CEA is the defensible best offered plan after reassessing recurrent ipsilateral events during apparently adequate anticoagulation, with age and favorable neck anatomy distinguishing it from transfemoral CAS. Continued warfarin-based management is a credible anchoring error; transfemoral CAS is a credible procedure-selection error. AF remains a separate treatment indication, as the shared context and explanation acknowledge.

The first consequential step is integrating event territory and treatment adequacy to reconsider anticoagulation-based management. The second is choosing the revascularization route using the patient-specific operative context. These are different decisions, not two names for the same finding. Predicted difficulty is moderate, not measured.

No unique wording overlap, length outlier, absolute, explanatory distractor or convergence pattern identifies CEA without clinical knowledge. The common prevention wording is balanced. The initial cardiac attribution is historical information, not an author-supplied current diagnosis.

No confident clinical error identified. These observations do not prove that every embolus originated in the carotid, and the explanation appropriately calls for reassessment rather than claiming proof. The exact ESVS recurrence recommendation was not independently source-verified in this no-network, candidate-content review; clinical sign-off remains required.

Symptomatic-carotid management, competing embolic sources and age-sensitive procedure selection are high-yield. This is one self-contained node; no prior answer or later part supplies its discriminator. Name, age, sex, complaint and complete task are consistent.
suggestions: Retain the competing AF history, serial INR observations, new ipsilateral cortical events and explicit transfemoral comparator. Avoid replacing those observations with labels such as therapeutic-anticoagulation failure or proven carotid embolism.

Keep the statement that AF prevention requires its own perioperative plan. Editorial PASS does not approve uninterrupted perioperative warfarin or a specific anticoagulation protocol, and the exact version remains needs_clinician_review.

record.title: Reassessing carotid treatment after neurologic recovery
fairness: Serial absence of a cervical lumen on arterial and delayed imaging, with intracranial collateral filling, supports chronic complete occlusion rather than an ordinary severe stenosis with a reconstructible lumen.

The update changes the decision: neurologic recovery removes the earlier timing problem, but current vessel anatomy defeats routine CEA. EC-IC bypass is a clinically recognizable competing error rather than a spelling or length cue.

Medical prevention without carotid reconstruction is the defensible best offered routine plan. The explanation correctly distinguishes intracranial collateral filling from patency of the cervical ICA and limits its bypass statement to routine practice.

The progression from severe stenosis to later documented occlusion is possible and explicitly supported by interval imaging. The node stands alone with its shared presentation and current update; it need not rely on choosing the previous answer correctly.

High-yield distinction between chronic occlusion and severe stenosis, with a meaningful second decision after recovery. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; PASS is editorial and offline, not fresh evidence verification or named-clinician approval.
suggestions: Preserve the serial and delayed-imaging observations; do not replace them with a pre-answer 'chronic occlusion' label.
Preserve the update's recovery context and the explanation's 'routine' qualification for bypass.

case.presentation: Jonah Price, a 68-year-old man, attends clinic after resolved right arm weakness six days ago. Outside brain imaging shows no infarct or hemorrhage. Two expert reviews leave a left ICA duplex report below 50% and a CTA report above 70% in disagreement; calcific blooming obscures the CTA lumen. Renal function is at baseline. Aspirin, statin therapy and risk-factor treatment have begun.

case.presentation: The founder reviews Nora Lewis's outside hospital records in clinic. Nora is a 71-year-old woman admitted yesterday with persistent right arm and leg weakness and difficulty speaking. She needs help dressing and cannot walk independently. CTA shows left ICA stenosis of 84% with a patent distal lumen. CT shows infarction and edema involving about half the left MCA territory, without hemorrhage. The hospital stroke team is providing medical treatment.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Eight weeks later, Nora attends clinic independently after rehabilitation. Interval brain imaging shows the established infarct without edema or hemorrhage. CTA and expert duplex show no cervical left ICA lumen from its origin to the skull base on arterial or delayed imaging. The intracranial left ICA fills through communicating arteries. This appearance was also present on imaging four weeks earlier; she has had no new events.
decisionNodes.stem: Which long-term left carotid plan best fits Nora Lewis's current vascular findings?

answerChoices.label: Continue medical prevention without carotid reconstruction
answerChoices.rationale: The persistent absent cervical lumen represents established occlusion, not an ordinary severe stenosis to reopen through CEA.

answerChoices.label: Perform CEA with continued medical prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Distal collateral opacification does not establish a patent cervical lumen suitable for routine endarterectomy.

answerChoices.label: Perform EC-IC bypass with continued medical prevention
answerChoices.rationale: Bypass has not established a stroke-prevention advantage for this atherosclerotic occlusion indication.

decisionNodes.explanation: The serial absence of a cervical lumen on adequate arterial and delayed imaging establishes chronic occlusion. Communicating arteries explain intracranial filling without reopening the cervical ICA. Neurologic recovery removes the earlier timing barrier but does not create a CEA target. Continue medical prevention; routine EC-IC bypass is not recommended for atherosclerotic ICA occlusion.

concept.displayName: Distinguish chronic ICA occlusion with distal collateral filling from a treatable severe residual stenosis after stroke recovery.
concept.learningObjective: Distinguish chronic ICA occlusion with distal collateral filling from a treatable severe residual stenosis after stroke recovery.

record.title: Reassessing carotid treatment after neurologic recovery
fairness: Serial absence of a cervical lumen on arterial and delayed imaging, with intracranial collateral filling, supports chronic complete occlusion rather than an ordinary severe stenosis with a reconstructible lumen.

The update changes the decision: neurologic recovery removes the earlier timing problem, but current vessel anatomy defeats routine CEA. EC-IC bypass is a clinically recognizable competing error rather than a spelling or length cue.

Medical prevention without carotid reconstruction is the defensible best offered routine plan. The explanation correctly distinguishes intracranial collateral filling from patency of the cervical ICA and limits its bypass statement to routine practice.

The progression from severe stenosis to later documented occlusion is possible and explicitly supported by interval imaging. The node stands alone with its shared presentation and current update; it need not rely on choosing the previous answer correctly.

High-yield distinction between chronic occlusion and severe stenosis, with a meaningful second decision after recovery. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; PASS is editorial and offline, not fresh evidence verification or named-clinician approval.
suggestions: Preserve the serial and delayed-imaging observations; do not replace them with a pre-answer 'chronic occlusion' label.
Preserve the update's recovery context and the explanation's 'routine' qualification for bypass.

case.presentation: Ruth Carter, a 70-year-old woman, attends clinic after outside assessment for a brief right-eye visual loss eight days ago. CTA shows a very tight right bulb lumen, a threadlike distal right cervical ICA, and delayed intracranial filling. The distal right ICA is smaller than both the opposite ICA and the right external carotid artery. Brain imaging shows no infarct. She has had no recurrence since starting medical prevention.

record.title: Distal ICA collapse and the limits of ordinary stenosis rules
fairness: The threadlike distal ICA, delayed filling and comparison with both the opposite ICA and ipsilateral external carotid provide observations from which the learner must infer distal collapse. The diagnosis is not stated before the answer.

The second consequential step is recognizing that the usual severe-symptomatic-stenosis intervention rule does not transfer directly to this anatomy, while considering the absence of recurrent events on prevention.

The three options are parallel treatment plans with background prevention shared. The medical option's distinct action is the tested clinical distinction, not a unique explanatory qualifier or convergence cue.

Continued prevention and neurovascular follow-up is a defensible best offered plan for the described nonrecurrent presentation. The explanation explicitly attributes its management recommendation to ESVS and preserves ESO uncertainty; absence of an ESO recommendation does not by itself establish that either routine early procedure is equally correct.

The narrower guideline recommendation and its current status were not independently verified in this no-network review. This editorial PASS is conditional on clinical confirmation of that evidence boundary and does not certify consensus or approve the exact version clinically.
High-yield severe-stenosis exception, though more specialized than routine CEA selection. It is a complete single-node case; no preceding feedback supplies the diagnosis.
suggestions: Preserve the explicit evidence limitation and named-guideline attribution in feedback; do not expand this into a universal near-occlusion prohibition.
Retain separate clinician review for recurrent events despite treatment. Do not import a recurrent-case intervention rule into this nonrecurrent item.

case.presentation: Martin Bell, a 74-year-old man, attends clinic after another resolved episode of left-arm weakness yesterday. Four weeks earlier, a similar event led to detection of atrial fibrillation. The initial team favored cardiac embolism and started warfarin. Recorded INRs since then are 2.4, 2.6 and 2.5, with the latest drawn during yesterday's assessment. Brain MRI shows two small recent right cortical infarcts without hemorrhage or edema. CTA shows ordinary 81% right ICA stenosis with a patent normal-caliber distal vessel and a low cervical lesion. He lives independently, walks without angina or dyspnea, and has no prior neck surgery or radiation. The procedural teams meet audited guideline risk criteria. Lipid treatment and the indicated AF prevention continue under the treating teams' perioperative protocol.

answerChoices.rationale: Revascularization is reasonable, but transfemoral CAS has a less favorable peri-procedural neurologic comparison in an otherwise operable patient older than 70.

answerChoices.rationale: Maintaining AF prevention is necessary, but it does not resolve the new carotid decision after recurrent ipsilateral events during therapeutic anticoagulation.

ESVS recommends carotid revascularization for recurrent ipsilateral events during therapeutic anticoagulation in this setting. Age 74 and the accessible neck favor CEA over transfemoral CAS. AF prevention still requires its own perioperative plan.

record.title: Recurrent weakness
fairness: The chronology distinguishes the earlier team's attribution from the current evidence. The INR observations require interpretation; the presentation does not label anticoagulation therapeutic. Recurrent left-arm events and right cortical infarcts make the severe right carotid lesion consequential despite the competing AF history.

CEA is the defensible best offered plan after reassessing recurrent ipsilateral events during apparently adequate anticoagulation, with age and favorable neck anatomy distinguishing it from transfemoral CAS. Continued warfarin-based management is a credible anchoring error; transfemoral CAS is a credible procedure-selection error. AF remains a separate treatment indication, as the shared context and explanation acknowledge.

The first consequential step is integrating event territory and treatment adequacy to reconsider anticoagulation-based management. The second is choosing the revascularization route using the patient-specific operative context. These are different decisions, not two names for the same finding. Predicted difficulty is moderate, not measured.

No unique wording overlap, length outlier, absolute, explanatory distractor or convergence pattern identifies CEA without clinical knowledge. The common prevention wording is balanced. The initial cardiac attribution is historical information, not an author-supplied current diagnosis.

No confident clinical error identified. These observations do not prove that every embolus originated in the carotid, and the explanation appropriately calls for reassessment rather than claiming proof. The exact ESVS recurrence recommendation was not independently source-verified in this no-network, candidate-content review; clinical sign-off remains required.

Symptomatic-carotid management, competing embolic sources and age-sensitive procedure selection are high-yield. This is one self-contained node; no prior answer or later part supplies its discriminator. Name, age, sex, complaint and complete task are consistent.
suggestions: Retain the competing AF history, serial INR observations, new ipsilateral cortical events and explicit transfemoral comparator. Avoid replacing those observations with labels such as therapeutic-anticoagulation failure or proven carotid embolism.

Keep the statement that AF prevention requires its own perioperative plan. Editorial PASS does not approve uninterrupted perioperative warfarin or a specific anticoagulation protocol, and the exact version remains needs_clinician_review.

record.title: Initial investigation of recurrent urinary infection with pneumaturia and abdominal findings
fairness: Best offered answer: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis. First interpret recurrent treated infections, bubbles during urination without instrumentation, and focal abdominal tenderness as concern for a bowel-bladder process; then choose an investigation that evaluates its cause and surrounding anatomy rather than limiting the initial examination to the urinary lumen or collecting system. Cystoscopy is the closest credible error for a resident anchoring on recurrent urinary infection.

The findings raise suspicion rather than prove diverticular fistulization. Other causes of urinary gas are possible, but that uncertainty does not create a better offered initial investigation. The explanation appropriately calls for assessment instead of declaring a confirmed fistula or its cause.

Cystoscopy can be useful in subsequent bladder evaluation and ultrasound can assess urinary obstruction; neither is the best offered initial assessment of this combined abdominal and urinary presentation. Their usefulness in other circumstances does not make them coequal keys here.

Cue attack: 'bubbles during urination' is a clinical discriminator, not a lexical match to the CT option. 'There had been no urinary catheterization' is necessary interpretation context for urinary gas. 'initial combination of findings' modestly favors a broad evaluation conceptually, but identifying the appropriate modality still requires clinical knowledge. No diagnosis label, rationale embedded in a choice, absolute, convergence pattern or decisive length outlier supplies the answer.

Standalone check: Daniel Mercer has a consistent age, sex and short complaint; the update contains the relevant prior treatment, symptoms and investigation history. The task clearly asks for the initial investigation in this retrospective clinic review. There is one node, no exhibit and no preceding feedback or later part to supply missing information or rehearse the answer.

Moderate, toward the easier end: the syndrome is recognizable, but choosing cross-sectional assessment over a plausible bladder-directed investigation is a consequential second decision. This is a high-yield general-surgery diagnostic concept; that rating is an editorial judgment, not a measured exam-frequency claim.

Offline review of the candidate text only. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; exact fistula-oriented contrast protocols and current guideline wording were not independently verified. PASS is editorial and does not confer clinical approval; the draft remains needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: No required repair for this standalone version. Keep the no-instrumentation history and avoid adding a pre-answer fistula label or a sentence telling the learner to evaluate both organs.

If feedback is expanded in a future authorized version, explain why cystoscopy may contribute later without replacing the initial assessment of adjacent bowel and bladder. Do not imply that the broad CT option specifies every protocol detail needed to demonstrate a tract.

record.title: Initial CT selection for overlapping abdominal and urinary symptoms
fairness: Best offered answer: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis. First weigh focal left-lower-quadrant tenderness and fever against dysuria and limited urinalysis abnormalities; then select an imaging approach that assesses a possible colonic inflammatory process and its complications rather than committing to a ureteric-stone protocol.

The urinalysis does not prove or exclude a urinary source. Absence of blood does not rule out a stone, and absence of nitrites does not rule out urinary infection. The broader clinical pattern makes contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT the best offered choice without requiring either false exclusion. Normal creatinine supports the stated contrast choice without inventing a renal-function cutoff.

Noncontrast stone-protocol CT can also show some alternative abdominal findings; it should not be taught as incapable of detecting diverticulitis. It remains less appropriate than the offered contrast-enhanced study for this uncertain first inflammatory presentation. Colonoscopy is a plausible stage-of-care error, but does not replace initial assessment of an acute extraluminal inflammatory process.

Cue attack: 'discomfort during urination' could attract the stone distractor rather than reveal the key. 'Creatinine was within the laboratory reference interval' is contrast-related context, but two CT options remain and the finding does not itself establish the suspected source. The options have comparable length, name investigations and contain no self-discrediting explanations. Neither the complaint nor the presentation supplies a diverticulitis diagnosis.

Standalone check: Elena Brooks has a consistent age, sex and short complaint. 'At that visit' resolves to the first episode described in the presentation, and 'initial presentation' distinguishes the historical investigation from a test to order at today's follow-up. The solitary node requires no missing treatment result, companion explanation or exhibit.

Moderate at the lower boundary, not hard: the conventional CT choice will be familiar, but the urinary findings create a real anchoring error and require choosing between two CT protocols. The competing urinary and colonic interpretations make the second decision meaningful. Initial investigation and complication assessment of suspected diverticulitis are high-yield surgical learning objectives.

Offline review of the candidate text only. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, and no new probability, threshold or diagnostic exclusion is asserted. Guideline currency was not independently verified. Editorial PASS leaves needs_clinician_review unchanged.
suggestions: No required standalone repair. Preserve the urinary findings and uncertainty of the first episode; removing them would reduce this to an easier diagnosis-to-test association.

For a future authorized feedback revision, explicitly distinguish the preferred broader inflammatory evaluation from a stone-focused protocol while acknowledging that noncontrast CT can detect other pathology. Do not claim that the negative urine findings exclude urinary disease.

record.title: Persistent alarm findings despite a recent adequate colonoscopy

cues.phrase: She tolerated that examination without a procedural problem.
cues.why: Minor, nonfatal feasibility cue: it reassures the learner about repeating the prior optical examination immediately before that option is offered. It adds little beyond the documented complete, adequately prepared examination. Removing it would preserve the clinical ranking; it does not independently settle why optical colonoscopy is preferred to CT colonography.

fairness: Best offered answer: optical colonoscopy. First distinguish persistent caliber change, weight loss and focal thickening from uncomplicated recovery despite the recent reassuring examination; then select direct luminal assessment with the ability to sample a suspicious abnormality rather than another structural imaging study.

The recent colonoscopy's date, completion and preparation are supplied, so the learner cannot solve the case simply by assuming the prior examination was inadequate. New alarm findings create the diagnostic indication. The known diverticulitis-with-abscess label supplies legitimate background and does not resolve this new investigation decision.

CT colonography is a credible competitor for structural colonic evaluation, but cannot obtain tissue and is less appropriate as the first offered investigation when optical examination is feasible and new focal pathology requires assessment. Conventional CT has already shown the persistent abnormality and resolved collection; repeating it does not address the principal remaining luminal question as directly. Neither distractor is categorically useless.

The task says 'post-recovery', and the update supplies resolution of fever, acute tenderness and the collection. Together these support a diagnostic examination after the acute episode rather than urgent endoscopy during active diverticulitis. The text does not establish a fixed safe interval or prove that every inflammatory change has vanished, and the review does not infer either claim. No confident clinical error or second equally defensible best answer identified.

Other cue attacks: 'colonoscopy report documented cecal intubation, good preparation and no mass' repeats a term in the key but is decision-critical competing evidence, not an unfair answer announcement. 'Optical colonoscopy' and 'CT colonography' are similarly concise procedure names; the longer conventional-CT distractor does not create a key-length cue. No pre-answer teaching sentence says that tissue is required or names the new diagnosis.

Standalone check: Nora Bennett has a consistent age, sex and short complaint. Her admission, recovery, current symptoms and earlier colonoscopy are all contained in this single case. There is no dependence on an absent companion's stricture findings or management decision, no prior explanation and no missing exhibit. The task is complete when displayed separately with its presentation and update.

Moderate: the recent high-quality examination creates meaningful competing reassurance, and modality selection then requires a capability distinction. Persistent alarm features and the limits of a prior negative examination are high-yield concepts. This is not hard solely because several observations are supplied.

Offline review of the candidate text only; guideline currency and exact timing recommendations were not independently verified. The verdict does not endorse a blanket repeat-colonoscopy rule after every abscess despite a recent adequate examination. Editorial PASS is limited to these symptomatic findings and leaves needs_clinician_review unchanged.
suggestions: No required repair for standalone coherence or answer uniqueness. In a future authorized wording version, remove the prior-tolerance sentence to reduce redundant feasibility cueing while retaining the examination's date, completeness and preparation quality.

Make the reusable distinction explicit in post-answer feedback: new alarm findings warrant diagnostic reassessment despite a recent adequate examination, and optical colonoscopy permits tissue sampling whereas CT colonography does not. Avoid inventing a waiting interval or treating persistent thickening as proof of malignancy.
