record.title: Initial CT selection for overlapping abdominal and urinary symptoms
fairness: Best offered answer: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis. First weigh focal left-lower-quadrant tenderness and fever against dysuria and limited urinalysis abnormalities; then select an imaging approach that assesses a possible colonic inflammatory process and its complications rather than committing to a ureteric-stone protocol.

The urinalysis does not prove or exclude a urinary source. Absence of blood does not rule out a stone, and absence of nitrites does not rule out urinary infection. The broader clinical pattern makes contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT the best offered choice without requiring either false exclusion. Normal creatinine supports the stated contrast choice without inventing a renal-function cutoff.

Noncontrast stone-protocol CT can also show some alternative abdominal findings; it should not be taught as incapable of detecting diverticulitis. It remains less appropriate than the offered contrast-enhanced study for this uncertain first inflammatory presentation. Colonoscopy is a plausible stage-of-care error, but does not replace initial assessment of an acute extraluminal inflammatory process.

Cue attack: 'discomfort during urination' could attract the stone distractor rather than reveal the key. 'Creatinine was within the laboratory reference interval' is contrast-related context, but two CT options remain and the finding does not itself establish the suspected source. The options have comparable length, name investigations and contain no self-discrediting explanations. Neither the complaint nor the presentation supplies a diverticulitis diagnosis.

Standalone check: Elena Brooks has a consistent age, sex and short complaint. 'At that visit' resolves to the first episode described in the presentation, and 'initial presentation' distinguishes the historical investigation from a test to order at today's follow-up. The solitary node requires no missing treatment result, companion explanation or exhibit.

Moderate at the lower boundary, not hard: the conventional CT choice will be familiar, but the urinary findings create a real anchoring error and require choosing between two CT protocols. The competing urinary and colonic interpretations make the second decision meaningful. Initial investigation and complication assessment of suspected diverticulitis are high-yield surgical learning objectives.

Offline review of the candidate text only. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, and no new probability, threshold or diagnostic exclusion is asserted. Guideline currency was not independently verified. Editorial PASS leaves needs_clinician_review unchanged.
suggestions: No required standalone repair. Preserve the urinary findings and uncertainty of the first episode; removing them would reduce this to an easier diagnosis-to-test association.

For a future authorized feedback revision, explicitly distinguish the preferred broader inflammatory evaluation from a stone-focused protocol while acknowledging that noncontrast CT can detect other pathology. Do not claim that the negative urine findings exclude urinary disease.

record.title: Persistent alarm findings despite a recent adequate colonoscopy

cues.phrase: She tolerated that examination without a procedural problem.
cues.why: Minor, nonfatal feasibility cue: it reassures the learner about repeating the prior optical examination immediately before that option is offered. It adds little beyond the documented complete, adequately prepared examination. Removing it would preserve the clinical ranking; it does not independently settle why optical colonoscopy is preferred to CT colonography.

fairness: Best offered answer: optical colonoscopy. First distinguish persistent caliber change, weight loss and focal thickening from uncomplicated recovery despite the recent reassuring examination; then select direct luminal assessment with the ability to sample a suspicious abnormality rather than another structural imaging study.

The recent colonoscopy's date, completion and preparation are supplied, so the learner cannot solve the case simply by assuming the prior examination was inadequate. New alarm findings create the diagnostic indication. The known diverticulitis-with-abscess label supplies legitimate background and does not resolve this new investigation decision.

CT colonography is a credible competitor for structural colonic evaluation, but cannot obtain tissue and is less appropriate as the first offered investigation when optical examination is feasible and new focal pathology requires assessment. Conventional CT has already shown the persistent abnormality and resolved collection; repeating it does not address the principal remaining luminal question as directly. Neither distractor is categorically useless.

The task says 'post-recovery', and the update supplies resolution of fever, acute tenderness and the collection. Together these support a diagnostic examination after the acute episode rather than urgent endoscopy during active diverticulitis. The text does not establish a fixed safe interval or prove that every inflammatory change has vanished, and the review does not infer either claim. No confident clinical error or second equally defensible best answer identified.

Other cue attacks: 'colonoscopy report documented cecal intubation, good preparation and no mass' repeats a term in the key but is decision-critical competing evidence, not an unfair answer announcement. 'Optical colonoscopy' and 'CT colonography' are similarly concise procedure names; the longer conventional-CT distractor does not create a key-length cue. No pre-answer teaching sentence says that tissue is required or names the new diagnosis.

Standalone check: Nora Bennett has a consistent age, sex and short complaint. Her admission, recovery, current symptoms and earlier colonoscopy are all contained in this single case. There is no dependence on an absent companion's stricture findings or management decision, no prior explanation and no missing exhibit. The task is complete when displayed separately with its presentation and update.

Moderate: the recent high-quality examination creates meaningful competing reassurance, and modality selection then requires a capability distinction. Persistent alarm features and the limits of a prior negative examination are high-yield concepts. This is not hard solely because several observations are supplied.

Offline review of the candidate text only; guideline currency and exact timing recommendations were not independently verified. The verdict does not endorse a blanket repeat-colonoscopy rule after every abscess despite a recent adequate examination. Editorial PASS is limited to these symptomatic findings and leaves needs_clinician_review unchanged.
suggestions: No required repair for standalone coherence or answer uniqueness. In a future authorized wording version, remove the prior-tolerance sentence to reduce redundant feasibility cueing while retaining the examination's date, completeness and preparation quality.

Make the reusable distinction explicit in post-answer feedback: new alarm findings warrant diagnostic reassessment despite a recent adequate examination, and optical colonoscopy permits tissue sampling whereas CT colonography does not. Avoid inventing a waiting interval or treating persistent thickening as proof of malignancy.

record.title: Failed dilation and POEM: salvage before esophagectomy
fairness: Referral for Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication is the best offered plan at the explicitly identified earlier referral. Persistent junctional hold-up, reduced distensibility, relatively straight anatomy and an operative report showing inadequate gastric extension support a potentially correctable residual outflow problem. Failure of dilation and POEM alone does not establish that esophagectomy is the next best step. Botulinum toxin is a less suitable durable salvage strategy in the stated patient who was fit for major surgery.

The explanation appropriately recommends considering Heller salvage and specialized foregut assessment rather than promising success or claiming this operation is mandatory after every failed POEM. Other specialist salvage approaches may exist, but they are not competing offered keys. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The exact procedural ranking and suitability remain subject to clinician review; no fresh guideline or source verification was performed.

Cover-the-key attack: 'the muscle division had stopped short of the gastric extension' is a concrete operative observation, not a named recommendation or a wording match to the Heller option. It is legitimately decision-critical. 'fit for major surgery' favors a durable intervention only with clinical knowledge and still leaves two surgical referrals competing. The relatively straight anatomy and focal hold-up must be interpreted together. Options consistently use 'Refer for', name actual interventions, and do not contain explanatory distractor wording, absolutes, unique caution, an outlier-length key or a convergence shortcut.

Two consequential steps remain: infer an incompletely treated junctional obstruction with potentially useful esophageal anatomy, then choose organ-preserving surgical salvage over resection despite two previous treatment failures. This is a high-yield surgical principle applied to a moderately difficult salvage scenario. Botulinum toxin is the weaker distractor, but esophagectomy is a credible escalation error. The item is not hard merely because several procedures appear in the history.

The standalone presentation identifies a named 54-year-old woman in clinic after discharge. 'At that earlier referral' and the task's 'earlier referral after dilation and POEM had failed' consistently locate the decision in the prior record. Fitness for surgery applies at that earlier time; the task does not ask the learner to operate during the current respiratory illness. The original preceding or subsequent nodes are unnecessary. No exhibit is supplied or promised and there is no later scored part whose answer is disclosed by this explanation.

This independent editorial assessment applies to the supplied standalone candidate, without relying on its recorded prior PASS. It confers neither clinical approval nor verification of runtime randomization, wait previews or source mappings. Clinical review remains pending Melissa Rowland's approval of the exact version.
suggestions: Optional presentation polish: shorten the framing about reviewing 'earlier and current outside foregut records' while preserving the explicit retrospective time point. Do not recast this as a decision about current operative fitness after the respiratory illness.
Preserve the operative-report observation and anatomical findings; deleting them would turn the question into an unsupported blanket choice of Heller after failed POEM.

record.title: Failed dilation and POEM: salvage before esophagectomy
fairness: Referral for Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication is the best offered plan at the explicitly identified earlier referral. Persistent junctional hold-up, reduced distensibility, relatively straight anatomy and an operative report showing inadequate gastric extension support a potentially correctable residual outflow problem. Failure of dilation and POEM alone does not establish that esophagectomy is the next best step. Botulinum toxin is a less suitable durable salvage strategy in the stated patient who was fit for major surgery.

The explanation appropriately recommends considering Heller salvage and specialized foregut assessment rather than promising success or claiming this operation is mandatory after every failed POEM. Other specialist salvage approaches may exist, but they are not competing offered keys. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The exact procedural ranking and suitability remain subject to clinician review; no fresh guideline or source verification was performed.

Cover-the-key attack: 'the muscle division had stopped short of the gastric extension' is a concrete operative observation, not a named recommendation or a wording match to the Heller option. It is legitimately decision-critical. 'fit for major surgery' favors a durable intervention only with clinical knowledge and still leaves two surgical referrals competing. The relatively straight anatomy and focal hold-up must be interpreted together. Options consistently use 'Refer for', name actual interventions, and do not contain explanatory distractor wording, absolutes, unique caution, an outlier-length key or a convergence shortcut.

Two consequential steps remain: infer an incompletely treated junctional obstruction with potentially useful esophageal anatomy, then choose organ-preserving surgical salvage over resection despite two previous treatment failures. This is a high-yield surgical principle applied to a moderately difficult salvage scenario. Botulinum toxin is the weaker distractor, but esophagectomy is a credible escalation error. The item is not hard merely because several procedures appear in the history.

The standalone presentation identifies a named 54-year-old woman in clinic after discharge. 'At that earlier referral' and the task's 'earlier referral after dilation and POEM had failed' consistently locate the decision in the prior record. Fitness for surgery applies at that earlier time; the task does not ask the learner to operate during the current respiratory illness. The original preceding or subsequent nodes are unnecessary. No exhibit is supplied or promised and there is no later scored part whose answer is disclosed by this explanation.

This independent editorial assessment applies to the supplied standalone candidate, without relying on its recorded prior PASS. It confers neither clinical approval nor verification of runtime randomization, wait previews or source mappings. Clinical review remains pending Melissa Rowland's approval of the exact version.
suggestions: Optional presentation polish: shorten the framing about reviewing 'earlier and current outside foregut records' while preserving the explicit retrospective time point. Do not recast this as a decision about current operative fitness after the respiratory illness.
Preserve the operative-report observation and anatomical findings; deleting them would turn the question into an unsupported blanket choice of Heller after failed POEM.

record.title: Indefinite biopsy review
fairness: The current update specifies omeprazole once daily before breakfast with adherence confirmed at the time of biopsy. The key now names the change to administration before breakfast and dinner, followed by repeat mapped endoscopy. Both the medication decision and the reassessment sequence are concrete; no missing prior encounter is needed.

The two consequential steps are to interpret the expert indefinite grade in markedly inflamed tissue as unresolved neoplasia status, then increase acid suppression and obtain reassessment before choosing routine surveillance or ablation. Expert agreement does not convert indefinite findings into confirmed dysplasia. The current once-daily regimen makes the treatment modification consequential, rather than an unspecified instruction to optimize therapy.

Exactly one offered plan is best: twice-daily premeal omeprazole followed by repeat mapped endoscopy. Continuing the current regimen with routine surveillance prematurely treats the uncertain grade as settled; increasing treatment and then ablating bypasses histologic reassessment. No confident clinical inaccuracy or equally defensible competing key was identified. This review does not establish a dose or a required repeat interval.

Cue attack: 'Omeprazole before breakfast and dinner' occurs in both the key and the ablation option, so escalation wording does not uniquely disclose the answer. 'Mapped biopsies' and 'repeat mapped endoscopy' have some natural repetition, but surveillance also involves reassessment and the overlap does not settle the sequencing decision without clinical knowledge. Options have comparable grammar, scope and specificity; no decisive length, absolute, convergence or teaching-sentence shortcut was found. 'Indefinite for dysplasia' is a legitimate pathology result for a management task.

The named 59-year-old woman, biopsy-review complaint, outside-treatment history and current pathology are consistent. This single-node case stands alone and has no later part or preceding feedback to supply its answer. The explanation correctly places management interpretation after the choice. The task remains complete when separated from the presentation.

This is a high-yield Barrett management boundary and a moderate application item, not a hard item. The competing errors are undertreating unresolved inflammation and overcalling indefinite atypia as an ablation indication. Difficulty and high-yield ratings are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified exam frequencies.

Scope: all five entries still marked salvage were assessed at their current candidate versions. The two newer revisions replace their obsolete review rows; the three unchanged salvage contexts retain their existing findings, which remain consistent with this review. Kept-unchanged, retired, parked and held records are outside scope. This offline review uses candidate presentation, update, exhibit, task, options and explanation only for clinical judgments; it is not fresh source verification, runtime validation or clinical approval. All drafts remain needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: Retain the current medication, meal-based administration and confirmed adherence alongside the expert indefinite grade and active inflammation; together these resolve the former ambiguity.

Optional clarity polish: 'repeat endoscopy with mapped biopsies' would make the intended tissue reassessment explicit in the answer label. The current biopsy context and explanation already make that meaning clear.
Do not add an invented dose or repeat interval to make the item appear harder. Preserve the two concrete competing errors and keep their rationales after the answer.

record.title: Treated reflux review
fairness: The prior off-treatment LA grade C esophagitis supplies objective GERD evidence despite subsequent mucosal healing. Persistent regurgitation after documented twice-daily premeal omeprazole with confirmed adherence makes on-PPI impedance-pH the best offered investigation of residual reflux and symptom association.

The resident must first interpret the original versus treated endoscopic findings, then choose testing conditions appropriate to established disease with persistent symptoms. Off-PPI wireless monitoring tempts the error of treating healed mucosa as an unproven diagnosis. Manometry is relevant in foregut assessment but does not answer the immediate residual reflux question. No second equally strong key is apparent from the supplied clinical situation.

The options are specific investigations of comparable length. The exhibit's 'off-treatment' wording overlaps the wrong wireless option rather than uniquely cueing the key. 'Established history' is an unnecessary interpretive heading, but it does not state the test or the on-treatment rule; the resident must still know what LA grade C establishes.

The presentation, age/sex and complaint are consistent. All relevant medication, response and prior-disease information is present in this single node. 'At a later clinic visit' can refer to outside care and does not require an earlier game decision; no later part is present.

The explanation accurately distinguishes the persistent-symptom question from initial GERD confirmation. The stated 8 weeks is a fictional treatment history, not a runtime wait. Its exact evidentiary basis was not independently verified in this no-network review and should not be generalized into a universal threshold. This is a high-yield, moderate application item rather than a hard one.
suggestions: Retain the prior severe erosive finding, healed follow-up examination and actual optimized administration; together they support the two-step distinction.
Optional clarity polish: use 'Prior endoscopy' instead of 'Established history' and remove 'At a later clinic visit' if the standalone screen otherwise suggests an unseen game encounter.
Keep the explanation focused on the test's purpose; do not imply that all persistent symptoms are caused by reflux or that positive procedural eligibility has already been established.

record.title: Residual Barrett review
fairness: The favorable intramucosal cancer pathology, negative deep and lateral margins and absent lymphovascular invasion support continuing endoscopic management. The residual flat Barrett field after neoplasia is not equivalent to never-neoplastic nondysplastic Barrett; ablation is the best offered next field treatment.

Two meaningful interpretations remain: distinguish completed local treatment from a lesion requiring further resection, then use the prior neoplasia history rather than the residual nondysplastic biopsies to choose ablation over surveillance. Surveillance is a credible misapplication of the usual nondysplastic-Barrett rule. Resection of the remaining flat segment is a less attractive alternative than ablation and is not an equally preferred plan here.

'Which endoscopic plan' and 'fit for endoscopic treatment' constrain the broader surgery-versus-endoscopy decision, so this should not be advertised as a hard cancer-staging item. They do not choose between the three offered endoscopic plans. All options repeat 'the remaining Barrett segment' and differ by one parallel action verb; there is no key-only wording overlap, length outlier or component-convergence shortcut.

The completed-resection presentation and pathology/residual map provide the necessary standalone history. No earlier lesion-treatment answer or explanation is needed, and there is no later part. The named Barrett diagnosis is legitimate background for a post-neoplasia management task.

The explanation correctly separates complete resection of the visible cancer from risk in the remaining Barrett field. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the supplied fields. cues.phrase: Which next endoscopic intervention / Endoscopic ultrasound before lesion treatment
cues.why: Minor category cue: 'intervention' sounds therapeutic, while this ultrasound option is explicitly a pretreatment diagnostic step. That can make the ultrasound distractor easier to discount without knowing its staging limitations. It does not distinguish resection from ablation and does not collapse the clinical decision.

fairness: A discrete visible abnormality with forceps-biopsy high-grade dysplasia needs a resection specimen for histologic assessment before subsequent ablation is selected. The absence of represented submucosa limits the biopsy's staging information; it does not prove submucosal invasion. The explanation respects that distinction.

The resident must interpret the biopsy's depth limitation in a visible lesion, then select tissue resection rather than treating the entire segment or using ultrasound as the next superficial-staging step. Direct ablation is a credible error after seeing confirmed high-grade dysplasia; ultrasound is a credible staging misconception. Neither is an equally strong next answer for the described discrete lesion.

'A discrete raised lesion with shallow depression' does not by itself establish deep invasion or unresectability. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified, but a later change to lesion morphology or a technique-specific key would require a new resectability/staging review. The present generic endoscopic-resection option avoids an unsupported EMR-versus-ESD ranking.

The presentation supplies expert-confirmed grade and fitness, while the exhibit supplies the lesion and biopsy limitations. The patient, age/sex and clinic review setting are coherent. The standalone node requires no earlier answer and exposes no later resection result.

'Visible lesion' overlaps the resection option, but the other choices also address that lesion or its containing segment; the phrase is clinically necessary to the sequencing distinction. The known dysplasia label is appropriate for this management task. There is no decisive key-only length, absolute or convergence cue.

This is a high-yield, moderate Barrett treatment-sequencing item, not a hard exercise. The pathology limitation and choice between a staging specimen, imaging and ablation provide meaningful reasoning despite the minor task-category cue.

Options have comparable grammar, scope and specificity; no decisive length, absolute, convergence or teaching-sentence shortcut was found. 'Indefinite for dysplasia' is a legitimate pathology result for a management task.

The named 59-year-old woman, biopsy-review complaint, outside-treatment history and current pathology are consistent. This single-node case stands alone and has no later part or preceding feedback to supply its answer. The explanation correctly places management interpretation after the choice. The task remains complete when separated from the presentation.

This is a high-yield Barrett management boundary and a moderate application item, not a hard item. The competing errors are undertreating unresolved inflammation and overcalling indefinite atypia as an ablation indication. Difficulty and high-yield ratings are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified exam frequencies.

The two newer revisions replace their obsolete review rows; the three unchanged salvage contexts retain their existing findings, which remain consistent with this review. record.title: Treated reflux review
fairness: The prior off-treatment LA grade C esophagitis supplies objective GERD evidence despite subsequent mucosal healing. Persistent regurgitation after documented twice-daily premeal omeprazole with confirmed adherence makes on-PPI impedance-pH the best offered investigation of residual reflux and symptom association.

The resident must first interpret the original versus treated endoscopic findings, then choose testing conditions appropriate to established disease with persistent symptoms. Off-PPI wireless monitoring tempts the error of treating healed mucosa as an unproven diagnosis. Manometry is relevant in foregut assessment but does not answer the immediate residual reflux question. No second equally strong key is apparent from the supplied clinical situation.

The options are specific investigations of comparable length. The exhibit's 'off-treatment' wording overlaps the wrong wireless option rather than uniquely cueing the key. 'Established history' is an unnecessary interpretive heading, but it does not state the test or the on-treatment rule; the resident must still know what LA grade C establishes.

The presentation, age/sex and complaint are consistent. All relevant medication, response and prior-disease information is present in this single node. 'At a later clinic visit' can refer to outside care and does not require an earlier game decision; no later part is present.

The explanation accurately distinguishes the persistent-symptom question from initial GERD confirmation. The stated 8 weeks is a fictional treatment history, not a runtime wait. Its exact evidentiary basis was not independently verified in this no-network review and should not be generalized into a universal threshold. This is a high-yield, moderate application item rather than a hard one.
suggestions: Retain the prior severe erosive finding, healed follow-up examination and actual optimized administration; together they support the two-step distinction.
Optional clarity polish: use 'Prior endoscopy' instead of 'Established history' and remove 'At a later clinic visit' if the standalone screen otherwise suggests an unseen game encounter.
Keep the explanation focused on the test's purpose; do not imply that all persistent symptoms are caused by reflux or that positive procedural eligibility has already been established.

record.title: Residual Barrett review
fairness: The favorable intramucosal cancer pathology, negative deep and lateral margins and absent lymphovascular invasion support continuing endoscopic management. The residual flat Barrett field after neoplasia is not equivalent to never-neoplastic nondysplastic Barrett; ablation is the best offered next field treatment.

Two meaningful interpretations remain: distinguish completed local treatment from a lesion requiring further resection, then use the prior neoplasia history rather than the residual nondysplastic biopsies to choose ablation over surveillance. Surveillance is a credible misapplication of the usual nondysplastic-Barrett rule. Resection of the remaining flat segment is a less attractive alternative than ablation and is not an equally preferred plan here.

'Which endoscopic plan' and 'fit for endoscopic treatment' constrain the broader surgery-versus-endoscopy decision, so this should not be advertised as a hard cancer-staging item. They do not choose between the three offered endoscopic plans. All options repeat 'the remaining Barrett segment' and differ by one parallel action verb; there is no key-only wording overlap, length outlier or component-convergence shortcut.

The completed-resection presentation and pathology/residual map provide the necessary standalone history. No earlier lesion-treatment answer or explanation is needed, and there is no later part. The named Barrett diagnosis is legitimate background for a post-neoplasia management task.

The explanation correctly separates complete resection of the visible cancer from risk in the remaining Barrett field. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified in the supplied fields. This is a high-yield, moderate treatment-sequencing decision; exact technique and timing are not being tested or freshly verified.
suggestions: Preserve the original neoplastic histology, favorable resection findings and nondysplastic residual map together. Removing the neoplasia history would change the answer; omitting the resection findings would leave treatment adequacy uncertain.
Keep any preceding feedback from naming residual-field ablation if this node is later recombined into a multi-part case. The current standalone version has no such sequence cue.
In subsequent teaching feedback, distinguish ablation of the residual field from surveillance after treatment; do not imply that choosing ablation eliminates later surveillance.

record.title: Reflux evidence review

cues.phrase: Complete off-treatment esophageal inspection / Wireless distal pH monitoring off PPI
cues.why: Limited lexical cue: the only off-PPI option echoes the prior off-treatment examination, whereas both other options use on-PPI testing. This permits a wording-match guess but does not logically select the answer. Prior acquisition conditions are legitimate data; deleting them would weaken interpretation. The task does not teach that a prior off-treatment test determines the conditions for the next one.

fairness: The new factual history states that acid suppression preceded any testing, this was the first upper endoscopy and no ambulatory reflux monitoring has occurred. Together with the normal off-treatment inspection, this resolves the former possibility of earlier conclusive GERD evidence. The case no longer relies on its title, slug or an absent companion to establish diagnostic history.

The resident must first distinguish partial symptom response and a normal examination from objective confirmation of GERD, then choose monitoring conditions that establish baseline reflux burden before a procedural decision. Wireless distal pH monitoring off PPI is the single best offered strategy. Persistent symptoms do not by themselves make on-PPI impedance-pH the appropriate initial confirmation study.

On-PPI impedance-pH is the closest credible error because symptoms persist during treatment; it answers a different question in established GERD. Wireless pH monitoring on PPI is a weaker but recognizable mistake about how treatment affects acid measurement. Neither is equally appropriate for this explicitly supplied first-workup history. The explanation now follows from the visible data rather than assuming a missing history. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified.

The neutral monitoring-strategy task is complete and all three options answer it with specific, similarly sized investigation plans. The option components do not converge on the key: their majority components would produce wireless monitoring on PPI, which is a distractor. No key-only length, absolute or explanatory-option cue was found. The prior 'never undergone ambulatory reflux monitoring' history is decision-critical and does not uniquely favor any of the three monitoring options.

The named 41-year-old man, regurgitation complaint, treatment response and prior endoscopy are coherent. All required history is present in this standalone node; no prior answer or later result is needed. There is no later part. The examination excludes visible erosive disease but is not misrepresented as excluding GERD.

This is a high-yield, moderate preprocedural evidence-and-test-selection item with two consequential steps. A hypothetical prior conclusive GERD study would change the testing question, so the added history earns its place. It is not a hard item, and the residual lexical vulnerability should not be mistaken for strong difficulty. Clinical assessment is offline; no numerical protocol or external guideline currency was independently verified.
suggestions: Preserve the factual first-endoscopy and never-monitored history rather than replacing it with the interpretive label 'unproven GERD' or a statement that records are unavailable.
Retain clinically necessary treatment conditions despite the minor overlap; do not add a pre-answer sentence explaining why testing must be off therapy.
Keep the task limited to the appropriate monitoring strategy. A positive diagnostic study would still require subsequent patient-specific assessment before selecting an antireflux procedure.

record.title: Visible lesion review

cues.phrase: Which next endoscopic intervention / Endoscopic ultrasound before lesion treatment
cues.why: Minor category cue: 'intervention' sounds therapeutic, while this ultrasound option is explicitly a pretreatment diagnostic step. That can make the ultrasound distractor easier to discount without knowing its staging limitations. It does not distinguish resection from ablation and does not collapse the clinical decision.

fairness: A discrete visible abnormality with forceps-biopsy high-grade dysplasia needs a resection specimen for histologic assessment before subsequent ablation is selected. The absence of represented submucosa limits the biopsy's staging information; it does not prove submucosal invasion. The explanation respects that distinction.

The resident must interpret the biopsy's depth limitation in a visible lesion, then select tissue resection rather than treating the entire segment or using ultrasound as the next superficial-staging step. Direct ablation is a credible error after seeing confirmed high-grade dysplasia; ultrasound is a credible staging misconception. Neither is an equally strong next answer for the described discrete lesion.

'A discrete raised lesion with shallow depression' does not by itself establish deep invasion or unresectability. No confident clinical inaccuracy was identified, but a later change to lesion morphology or a technique-specific key would require a new resectability/staging review. The present generic endoscopic-resection option avoids an unsupported EMR-versus-ESD ranking.

The presentation supplies expert-confirmed grade and fitness, while the exhibit supplies the lesion and biopsy limitations. The patient, age/sex and clinic review setting are coherent. The standalone node requires no earlier answer and exposes no later resection result.

'Visible lesion' overlaps the resection option, but the other choices also address that lesion or its containing segment; the phrase is clinically necessary to the sequencing distinction. The known dysplasia label is appropriate for this management task. There is no decisive key-only length, absolute or convergence cue.

This is a high-yield, moderate Barrett treatment-sequencing item, not a hard exercise. The pathology limitation and choice between a staging specimen, imaging and ablation provide meaningful reasoning despite the minor task-category cue.
suggestions: Optional wording polish: ask for the 'next endoscopic step' so diagnostic ultrasound and therapeutic procedures answer the same task without a semantic disadvantage.
Preserve the actual biopsy limitation; do not replace it with a teaching sentence such as 'depth cannot be staged until resection'.
Keep the resection technique generic unless supported lesion characteristics and verified criteria are added for a technique-specific decision.

record.title: Antibacterial endpoint after pelvic source control
fairness: Standalone case v2 supplies the prior drainage, completion findings, current imaging, recovery and treatment clock. The task explicitly refers to the recorded fourth-day reassessment, so the later clinic visit does not change the decision time. No preceding question or explanation is needed; there are no later parts.

Stopping antibacterial therapy is the single defensible best answer among these choices: the supplied observations support controlled infection and clinical recovery without a separate treatment indication. Neither a retained catheter nor residual fat stranding, in this stated context, independently justifies continuing treatment. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

Two consequential steps remain: distinguish residual inflammation and device retention from an inadequately controlled collection, then apply the treatment endpoint to that interpretation. Continuing until catheter removal is a recognizable practice error; waiting for radiographic inflammatory changes to disappear is a second plausible over-treatment error. This supports moderate, not hard, predicted resident difficulty.

Cue attack found no nonmedical route to a unique answer. The two continue options share their grammar; the stop option is not uniquely elaborate. The fourth-day timing is necessary decision data, not a numerical cutoff invented by this review. The statement excluding another treatment indication limits the question fairly rather than identifying one option by wording.

record.title: Persistent pelvic infection after incisional drainage
fairness: Standalone case v2 contains the original incisional drainage, differential symptom response, hemodynamic and abdominal findings, and current CT report. The task asks about that recorded reassessment rather than the later clinic visit. The exhibit explicitly identifies itself as a constructed report, so no absent scan image must be interpreted. No prior question or subsequent part is needed.

Image-guided pelvic drainage is the single defensible best answer among the stated plans. The symptomatic rim-enhancing pelvic collection remains separate from the decompressed subcutaneous pocket; the patient lacks the stated findings that would favor immediate generalized abdominal exploration, and the report supplies a posterior access corridor. Antibacterial treatment and wound care are appropriately shared across plans.

Two consequential steps are present: infer that improvement of the superficial compartment does not establish control of the deeper infection, then integrate confinement, clinical stability and competing access paths to choose directed drainage rather than continued medical reassessment or exploration. Misreading anterior bowel interposition as excluding all image-guided access is a credible competing error. Predicted difficulty is moderate, not hard.

The phrases describing intact fascia and the anterior and posterior paths are necessary anatomical observations, not a diagnosis label or a statement that a named procedure is available. No key-only lexical match, convergence, uniquely qualified answer or rhetorical absolute supplies a nonmedical solution. Removing the access findings would weaken the fairness of the procedure comparison, so they should remain.

The explanation correctly limits a negative contrast finding: it does not claim that failure to demonstrate enteric escape excludes an occult communication. The 6-cm measurement is a case observation, not a general drainage threshold. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; exact technical access feasibility still depends on clinical procedural assessment rather than this simplified teaching report.

Source control, infection compartments and percutaneous versus operative management are high-yield general-surgery concepts. This is an offline editorial assessment of the supplied text, without fresh evidence verification or runtime preview validation. PASS does not confer clinical approval; retain needs_clinician_review.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: During the outside admission, a purulent subcutaneous incisional pocket was opened and decompressed, and piperacillin-tazobactam was administered. Across the examinations before that procedure and at the recorded reassessment, {patientName}'s fever and deep left pelvic pain persisted while incisional pain and redness diminished. Blood pressure was maintained without vasopressors, and tenderness remained confined to the lower abdomen without generalized guarding. The CT report obtained at that reassessment is shown below. Antibacterial therapy and incisional wound care continued under all plans.
decisionNodes.stem: At that recorded reassessment, which management plan was most appropriate for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Image-guided pelvic drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Improvement at the opened incision does not establish drainage of the pelvic compartment. The persisting deep symptoms and the fluid, debris and inflammatory findings in a different compartment support an unaddressed focal infection. Its confined distribution, the examination and the reported access anatomy favor image-guided drainage while antibacterial care continues. Failure to demonstrate contrast escape does not exclude an occult communication; deterioration or diffuse contamination would require renewed operative assessment.

answerChoices.label: Antibacterial treatment with reassessment
answerChoices.rationale: The observed local improvement concerns the decompressed incisional pocket. The deeper collection and continuing pelvic symptoms are not accounted for by that procedure, so another medical-only reassessment leaves this source unaddressed.

answerChoices.label: Operative abdominal exploration
answerChoices.rationale: The anterior route crosses bowel, but the same report describes a posterior soft-tissue corridor. With confined disease and the documented examination, that alternative access supports a directed procedure rather than abdominal exploration.

record.title: Persistent pelvic infection after incisional drainage
fairness: Standalone case v2 contains the original incisional drainage, differential symptom response, hemodynamic and abdominal findings, and current CT report. The task asks about that recorded reassessment rather than the later clinic visit. The exhibit explicitly identifies itself as a constructed report, so no absent scan image must be interpreted. No prior question or subsequent part is needed.

Image-guided pelvic drainage is the single defensible best answer among the stated plans. The symptomatic rim-enhancing pelvic collection remains separate from the decompressed subcutaneous pocket; the patient lacks the stated findings that would favor immediate generalized abdominal exploration, and the report supplies a posterior access corridor. Antibacterial treatment and wound care are appropriately shared across plans.

Two consequential steps are present: infer that improvement of the superficial compartment does not establish control of the deeper infection, then integrate confinement, clinical stability and competing access paths to choose directed drainage rather than continued medical reassessment or exploration. Misreading anterior bowel interposition as excluding all image-guided access is a credible competing error. Predicted difficulty is moderate, not hard.

The phrases describing intact fascia and the anterior and posterior paths are necessary anatomical observations, not a diagnosis label or a statement that a named procedure is available. No key-only lexical match, convergence, uniquely qualified answer or rhetorical absolute supplies a nonmedical solution. Removing the access findings would weaken the fairness of the procedure comparison, so they should remain.

The explanation correctly limits a negative contrast finding: it does not claim that failure to demonstrate enteric escape excludes an occult communication. The 6-cm measurement is a case observation, not a general drainage threshold. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; exact technical access feasibility still depends on clinical procedural assessment rather than this simplified teaching report.

Source control, infection compartments and percutaneous versus operative management are high-yield general-surgery concepts. This is an offline editorial assessment of the supplied text, without fresh evidence verification or runtime preview validation. PASS does not confer clinical approval; retain needs_clinician_review.

claims.statement: Rectus diastasis widens the linea alba rather than creating the focal fascial opening of a hernia; a separate focal defect can coexist.

claims.statement: Activity-limiting symptoms from a reducible hernia support elective surgical evaluation, with repair weighed against operative risks and the patient's goals.

claims.statement: A reducible incisional hernia without troublesome symptoms can be managed with observation after discussing repair risks and acute warning symptoms.

claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the exact constructed clinic encounters and outside-hospital chart reviews; see individual scope boundaries.

claims.statement: Persistent mesh infection after a completed conservative source-control attempt supports mesh excision assessment; sepsis requires urgent surgical source control.

claims.statement: Postoperative skin erythema does not by itself establish infection of a prosthesis; a draining deep tract or periprosthetic infected collection warrants evaluation of the implant plane.

claims.statement: Selected stable patients with infected hernia mesh may undergo a specialist-directed salvage attempt using antibiotics, drainage and/or wound debridement.

claims.statement: Watchful waiting can be considered for an asymptomatic reducible umbilical or epigastric hernia.

claims.statement: Physiotherapy may be considered before surgical management of rectus diastasis; no particular exercise programme or improvement in symptoms can be guaranteed from the guideline evidence.

claims.statement: For isolated rectus diastasis selected for surgery, plication with or without mesh augmentation is described, without an established universal preference among techniques.

claims.statement: After adequate source control in a stable selected single-stage ventral repair, a controlled bowel entry does not automatically require a biologic implant; current emergency guidance favors permanent macroporous synthetic mesh when mesh repair is selected.

claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.

claims.statement: Source control must address the actual infected compartment and ongoing contamination. Drain output from one space does not establish control of a separate collection.

claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated postoperative or perioperative context. Constructed cases fix age, sex, anatomy and treatment phase.

claims.statement: Continuing or recurrent abdominal infection after source-control treatment requires reassessment for an uncontrolled focus and microbiological mismatch.

claims.statement: Longstanding abdominal drains and collection systems can become colonized, so their culture results may misrepresent organisms causing an active intra-abdominal infection.

concepts.displayName: Pulmonary optimization before elective incisional-hernia repair
concepts.learningObjective: For a stable adult with a reducible, nonemergent incisional hernia and poorly controlled COPD, select pulmonary optimization before finalizing elective repair.

concepts.displayName: Initial imaging of a palpable breast mass under age 30
concepts.learningObjective: Select targeted breast ultrasound as the initial imaging study for the scoped adult patient younger than 30 with a new palpable breast mass.

concepts.displayName: Management of an asymptomatic simple breast cyst
concepts.learningObjective: Select no cyst-directed procedure for an imaging-concordant simple breast cyst that is not painful or bothersome.

concepts.displayName: Initial treatment of a painful simple breast cyst
concepts.learningObjective: Offer needle aspiration for symptom relief from a persistently painful or bothersome, imaging-concordant simple breast cyst.

concepts.displayName: Recognition of EBV-associated malignancies
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize canonical EBV-associated malignancies while preserving the boundary that an association is neither universal across every tumor nor an individual cancer-risk prediction.

concepts.displayName: Apply standard Milan criteria to HCC referral
concepts.learningObjective: Apply standard Milan tumor-number, size, macrovascular-invasion, and extrahepatic-disease criteria to recognize when HCC tumor burden supports transplant-center evaluation without treating the criteria as automatic listing.

concepts.displayName: Clinical recognition of Mondor disease
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize the characteristic superficial breast or chest-wall venous cord and its underlying superficial thrombophlebitis.

concepts.displayName: Selective imaging evaluation of suspected Mondor disease
concepts.learningObjective: Select targeted Doppler ultrasound when the superficial venous diagnosis is uncertain and age-appropriate diagnostic breast imaging when focal symptoms require evaluation for underlying pathology.

concepts.displayName: Supportive management of uncomplicated Mondor disease
concepts.learningObjective: Use supportive care for concordant uncomplicated Mondor disease while recognizing findings that require renewed evaluation.

concepts.displayName: Female sex and perioperative mortality after elective AAA repair
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize that women have higher observed perioperative mortality after elective intact AAA repair at the group level, while preserving the boundary that this association does not determine an individual outcome or select a repair approach.

concepts.displayName: Initial active surveillance for selected desmoid tumors
concepts.learningObjective: Choose specialist active surveillance as the initial strategy for newly diagnosed, stable or minimally symptomatic desmoid disease without critical threat or meaningful functional deterioration.

concepts.displayName: Surgical option for progressing symptomatic abdominal-wall desmoid
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize function-preserving resection after multidisciplinary review as an option for progressing symptomatic abdominal-wall desmoid when expected morbidity is acceptably low.

concepts.displayName: Distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy for resectable tail adenocarcinoma
concepts.learningObjective: Select oncologic distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy when a fit patient with pancreatic-tail adenocarcinoma has been judged resectable and is proceeding to surgery.

concepts.displayName: Recognize Felty syndrome
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize Felty syndrome from rheumatoid arthritis with persistent neutropenia, usually with splenomegaly, after important alternative causes have been excluded.

concepts.displayName: First-line methotrexate for Felty syndrome
concepts.learningObjective: Select specialist-monitored methotrexate as the usual first-line disease-modifying treatment and distinguish bridging therapy from the long-term plan.

concepts.displayName: Splenectomy for medically refractory Felty syndrome
concepts.learningObjective: Consider splenectomy only after recurrent infections persist despite adequate medical therapy and multidisciplinary review.

concepts.displayName: Biochemical evaluation for suspected FHH
concepts.learningObjective: Order paired 24-hour urine and serum calcium-creatinine measurements before parathyroid localization when FHH is suspected.

concepts.displayName: Recognize and confirm FHH
concepts.learningObjective: Use relative hypocalciuria, family context, and appropriate genetic evaluation without treating a low clearance ratio as independently diagnostic.

concepts.displayName: Avoid unnecessary parathyroid surgery in FHH
concepts.learningObjective: Reassure and observe a patient with confirmed uncomplicated FHH rather than performing routine parathyroid surgery.

concepts.displayName: Acute lymphangitis clinical recognition
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize acute lymphangitis from a distal skin entry site, a tender erythematous streak extending proximally, and tender regional lymph nodes.

concepts.displayName: Initial gallbladder-polyp management category
concepts.learningObjective: Select the owner-approved initial management category for a completed incidental gallbladder-polyp ultrasound profile.

concepts.displayName: Distal cholangiocarcinoma resection selection
concepts.learningObjective: For the approved resectable distal common-bile-duct profile, select hospital HPB referral for pancreaticoduodenectomy and distinguish the represented distal location.

concepts.displayName: Obstructive jaundice, vitamin K, and coagulopathy
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize the approved relationship between obstructive jaundice, reduced vitamin K absorption, and vitamin K-related coagulopathy.

concepts.displayName: HCC resection selection in compensated cirrhosis
concepts.learningObjective: For the approved favorable compensated-cirrhosis profile, select hospital HPB-surgery referral for hepatic resection evaluation without treating Child-Pugh A status or Milan classification alone as sufficient.

concepts.displayName: Accessory spleen common location
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize the splenic hilum as the most common location represented for an accessory spleen without treating one location as a complete splenectomy plan.

concepts.displayName: Persistent hemolysis after splenectomy evaluation
concepts.learningObjective: For the approved persistent-hemolysis presentation after total splenectomy, reassess and evaluate for functioning accessory splenic tissue without relying on MCV, RDW, or Howell-Jolly bodies alone.

concepts.displayName: Confirmed accessory splenic tissue management
concepts.learningObjective: For confirmed functioning accessory splenic tissue causing persistent symptomatic hemolysis, refer to hospital surgery for removal without treating incidental tissue as an indication.

concepts.displayName: Pouchitis after IPAA
concepts.learningObjective: Identify pouchitis as the approved common inflammatory pouch complication after IPAA for ulcerative colitis.

concepts.displayName: Type IVA congenital bile duct cyst anatomy
concepts.learningObjective: Identify Type IVA as the approved combined intrahepatic and extrahepatic cystic-dilatation pattern.

concepts.displayName: Anal HSIL and high-risk HPV
concepts.learningObjective: Identify high-risk human papillomavirus as the approved etiologic association of anal HSIL.

concepts.displayName: MEN2A manifestation pattern
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize the approved MEN2A pattern of medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism.

concepts.displayName: Pheochromocytoma before thyroid intervention
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize that a functioning pheochromocytoma must be excluded or addressed before thyroid intervention in the approved MEN2A scope.

concepts.displayName: Alpha blockade before beta blockade
concepts.learningObjective: When both are indicated for a functioning pheochromocytoma, establish alpha blockade before adding beta blockade.

concepts.displayName: Endoscopic recognition of colonic lipoma
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize the characteristic soft, yellowish, deformable subepithelial phenotype of a colonic lipoma while preserving the boundary that an absent cushion sign does not exclude it.

concepts.displayName: Management of a clearly characterized asymptomatic colonic lipoma
concepts.learningObjective: Choose no lipoma-directed treatment or dedicated surveillance for a clearly characterized asymptomatic colonic lipoma and recognize features that make that pathway inapplicable.

concepts.displayName: Vitamin C in collagen hydroxylation
concepts.learningObjective: Identify vitamin C as a cofactor for proline and lysine hydroxylation in collagen biosynthesis and connect inadequate hydroxylation with reduced collagen stability and impaired healing.

concepts.displayName: Pathologic recognition of gastric MALT lymphoma
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize gastric MALT lymphoma from integrated small B-cell morphology, lymphoepithelial lesions, and compatible immunophenotyping while avoiding diagnosis from CD20 alone.

concepts.displayName: H. pylori eradication as initial treatment for localized gastric MALT lymphoma
concepts.learningObjective: Select H. pylori eradication as initial treatment for the classic localized low-grade presentation and preserve confirmation and response-reassessment boundaries.

concepts.displayName: Confirmatory gastric-emptying testing for suspected gastroparesis
concepts.learningObjective: Select four-hour solid-meal gastric emptying scintigraphy to document delayed gastric emptying after mechanical obstruction has been excluded.

concepts.displayName: Avoid routine prophylactic splenectomy in proximal gastric cancer
concepts.learningObjective: Preserve the spleen during curative gastrectomy for proximal gastric adenocarcinoma when there is no greater-curvature invasion, direct splenic invasion, or suspected splenic-hilar disease.

concepts.displayName: High-risk peptic-ulcer stigmata requiring endoscopic hemostasis
concepts.learningObjective: Distinguish active spurting, active oozing, and a nonbleeding visible vessel from low-risk clean-base or flat-spot findings when deciding whether endoscopic hemostasis is required.

concepts.displayName: Endoscopic hemostasis modality selection for peptic-ulcer bleeding
concepts.learningObjective: Select an accepted definitive thermal or mechanical modality, recognize that epinephrine is never definitive monotherapy, and apply the conventional epinephrine-plus-definitive-modality pathway without making all monotherapies universally wrong.

concepts.displayName: Operable distal cholangiocarcinoma tissue evaluation
concepts.learningObjective: For the approved completed-imaging distal-obstruction profile, select the constrained combined endoscopic tissue-evaluation plan without treating CA 19-9 as confirmation.

concepts.displayName: Graves clinical-pattern recognition
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize an adult clinical pattern that supports Graves disease: symptoms compatible with thyroid-hormone excess together with diffuse thyroid enlargement and characteristic eye or pretibial skin findings when present, without requiring every feature in every patient.

concepts.displayName: TRAb diagnostic support for Graves disease
concepts.learningObjective: Use TRAb as etiologic support for Graves disease when a patient already has biochemical thyrotoxicosis; distinguish thyroid function from cause and recognize that a negative TRAb result does not fully exclude Graves disease.

concepts.displayName: RAI evaluation for recurrent Graves hyperthyroidism
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize recurrent hyperthyroidism after antithyroid-drug withdrawal as a setting where RAI evaluation is a reasonable counseling option, while retaining surgery and antithyroid-drug treatment as preference-sensitive alternatives.

concepts.displayName: RAI contraindication during pregnancy
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize current pregnancy as a contraindication to RAI treatment for Graves disease while continuing appropriate endocrine and obstetric assessment without RAI during pregnancy.

concepts.displayName: RAI contraindication during lactation
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize current breastfeeding as a contraindication to therapeutic iodine-131 for Graves disease and recognize the pre-treatment counseling boundary for feeding the current child.

concepts.displayName: RAI avoidance with active moderate-to-severe TED
concepts.learningObjective: Generally avoid therapeutic iodine-131 in ordinary Graves treatment counseling when specialist assessment documents active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease.

concepts.displayName: Initial ultrasound for suspected gallstones
concepts.learningObjective: Select abdominal ultrasound as the initial imaging study for a stable outpatient with recurrent symptoms compatible with uncomplicated gallstones.

concepts.displayName: Elective referral for symptomatic gallstones
concepts.learningObjective: Use compatible recurrent symptoms and uncomplicated ultrasound-confirmed gallstones to support elective surgical assessment and cholecystectomy counseling.

concepts.displayName: Observation of uncomplicated incidental gallstones
concepts.learningObjective: Choose observation and counseling for uncomplicated incidental gallstones in an asymptomatic adult without suspicious gallbladder features.

concepts.displayName: Noncontrast CT for unresolved suspected stone disease
concepts.learningObjective: Select noncontrast CT to resolve stone presence, location, and obstruction in a stable nonpregnant adult after indeterminate ultrasound.

concepts.displayName: Metabolic evaluation after recurrent kidney stones
concepts.learningObjective: Select stone analysis when available together with urine and blood metabolic assessment for prevention planning after recurrent confirmed stone disease.

concepts.displayName: Initial serology for suspected celiac disease
concepts.learningObjective: Select tTG-IgA with total-IgA context as a usual initial serologic assessment while a patient with compatible symptoms continues eating gluten.

concepts.displayName: Usual adult duodenal-biopsy confirmation
concepts.learningObjective: Select upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies as the usual confirmation step for an adult with compatible positive celiac serology and adequate IgA.

concepts.displayName: Dietitian-supported gluten-free treatment
concepts.learningObjective: Recommend a gluten-free diet with dietitian support after celiac disease is confirmed in the completed diagnostic pathway.

concepts.displayName: Diagnostic colonoscopy after a positive FIT
concepts.learningObjective: Select diagnostic colonoscopy after a positive screening FIT while recognizing that the stool result alone does not diagnose colorectal cancer.

concepts.displayName: Histologic confirmation of a colorectal lesion
concepts.learningObjective: Identify histologic examination of sampled lesion tissue as the confirming evidence after colonoscopy identifies a suspicious colorectal lesion.

concepts.displayName: Iron studies in established anemia
concepts.learningObjective: Choose ferritin and complementary iron studies to determine whether iron deficiency explains established anemia without relying on a numeric threshold.

concepts.displayName: Gastrointestinal evaluation of unexplained IDA
concepts.learningObjective: Recommend suitability assessment for upper endoscopy and colonoscopy in adult men or postmenopausal patients with otherwise unexplained confirmed iron-deficiency anemia.

concepts.displayName: MRI characterization of a concerning extremity mass
concepts.learningObjective: Select dedicated extremity MRI before biopsy for a deep, enlarging, or ultrasound-indeterminate soft-tissue mass while recognizing that imaging does not prove sarcoma.

concepts.displayName: Specialist-planned biopsy of a suspicious soft-tissue mass
concepts.learningObjective: Refer a suspicious extremity mass to an experienced sarcoma team for planned image-guided core biopsy that preserves the future surgical approach.

concepts.displayName: FNA selection for a suspicious thyroid nodule
concepts.learningObjective: Select ultrasound-guided FNA after normal TSH and ultrasound findings meeting biopsy criteria in the scoped stable outpatient pathway.

concepts.displayName: Follicular invasion requires histology
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize that capsular or vascular invasion distinguishing follicular adenoma from carcinoma requires histologic evaluation rather than follicular cytology alone.

concepts.displayName: Biochemical confirmation of primary hyperparathyroidism
concepts.learningObjective: Use repeat serum calcium with intact PTH to establish the biochemical pattern before localization planning in the scoped stable outpatient pathway.

concepts.displayName: Surgical assessment for complicated primary hyperparathyroidism
concepts.learningObjective: Recommend parathyroid surgical assessment for biochemically confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism with authored renal or skeletal complications.

concepts.displayName: Dynamic ultrasound after an equivocal inguinal-hernia examination
concepts.learningObjective: Select targeted dynamic groin ultrasound for the scoped stable patient with intermittent symptoms and an equivocal examination.

concepts.displayName: Elective planning for symptomatic inguinal hernia
concepts.learningObjective: Recommend elective repair discussion and planning after a reducible inguinal hernia is confirmed in a patient with meaningful activity-limiting symptoms.

concepts.displayName: Clinical recognition of acute anal fissure
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize an uncomplicated acute anal fissure from recent defecation-related pain, scant bleeding, and a superficial midline tear.

concepts.displayName: Initial conservative care for acute anal fissure
concepts.learningObjective: Select stool-regulating fiber, fluids, soft formed stools, and sitz baths as initial care for a typical uncomplicated acute fissure.

concepts.displayName: Anoscopy for suspected internal hemorrhoids
concepts.learningObjective: Select anoscopy to define local canal anatomy after an appropriate broader evaluation in a stable patient with suspected internal hemorrhoids.

concepts.displayName: Office banding for persistent internal hemorrhoids
concepts.learningObjective: Select office rubber-band ligation for uncomplicated bleeding or prolapsing internal hemorrhoids that persist after conservative care.

concepts.displayName: Upper endoscopy for persistent esophageal dysphagia
concepts.learningObjective: Select upper-GI endoscopy with appropriate esophageal biopsies for stable persistent esophageal dysphagia with a structural or mucosal concern.

concepts.displayName: Barrett esophagus on esophageal biopsy
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize Barrett esophagus from a sampled columnar esophageal segment with specialized intestinal metaplasia.

concepts.displayName: High-resolution manometry for suspected achalasia
concepts.learningObjective: Select high-resolution esophageal manometry after adequate structural evaluation for persistent solids-and-liquids dysphagia with regurgitation.

concepts.displayName: Manometric recognition of achalasia
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize achalasia from absent peristalsis and impaired esophagogastric-junction relaxation without relying on an unsupported numeric threshold.

concepts.displayName: Complete diagnostic biopsy of a suspicious pigmented lesion
concepts.learningObjective: Select complete diagnostic excision with narrow margins and adequate depth for a small accessible pigmented lesion concerning for melanoma.

concepts.displayName: Sentinel-node staging discussion for melanoma
concepts.learningObjective: Discuss sentinel lymph-node biopsy for pathological regional staging of intermediate-thickness clinically node-negative melanoma alongside definitive excision planning.

concepts.displayName: Ultrasound characterization of postoperative fullness
concepts.learningObjective: Select targeted ultrasound to characterize an uncertain superficial collection after benign breast excision.

concepts.displayName: Observation of an uncomplicated postoperative seroma
concepts.learningObjective: Observe a small simple asymptomatic postoperative seroma without infection, wound tension, implant, or functional limitation.

concepts.displayName: Clinical recognition of chronic pilonidal sinus
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize chronic pilonidal sinus disease from recurrent natal-cleft drainage and characteristic midline pits without a current abscess.

concepts.displayName: Off-midline closure planning for pilonidal disease
concepts.learningObjective: Plan an off-midline closure when excision with primary closure has already been selected for chronic pilonidal disease.

concepts.displayName: Targeted ultrasound for suspected lactational breast abscess
concepts.learningObjective: Select targeted breast ultrasound for a persistent focal inflammatory breast mass during lactation.

concepts.displayName: Selected drainage of a lactational breast abscess
concepts.learningObjective: Choose image-guided drainage with culture and individualized antibiotic care for a suitable uncomplicated lactational abscess while preserving feeding when contact precautions are met.

concepts.displayName: Laryngeal examination after thyroid surgery
concepts.learningObjective: Select laryngeal visualization for persistent voice change after thyroid surgery.

concepts.displayName: External superior laryngeal nerve localization
concepts.learningObjective: Localize loss of high pitch and projection with preserved ordinary vocal-fold mobility to external superior laryngeal nerve and cricothyroid dysfunction.

concepts.displayName: Contrast swallow for suspected Zenker diverticulum
concepts.learningObjective: Select contrast swallow with fluoroscopy for a classic proximal pouch presentation.

concepts.displayName: Zenker false-pouch anatomy
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize a posterior mucosa-and-submucosa pouch above the cricopharyngeus as Zenker anatomy.

concepts.displayName: Resting ABI for suspected peripheral arterial disease
concepts.learningObjective: Select resting ankle-brachial index testing for classic stable claudication symptoms and examination findings.

concepts.displayName: Structured exercise for stable claudication
concepts.learningObjective: Select supervised or structured exercise before invasive therapy for stable functionally limiting claudication after risk reduction is addressed.

concepts.displayName: Three-site skeletal assessment in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism
concepts.learningObjective: Select lumbar-spine, hip, and distal forearm DXA for skeletal assessment after primary hyperparathyroidism is confirmed.

concepts.displayName: Age-based surgical assessment in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize age under 50 years as an independent reason to discuss parathyroid surgery after confirmed asymptomatic disease.

concepts.displayName: ACTH classification after confirmed endogenous Cushing syndrome
concepts.learningObjective: Select plasma ACTH to classify the cause after endogenous hypercortisolism is already confirmed.

concepts.displayName: Adrenal imaging after suppressed ACTH
concepts.learningObjective: Select adrenal imaging for the suppressed-ACTH branch of confirmed endogenous Cushing syndrome.

concepts.displayName: MRCP duct assessment for an indeterminate pancreatic cyst
concepts.learningObjective: Use MRI/MRCP to assess communication between an indeterminate pancreatic cyst and the main duct.

concepts.displayName: MCN-compatible pancreatic-cyst pattern recognition
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize a body or tail cyst without main-duct communication as MCN-compatible without claiming definitive histology or automatic resection.

concepts.displayName: Preoperative cross-sectional staging for colon cancer
concepts.learningObjective: Select contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis before treatment planning for confirmed colon cancer.

concepts.displayName: Oncologic regional resection for colon cancer
concepts.learningObjective: Select resection of the tumor-bearing colon with its regional lymphatic drainage for localized resectable colon cancer.

concepts.displayName: Multimodal response assessment after rectal cancer treatment
concepts.learningObjective: Select combined digital rectal examination, endoscopy, and rectal-protocol MRI after neoadjuvant treatment.

concepts.displayName: Selected watch-and-wait after clinical complete response
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize intensive-surveillance watch-and-wait as an acceptable nonsurgical option for a fully informed adherent patient with a clinical complete response in an experienced program.

concepts.displayName: Confirmatory vascular imaging after carotid duplex
concepts.learningObjective: Select confirmatory CT angiography after duplex suggests severe symptomatic carotid stenosis.

concepts.displayName: Endarterectomy assessment for severe symptomatic carotid stenosis
concepts.learningObjective: Select prompt carotid endarterectomy assessment with best medical therapy for a suitable patient with severe ipsilateral symptomatic stenosis.

concepts.displayName: Germline polyposis evaluation after diffuse adenomas
concepts.learningObjective: Select hereditary counseling and APC/MUTYH germline testing after colonoscopy establishes diffuse adenomatous polyposis.

concepts.displayName: IPAA referral for uncontrolled rectal FAP burden
concepts.learningObjective: Select restorative proctocolectomy/IPAA referral when rectal adenomas cannot be controlled endoscopically and restoration is appropriate.

concepts.displayName: MRI mapping for recurrent complex fistula
concepts.learningObjective: Select pelvic MRI to map recurrent complex fistula anatomy.

concepts.displayName: Sphincter-preserving staged planning for high fistula
concepts.learningObjective: Choose loose-seton referral and staged sphincter-preserving planning for high transsphincteric anatomy.

concepts.displayName: Colonoscopy after recovered complicated diverticulitis
concepts.learningObjective: Select colonoscopy after first recovered complicated diverticulitis without recent adequate examination.

concepts.displayName: Individualized elective sigmoid discussion
concepts.learningObjective: Discuss elective sigmoid resection using recovery burden and patient context rather than episode count.

concepts.displayName: Biopsy with CT and MRI staging of an anal-canal lesion
concepts.learningObjective: Arrange tissue biopsy with CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and pelvic MRI for a suspicious anal-canal lesion.

concepts.displayName: Chemoradiation referral for localized anal-canal SCC
concepts.learningObjective: Refer nonmetastatic anal-canal SCC after CT and pelvic MRI for definitive chemoradiation planning.

concepts.displayName: Venous duplex for suspected postoperative DVT
concepts.learningObjective: Select prompt venous duplex/compression ultrasound for new unilateral postoperative leg symptoms.

concepts.displayName: Finite anticoagulation after surgery-provoked DVT
concepts.learningObjective: Select finite anticoagulation planning for a first uncomplicated major-surgery-provoked proximal DVT when safe.

concepts.displayName: HIV and hepatitis-C evaluation in presumed ITP
concepts.learningObjective: Select HIV and hepatitis-C testing before concluding primary ITP in compatible isolated thrombocytopenia.

concepts.displayName: Deferring elective splenectomy in persistent ITP
concepts.learningObjective: Defer elective splenectomy when feasible in stable persistent ITP of only several months.

concepts.displayName: EUS core and molecular evaluation of selected gastric GIST
concepts.learningObjective: Select EUS-guided core tissue and molecular testing when a challenging gastric mass may receive preoperative targeted therapy.

concepts.displayName: Mutation-guided neoadjuvant planning for challenging GIST
concepts.learningObjective: Select neoadjuvant imatinib only for an imatinib-sensitive GIST when shrinkage is expected to reduce operative morbidity.

concepts.displayName: Multiphasic MRI characterization of hepatic adenoma
concepts.learningObjective: Select multiphasic liver MRI to characterize a suspected hepatic adenoma while respecting imaging limitations.

concepts.displayName: Resection planning for hepatic adenoma in men
concepts.learningObjective: Refer a stable man with a characterized hepatic adenoma for elective resection planning regardless of lesion size.

concepts.displayName: CTA evaluation of chronic mesenteric ischemia
concepts.learningObjective: Select mesenteric CTA for compatible chronic postprandial symptoms after reasonable exclusion of alternatives.

concepts.displayName: Revascularization referral for symptomatic multivessel CMI
concepts.learningObjective: Refer symptomatic multivessel occlusive chronic mesenteric ischemia for expert revascularization planning.

concepts.displayName: Prepared ARR screening for primary aldosteronism
concepts.learningObjective: Select aldosterone and renin testing with ARR after potassium and medication preparation in resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalemia.

concepts.displayName: CT and AVS before lateralized adrenal surgery
concepts.learningObjective: Select adrenal CT plus AVS before deciding unilateral surgery in an appropriate adult with confirmed primary aldosteronism.

concepts.displayName: MRCP for an intermediate-risk duct stone
concepts.learningObjective: Select MRCP for stable intermediate-likelihood choledocholithiasis when the local route favors noninvasive imaging.

concepts.displayName: Therapeutic ERCP referral for a confirmed duct stone
concepts.learningObjective: Refer a confirmed duct stone for therapeutic ERCP when the selected local pathway clears the duct before cholecystectomy.

concepts.displayName: Hepatobiliary-contrast MRCP for bile-leak anatomy
concepts.learningObjective: Select hepatobiliary-contrast MRCP after CT to localize a stable postoperative bile leak and assess duct continuity.

concepts.displayName: ERCP stent referral for a persistent minor bile leak
concepts.learningObjective: Refer a persistent minor leak with preserved duct continuity for ERCP and plastic-stent treatment.

concepts.displayName: Contrast CT characterization of a pancreatic fluid collection
concepts.learningObjective: Order contrast-enhanced CT before classifying or planning drainage of a symptomatic post-pancreatitis collection.

concepts.displayName: Endoscopic drainage referral for a symptomatic pseudocyst
concepts.learningObjective: Recognize mature pseudocyst morphology on returned CT and refer a symptomatic suitably apposed collection for EUS-guided drainage.

concepts.displayName: Off-PPI reflux monitoring for unproven GERD
